バンドギャップ.desc: The energy difference between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band. About 1.12 eV for silicon at room temperature. A larger band gap means better tolerance to high temperatures and voltages.

ドナー.desc: An impurity that supplies electrons to a semiconductor. For silicon, group V elements such as phosphorus (P) and arsenic (As) act as donors and make n-type semiconductors.

アクセプタ.desc: An impurity that accepts electrons from a semiconductor and creates holes. For silicon, group III elements such as boron (B) act as acceptors and make p-type semiconductors.

移動度.desc: How easily carriers move when an electric field is applied. In silicon, electron mobility is higher than hole mobility.

空乏層.desc: A region near a PN junction boundary that contains almost no carriers. It widens under reverse bias.

ツェナーダイオード.desc: A diode that provides a constant voltage by using the nearly fixed reverse breakdown voltage.

電流増幅率(hFE).desc: The ratio of collector current to base current (IC/IB) in a bipolar transistor.

しきい値電圧.desc: The gate voltage at which a channel (inversion layer) forms in a MOSFET and current starts to flow. Written as Vth.

CMOS.desc: A circuit style that combines nMOS and pMOS transistors in a complementary way. Almost no current flows through it in steady state, so power consumption is low.

フリップフロップ.desc: The basic element of sequential circuits that stores one bit. A D flip-flop captures its input at a clock edge.

オペアンプ.desc: An amplifier with differential inputs and very high gain. Used with negative feedback in amplifiers, filters and more.

リフレッシュ.desc: The periodic reading and rewriting of DRAM data before the charge in its capacitors is lost through leakage.

センスアンプ.desc: A circuit that amplifies the tiny voltage difference read from a memory cell and decides whether it is 0 or 1.

NAND型フラッシュメモリ.desc: Non-volatile memory in which memory cells are connected in series. It is dense and easy to scale to large capacities, and is used in SSDs and memory cards.

MRAM.desc: Non-volatile memory that stores data as the difference in resistance caused by the magnetization direction of a magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ).

キャッシュメモリ.desc: Fast, small memory placed close to the CPU. It holds frequently used data to bridge the speed gap with main memory. Mostly built from SRAM.

IGBT.desc: Insulated-gate bipolar transistor. Driven by a MOS gate, it achieves a low on-state voltage even at high voltage ratings through conductivity modulation.

SiC(炭化ケイ素).desc: A wide-band-gap semiconductor with a band gap of about 3.3 eV. Its high breakdown field makes it suitable for high-voltage, low-loss power devices.

GaN(窒化ガリウム).desc: A III-V compound semiconductor with a band gap of about 3.4 eV. Used in blue LEDs and in high-frequency and power devices.

直接遷移型.desc: A band structure in which the bottom of the conduction band and the top of the valence band are at the same wave number. Electron-hole recombination emits light efficiently. Example: GaAs.

フォトダイオード.desc: A diode that generates charge (current) when it receives light. Used as the light-receiving element in image sensor pixels.

CZ法(チョクラルスキー法).desc: A method of making single-crystal silicon by dipping a seed crystal into molten silicon in a crucible and slowly pulling it up while rotating.

熱酸化.desc: A method of forming an SiO2 film on silicon by heating it in oxygen or water vapor. There are dry and wet oxidation.

about.p: Dry oxidation reacts silicon with oxygen gas, Si + O2 → SiO2, while wet oxidation uses steam, Si + 2H2O → SiO2 + 2H2. Water dissolves in SiO2 several hundred times more than O2, so wet oxidation grows oxide several to ten times faster: about 70 nm dry versus 400 nm wet after one hour at 1000 °C. Wet oxide retains some hydrogen and is slightly less dense, so it suits thick isolation and masking layers. Dry oxide grows slowly with precise thickness control and a low density of interface states, which made it the classic gate oxide.

The Deal-Grove model treats oxidation as oxidant moving from the gas to the oxide surface, diffusing through the oxide and reacting with silicon at the Si/SiO2 interface. Balancing these fluxes gives x² + Ax = B(t + τ). While the oxide is thin, the interface reaction limits growth and thickness rises linearly with time at rate B/A. Once the oxide is thicker than roughly A/2, diffusion limits growth and thickness follows the square root of time, so doubling it takes about four times as long. Higher temperature or oxidant pressure speeds both regimes.

Oxide grows by consuming the substrate: forming a film of thickness x uses about 0.44x of silicon, so 44 percent of the oxide lies below the original surface and 56 percent above. The roughly 2.2 times volume expansion leaves the oxide in compressive stress. Above about 950 °C the amorphous SiO2 can flow viscously and relax this stress; at lower temperatures stress retards oxidation at convex corners and leaves them sharp. Because new oxide always forms at a freshly created interface, thermal oxide has a cleaner interface than deposited oxide.

Oxidation runs at about 800 to 1,200 °C, usually in vertical furnaces holding around 100 wafers. The (111) surface oxidizes faster than (100), by about 1.5 times for thin oxides. Adding a few percent HCl getters sodium and metal contamination and suppresses oxidation-induced stacking faults, which grow from silicon interstitials injected during oxidation. Heavily doped polysilicon oxidizes faster and gives poorer oxide. Thermal SiO2 has a relative permittivity of about 3.9, the reference for equivalent oxide thickness (EOT). For thin, orientation-independent films, ISSG radical oxidation is used.

faq.q: How much silicon is consumed during thermal oxidation?
faq.a: About 0.44 times the final oxide thickness. Growing 100 nm of SiO2 consumes roughly 44 nm of silicon, and the surface rises by about 56 nm.

faq.q: Why is wet oxidation faster than dry oxidation?
faq.a: Water molecules dissolve in SiO2 at a concentration several hundred times higher than oxygen, so far more oxidant reaches the Si/SiO2 interface. This makes wet oxidation several to ten times faster at the same temperature.

faq.q: What is the difference between thermal oxide and CVD oxide?
faq.a: Thermal oxide is grown by converting the silicon substrate itself, giving a dense film and a high-quality interface. CVD oxide is deposited from precursor gases on top of any surface without consuming silicon, which allows lower temperatures and thick films on non-silicon layers but gives a poorer interface.

イオン注入.desc: A technique that ionizes impurities, accelerates them and implants them into the wafer. The dose and depth can be controlled precisely.

アニール.desc: Heat treatment. Used to repair crystal damage after ion implantation and to activate dopants, among other purposes.

CVD.desc: Chemical vapor deposition. A method of depositing thin films on a wafer through chemical reactions of source gases.

ALD.desc: Atomic layer deposition. A deposition method that repeats self-limiting surface reactions of precursor gases to control film thickness one atomic layer at a time.

about.p: Atomic layer deposition (ALD) splits a CVD reaction into two half-reactions separated in time. A precursor such as trimethylaluminum (TMA) is dosed and chemisorbs on surface sites until they are filled; excess gas is purged; a co-reactant such as water then reacts with the adsorbed layer; and a second purge follows. Because each half-reaction stops once the surface is saturated, growth per cycle is fixed, typically about 0.1 nm or less, since bulky precursor molecules block neighboring sites. Film thickness is set simply by counting cycles.

Self-limiting growth only holds within a temperature range called the ALD window. Too cold, precursors condense or react incompletely; too hot, they decompose and grow CVD-like, or adsorbed species desorb. Within the window growth per cycle is nearly constant, about 150–300 °C for Al2O3 from TMA and water. Precursor choice shifts it: HfO2 can be grown from HfCl4, which is stable around 300 °C but may leave chlorine, or from organometallics such as TEMAHf, which react at lower temperature but may leave carbon. Such residues affect threshold voltage and reliability.

about.h: Conformality compared with CVD and PVD
about.p: Because growth is controlled by surface saturation rather than gas transport, ALD reaches nearly 100% step coverage, coating the sidewalls and bottoms of features with aspect ratios of several tens. Sputtering may leave under 10% of the top thickness at the bottom of deep holes, and CVD sits in between. This is why ALD deposits high-k HfO2 gate dielectrics, TiN for metal gates and barriers, ZrO2/Al2O3/ZrO2 stacks in DRAM capacitors, the gate stack wrapped around GAA nanosheets, and the spacers used in self-aligned double and quadruple patterning.

The cost is speed: a cycle takes seconds to tens of seconds, so a few nanometers needs dozens of cycles. Batch reactors and spatial ALD, which moves wafers through separate gas zones, raise throughput. Plasma-enhanced ALD (PEALD) uses radicals in the reactant step to deposit at room temperature to a few hundred °C and to enable films such as SiN, at some cost in conformality inside deep features because radicals recombine. Atomic layer etching (ALE) applies the same self-limiting idea to removing material.

faq.q: What is the difference between ALD and CVD?
faq.a: In CVD all reactants are present together and the film grows continuously at a rate set by temperature and gas supply. In ALD the reactants are supplied separately with purges between them, so each step is self-limiting and thickness is set by the number of cycles.

faq.q: How thick is the film deposited in one ALD cycle?
faq.a: Typically about 0.1 nm, which is one atomic layer or less. A 2 nm film therefore needs on the order of 20 cycles.

faq.q: Why is ALD slow?
faq.a: Each cycle needs two precursor doses and two purges that must fully saturate and then fully clear the surface, taking seconds or longer, yet adds only a fraction of a nanometer.

スパッタリング.desc: A type of PVD in which ions in a plasma bombard a target and the ejected atoms are deposited on the wafer.

フォトレジスト.desc: A light-sensitive material whose solubility in developer changes when exposed. In positive resist the exposed areas dissolve; in negative resist they remain.

EUV露光.desc: Lithography using extreme ultraviolet light with a wavelength of 13.5 nm. It uses reflective optics and a vacuum environment.

開口数(NA).desc: A value that expresses the range of angles of light a lens can collect. A larger NA gives higher resolution.

異方性エッチング.desc: Etching that proceeds only in a particular direction (mainly vertically). Needed to pattern fine features.

about.p: Anisotropy compares lateral and vertical etch rates and is often expressed as A = 1 − (lateral rate / vertical rate): A = 1 is perfectly vertical, A = 0 is isotropic. In practice engineers quote the taper angle, the sidewall angle from the surface, with values near 90° meaning highly anisotropic. Anisotropic etching transfers the mask dimension into the film with almost no undercut, enabling features tens of nanometers wide and several micrometers deep. An isotropic etch would widen each opening by about the etch depth on each side.

An RF-driven wafer electrode charges to a negative DC self-bias, tens to hundreds of volts, because mobile electrons reach it more easily than ions. Positive ions accelerate across the sheath nearly perpendicular to the wafer, especially at low pressure where collisions are rare. Ion bombardment strongly enhances chemical etching where it lands, so feature bottoms etch much faster than sidewalls. Polymer or oxide-like passivation on the sidewalls blocks lateral attack while ions clear it from the bottom. Deep silicon etching often alternates an SF6 etch step with a C4F8 passivation step, the Bosch process, leaving small scallops on the walls.

Too much passivation narrows the bottom and tapers the profile; too little lets radicals and scattered ions bow the sidewalls outward. Ions reflecting off sloped walls or deflected by charging can cause microtrenching at the bottom corners. Etch rate also tends to fall as aspect ratio increases. Taper is chosen per application: features to be filled later often benefit from about 85° for void-free filling, while gates and fins are made nearly vertical to keep top and bottom dimensions equal.

The term also describes orientation-dependent wet etching of single-crystal silicon. Alkaline solutions such as KOH or TMAH etch the (111) planes far more slowly than (100) planes, so on a (100) wafer they form V-grooves and pits with sidewalls at about 54.7° to the surface. This crystallographic anisotropy is widely used in MEMS for cavities and membranes, but it is not the ion-driven vertical anisotropy used for patterning fine circuit features.

faq.q: What is the difference between anisotropic and isotropic etching?
faq.a: Anisotropic etching proceeds mainly in one direction, usually straight down, so the pattern keeps the mask's width. Isotropic etching proceeds equally in all directions and undercuts the mask, as most wet etches do.

faq.q: Can wet etching be anisotropic?
faq.a: Yes, in a crystallographic sense: KOH or TMAH etch silicon much more slowly along (111) planes, producing sloped facets at about 54.7° on (100) wafers. For vertical sidewalls in fine patterns, plasma dry etching is required.

faq.q: What is the Bosch process?
faq.a: It is a deep reactive ion etching method for silicon that alternates short SF6 etch steps with C4F8 passivation steps. It can etch very deep vertical trenches and through-silicon vias, leaving characteristic scalloped sidewalls.

選択比.desc: In etching, the ratio of the etch rate of the target film to that of the mask or underlying film. Higher selectivity means less damage to the underlayer.

CMP.desc: Chemical mechanical polishing. Planarizes the wafer surface by combining the chemical action of a slurry with mechanical polishing by a pad.

RCA洗浄.desc: A cleaning method that removes particles and organics with SC-1 (ammonia and hydrogen peroxide) and metal contamination with SC-2 (hydrochloric acid and hydrogen peroxide).

ダマシン法.desc: A method of forming interconnects by etching trenches in an insulating film, filling them with metal, and removing the excess metal by CMP. Used for copper wiring.

Low-k材料.desc: An interlayer dielectric with a low dielectric constant. It lowers the capacitance between wires, reducing signal delay and power consumption.

ワイヤボンディング.desc: A method of connecting the chip's bond pads to a lead frame or substrate with thin wires of gold, copper or similar metals.

about.p: In thermosonic ball bonding, the wire passes through a fine ceramic tube called a capillary. An electric spark melts the wire tip into a ball about twice the wire diameter, which is pressed onto the chip's bond pad with heat (roughly 150–200 °C), force and ultrasonic vibration to form the first bond. The capillary then draws a loop to the lead frame or substrate, where it presses the wire flat into a stitch, the second bond, and tears it off ready for the next ball. Because a ball has no orientation, wires can run in any direction.

Bonding wires are typically 15–50 µm in diameter, thinner than a human hair, to match pads only tens of micrometers across. Gold was the traditional choice, but copper has largely displaced it on cost and also conducts electricity and heat better. Copper oxidizes and is harder, so balls are formed under nitrogen–hydrogen gas, palladium-coated wire is common, and parameters are tuned to avoid damaging pads. Power devices use thick aluminum wire of about 100–500 µm, flat ribbons or copper clips, usually joined by wedge bonding, which presses the wire flat from the side.

Bond pads are usually aluminum about 1 µm thick, even on chips with copper interconnects, because aluminum's thin native oxide protects it and it bonds reliably. Excess force or ultrasound, or a hard copper wire, can crack the dielectric or silicon beneath the pad, a defect called cratering, which is a particular concern over mechanically weak low-k films. Probe marks left by wafer test must not spoil the bonding area. Over long high-temperature service, gold–aluminum intermetallics grow at the ball bond and can form voids if the joint is poorly controlled.

Wire bonding remains the most widely used chip interconnect by unit volume because the equipment is inexpensive and routing is flexible. Its limits are that connections sit only around the die edge and each wire adds resistance and inductance, a rule of thumb being about 1 nH per millimeter. Flip-chip places bumps across the whole die face for more I/O and shorter paths. Stacked packages for NAND flash and DRAM still wire-bond staircase-offset dies, sometimes more than 16, while very high bandwidth stacks use TSVs or hybrid bonding.

faq.q: Why is copper wire replacing gold wire in wire bonding?
faq.a: Copper is far cheaper than gold and has better electrical and thermal conductivity. Its drawbacks, easier oxidation and greater hardness, are handled with forming gas during ball formation, palladium-coated wire and carefully tuned bonding conditions.

faq.q: What is the difference between ball bonding and wedge bonding?
faq.a: Ball bonding melts the wire tip into a ball and bonds it with heat, force and ultrasound, so the wire can leave in any direction; it is used with gold and copper wire. Wedge bonding presses the side of the wire flat with a wedge tool, fixes the wire direction, and is common with aluminum wire and ribbons.

faq.q: Which end of the wire is bonded to the chip?
faq.a: Normally the ball (first bond) goes on the chip pad because it is compact, and the stitch (second bond) goes on the lead or substrate. The order is sometimes reversed to achieve very low loops in stacked-die packages.

フリップチップ.desc: A mounting method in which the chip is placed face down and connected directly to the substrate with bumps. Short connections make it suitable for high pin counts.

BGA.desc: Ball grid array. A high-pin-count package with solder balls arranged in a grid on its underside.

バーンイン.desc: A test that operates products under stress such as high temperature and high voltage to remove units prone to early failure before shipment.

about.p: Some chips pass every electrical test at time zero yet contain latent defects: a thin spot in a gate oxide, a marginal via, a particle bridging two lines, or contamination. Under normal use these weak parts fail early, producing the high, falling failure rate of the infant-mortality period at the start of the bathtub curve. Burn-in deliberately accelerates those failures in the factory so the weak units can be identified and removed, leaving a shipped population whose failure rate is already in the low, nearly constant random-failure period.

Parts are loaded onto burn-in boards inside ovens and operated for hours to tens of hours at around 125 °C with supply voltage set above nominal. Temperature accelerates thermally activated failure mechanisms roughly following the Arrhenius relation, and elevated voltage stresses dielectrics, so a short burn-in emulates a much longer period of field use. In static burn-in the device is only biased, while dynamic burn-in toggles internal nodes with test patterns so that more of the circuit is stressed. Conditions are chosen so that good parts lose only a small fraction of their wear-out lifetime.

about.h: Where it fits in the test flow
about.p: A typical flow is wafer test, assembly, final test and shipment. Burn-in is usually inserted around final test, followed by a post-burn-in electrical test that catches the units that failed under stress. Wafer-level burn-in, done before dicing, is used when bare known-good dies are needed for multi-chip packages. Because burn-in costs oven time, boards and floor space, it is applied mainly to high-reliability products such as automotive and server parts, while other products may rely on shorter elevated-voltage stress tests and statistical reliability data.

about.h: Not to be confused with display burn-in
about.p: In displays, burn-in means something different: permanent image retention when a static image is shown for a long time. OLED pixels emit their own light and age with accumulated current, so pixels that stay bright, such as a status bar, dim relative to their neighbors and leave a ghost image. Inorganic micro-LED displays are promoted partly because they do not suffer this effect. Semiconductor burn-in is a deliberate screening test, while display burn-in is an unwanted aging artifact.

faq.q: Why is burn-in done at high temperature and voltage?
faq.a: Most early-failure mechanisms, such as defective oxides and weak interconnects, are accelerated by heat and electric field. Stressing at around 125 °C and above-nominal voltage makes latent defects fail within hours instead of months in the field.

faq.q: Does burn-in shorten the life of good chips?
faq.a: It consumes a small part of their life, but the stress level and duration are chosen so that wear-out still begins well after the intended service life. The benefit of removing infant-mortality failures outweighs this small loss.

faq.q: What is the bathtub curve?
faq.a: It is a plot of failure rate versus time with three periods: a high, decreasing early-failure rate, a low and nearly constant random-failure rate, and a rising wear-out rate. Burn-in is used to get past the first period before shipment.

DFT(テスト容易化設計).desc: A design approach that builds test features such as scan chains and BIST into the circuit in advance.

歩留まり.desc: The proportion of good products to the total produced. A key factor in semiconductor manufacturing cost.

バスタブ曲線.desc: A curve showing how the failure rate changes over time. It consists of the early-failure, random-failure and wear-out periods and is shaped like a bathtub.

エレクトロマイグレーション.desc: The movement of metal atoms in interconnects caused by electric current. It creates voids and hillocks that lead to open or short circuits.

about.h: The electron wind and where damage forms
about.p: Conduction electrons scatter off metal ions and transfer momentum, pushing atoms in the direction of electron flow, which is opposite to conventional current. Atoms travel mostly along fast diffusion paths: grain boundaries in aluminum and the top interface between copper and its dielectric cap in copper. Damage appears where this atomic flux is interrupted, such as at a via bottom blocked by the barrier metal. Atoms leave the upstream side without replacement and a void forms, raising resistance or opening the line, while atoms pile up downstream as hillocks that can crack the dielectric and short to a neighboring line.

Black's equation, MTTF = A·J⁻ⁿ·exp(Ea/kT), says median lifetime falls with current density J, with n typically about 2, and falls exponentially with temperature. Reliability tests therefore stress lines at high current density and temperatures around 300 °C, then extrapolate to use conditions. Failure times follow a lognormal distribution, and because a chip holds hundreds of millions of wires, the design target is the time when a tiny fraction, such as 0.1 ppm, has failed. This sets per-wire current-density limits on the order of MA/cm².

about.h: Materials and structures that resist it
about.p: Adding about 0.5% copper to aluminum puts copper at grain boundaries and slows aluminum transport by an order of magnitude or more. Copper wiring, with resistivity about 1.7 µΩ·cm versus about 2.7 µΩ·cm for aluminum and a higher melting point, improved electromigration resistance further. Because copper moves mainly along its top surface, the dielectric cap (SiCN or SiN) and selective metal caps such as cobalt govern lifetime. A bamboo grain structure helps aluminum greatly but is not enough for copper. In short lines the Blech effect applies: back-stress stops net transport when current density times length is below a critical value.

Designers add redundant vias, widen metal around vias, and run electromigration analysis together with IR-drop analysis at sign-off. Self-heating in FinFET and SOI devices raises nearby wire temperature and speeds failure. In flip-chip solder bumps, current crowding at the trace-to-bump corner nucleates voids, one reason copper pillars are favored. Electromigration should not be confused with stress migration, where voids form from thermal stress without current, or with ion migration, where moisture lets metal ions grow dendrites between biased electrodes on boards.

faq.q: What is the difference between electromigration and stress migration?
faq.a: Electromigration is driven by current, as electrons push metal atoms along the wire. Stress migration forms voids without any current, as atoms move to relieve tensile stress left by thermal mismatch, and it is worst around 150–250 °C.

faq.q: Why does copper resist electromigration better than aluminum?
faq.a: Copper has a higher melting point, so its atoms are less mobile at operating temperatures, giving an order of magnitude or more improvement in lifetime. Its lower resistivity also means less heating for the same current.

faq.q: What is the Blech effect?
faq.a: In short wires, atoms pushed toward one end build up a stress gradient that drives a backflow. When the product of current density and line length is below a critical value, this backflow cancels the electron wind and the line does not degrade.

論理合成.desc: The design step that converts a circuit described in RTL into a netlist made of gates from a cell library.

STA(静的タイミング解析).desc: A method that calculates the delay of every path in a circuit without test patterns and checks that timing constraints are met.

FOUP.desc: A sealed container for transporting and storing 300 mm wafers.

SDS(安全データシート).desc: A document describing the hazards of a chemical, how to handle it, first-aid measures and more.

ファウンドリ.desc: A company or business model that specializes in manufacturing semiconductors designed by other companies.

ファブレス.desc: A company model that owns no fabrication plant and focuses on designing and selling semiconductors.

チップレット.desc: A small chip made for a specific function. Several chiplets are connected inside one package to build a larger system.

TSV(シリコン貫通電極).desc: An electrode that passes through the silicon substrate. It connects stacked chips vertically over a short distance.

HBM.desc: High Bandwidth Memory. Multiple DRAM dies stacked with TSVs, achieving very high bandwidth through an extremely wide bus.

サンプリング定理.desc: The theorem stating that a signal can be reconstructed if it is sampled at a frequency higher than twice its highest frequency component. Also called the Nyquist-Shannon theorem.

FinFET.desc: A 3D transistor whose channel stands up like a fin and is surrounded by the gate on three sides. It suppresses short-channel effects well.

High-k/メタルゲート.desc: The combination of a high-dielectric-constant gate insulator and a metal gate electrode. It keeps gate capacitance high while suppressing gate leakage.

MEMS.desc: Micro-electro-mechanical systems. Devices that integrate tiny mechanical structures and electronic circuits using semiconductor microfabrication.

about.p: MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical systems) borrow IC fabrication but add steps that free parts to move. Surface micromachining stacks a sacrificial film such as SiO2 under a structural film such as LPCVD polysilicon, then etches the sacrificial layer away to leave beams suspended a few µm above the substrate. Bulk micromachining carves the wafer itself, using KOH etching, which stops on (111) planes at about 54.7°, or deep RIE (the Bosch process) for vertical trenches with aspect ratios above 20. SOI wafers, anodic bonding and wafer-level vacuum sealing complete many devices.

Most MEMS sensors turn motion into a capacitance change. In an accelerometer a spring-suspended proof mass shifts by nanometers or less, changing comb-electrode capacitance by under a femtofarad. A gyroscope vibrates a mass at several to tens of kHz and senses the Coriolis displacement caused by rotation, usually in vacuum to raise Q. Resonant frequency is f = (1/2π)√(k/m), so stiffer springs raise bandwidth but lower sensitivity. Electrostatic actuators produce force proportional to V²/d², and parallel plates snap together (pull-in) after travelling about one third of the gap.

With structures from micrometers to millimeters, surface forces dominate over mass. Capillary forces during release drying, van der Waals forces and humidity can pin parts to the substrate, called stiction, prevented by vapor-phase HF release, supercritical drying, hydrophobic coatings and dimples. Gas trapped in narrow gaps causes squeeze-film damping, which scales inversely with the cube of the gap and is useful in accelerometers but harmful in resonators. Thermomechanical (Brownian) noise grows as the proof mass shrinks, limiting the resolution of very small sensors.

A smartphone contains several MEMS devices: accelerometers, gyroscopes, pressure sensors precise enough to resolve a change of one building floor, and microphones. Cars use MEMS accelerometers to trigger airbags and gyroscopes for stability control. Other examples include inkjet print heads, scanning mirrors for LiDAR and projection, silicon oscillators replacing quartz, RF switches, uncooled infrared microbolometers, ultrasonic transducers and MEMS probe cards for wafer test. MEMS are a typical More than Moore technology, often built on 200 mm or smaller wafers with mature equipment.

faq.q: What does MEMS stand for?
faq.a: MEMS stands for micro-electro-mechanical systems: tiny mechanical structures such as springs, membranes and mirrors built with semiconductor microfabrication and combined with electronics. Even smaller nanometer-scale mechanical devices are called NEMS.

faq.q: What is stiction in MEMS?
faq.a: Stiction is the permanent sticking of a movable MEMS part to the substrate or another surface, caused by capillary, electrostatic or van der Waals forces. It is fought with liquid-free release methods, anti-stiction coatings and small contact bumps.

faq.q: How does a MEMS accelerometer measure acceleration?
faq.a: A proof mass on springs lags behind when the package accelerates, changing its gap to fixed electrodes. The resulting capacitance change is converted to an acceleration reading, and at rest the sensor reads about 1 g because of gravity.

エピタキシャル成長.desc: A technique for growing a single-crystal thin film on a single-crystal substrate with the same crystal orientation as the substrate.

超純水.desc: Water from which ions, particles and organic matter have been removed to the extreme. Used in large amounts for wafer cleaning, with purity controlled by resistivity and other measures.

SIMS(二次イオン質量分析法).desc: A method that sputters a sample with primary ions and mass-analyzes the secondary ions to measure impurity depth profiles with high sensitivity.

CD-SEM.desc: A scanning electron microscope for measuring pattern line widths (critical dimensions). Used for dimensional control after lithography and etching.

フェルミ準位.desc: The energy at which the probability of an electron occupying a state is exactly one half. It lies closer to the conduction band in n-type material and closer to the valence band in p-type.

about.h: What the Fermi level means physically
about.p: The Fermi-Dirac function f(E) = 1/(1 + exp((E − EF)/kT)) gives the probability that a state at energy E holds an electron, and it equals exactly 1/2 at E = EF. A few kT above EF (kT is about 0.026 eV at room temperature) occupation falls off almost exponentially, which is why electron density is n = Nc·exp(−(Ec − EF)/kT) and hole density is p = Nv·exp(−(EF − Ev)/kT). EF is the electrochemical potential of the electrons, so it can sit in the band gap even though no allowed states exist there.

about.h: How doping and temperature move it
about.p: In intrinsic silicon the Fermi level lies about 0.01 eV below midgap, because the conduction band has a larger effective density of states than the valence band. Donors push EF toward the conduction band following Ec − EF ≈ kT·ln(Nc/ND), about 60 mV per tenfold increase in ND; acceptors push it toward the valence band. Above roughly 10¹⁸–10¹⁹ cm⁻³ it enters a band and the material becomes degenerate. Raising temperature increases the intrinsic carrier density and pulls EF back toward midgap, one reason MOSFET threshold voltage falls by about 1–2 mV/°C.

about.h: Fermi level alignment in junctions and MOS
about.p: In thermal equilibrium the Fermi level is flat across any structure, so when two materials with different Fermi levels are joined, charge flows until they line up. The resulting band bending gives the built-in potential of a PN junction and, in a MOS structure, the flat-band voltage set by the metal-semiconductor work-function difference. The work function is the energy from EF to the vacuum level and changes with doping, whereas the electron affinity, measured from the conduction band edge (about 4.05 eV for silicon), does not. An applied voltage V separates the Fermi levels of the two sides by qV.

Under illumination or current injection, electrons and holes are no longer described by one Fermi level. Separate quasi-Fermi levels, EFn and EFp, are used, with n = ni·exp((EFn − Ei)/kT) and p = ni·exp((Ei − EFp)/kT). Their separation sets np = ni²·exp((EFn − EFp)/kT), and in a forward-biased diode or an illuminated solar cell it corresponds to the terminal voltage. Current density is proportional to the gradient of each quasi-Fermi level, so a flat quasi-Fermi level means no net current for that carrier.

faq.q: Why can the Fermi level lie in the band gap where there are no states?
faq.a: The Fermi level is a statistical parameter, the electrochemical potential of electrons, not an occupied state. It only fixes the occupation probability of the states that do exist in the bands above and below it.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Fermi level and the work function?
faq.a: The Fermi level is an energy position, while the work function is the energy needed to move an electron from the Fermi level to the vacuum level. In a semiconductor, doping moves the Fermi level and therefore changes the work function.

faq.q: What is a degenerate semiconductor?
faq.a: It is a semiconductor doped so heavily, roughly above 10¹⁸–10¹⁹ cm⁻³ in silicon, that the Fermi level moves into the conduction or valence band. It then behaves almost like a metal, and simple relations such as np = ni² no longer hold accurately.

順方向バイアス.desc: Applying a positive voltage to the p side and a negative voltage to the n side. The barrier drops and current flows readily. The opposite is reverse bias, under which almost no current flows.

内蔵電位.desc: The potential difference across the depletion layer of a PN junction even with no external voltage applied. About 0.6 to 0.8 V in silicon, it forms the barrier that stops further carrier diffusion.

なだれ降伏.desc: A phenomenon in which carriers accelerated by a strong reverse field strike atoms and create new carriers, which multiply in a chain reaction so that a large current flows.

能動領域.desc: The state with the base-emitter junction forward-biased and the base-collector junction reverse-biased. A collector current proportional to the base current flows, and it is used for amplification.

アーリー効果.desc: A phenomenon in which raising the collector voltage widens the base-collector depletion layer, narrowing the effective base width and slightly increasing collector current.

エミッタ接地回路.desc: An amplifier circuit in which the emitter is the common terminal for input and output. It provides both current gain and voltage gain and is the most widely used configuration.

HBT(ヘテロ接合バイポーラトランジスタ).desc: A bipolar transistor using materials with different band gaps for the emitter and base. Types include SiGe and GaAs-based devices, used in high-frequency amplifiers.

反転層.desc: A layer formed at the semiconductor surface by the gate voltage, where carriers of the type opposite to the substrate gather. It becomes the MOSFET's channel.

about.p: Consider an n-channel MOS structure on a p-type substrate. A negative gate voltage pulls holes to the surface (accumulation). A small positive voltage pushes holes away and leaves a depletion region of ionized acceptors. At larger positive voltage the bands bend so far that electrons, the minority carriers, gather at the surface. Strong inversion is conventionally defined as the point where the surface potential reaches twice the bulk Fermi potential, so the surface electron density equals the bulk hole density. The gate voltage at that point is the threshold voltage.

about.h: The inversion layer as the MOSFET channel
about.p: In a MOSFET the inversion layer connects the heavily doped source and drain, which supply its carriers almost instantly. Its sheet charge is roughly Cox·(VGS − Vth), so drain current grows with gate overdrive. An nMOS forms an electron inversion layer and conducts when VGS exceeds a positive Vth; a pMOS forms a hole inversion layer in an n-well and has a negative Vth, for example −0.4 V. Electrons have higher mobility than holes, so an nMOS of the same size drives more current.

In a MOS capacitor without source and drain, inversion electrons must be generated thermally, which is slow. In a high-frequency C-V measurement, typically at 1 MHz, the inversion charge cannot follow the signal, so capacitance stays at its minimum: Cox in series with the depletion capacitance at maximum depletion width. In a low-frequency or quasi-static measurement the inversion layer responds and capacitance returns to Cox. The ratio of minimum to maximum capacitance gives the substrate doping.

The inversion layer is only a few nanometers thick and the strong interface field confines carriers in a narrow potential well. Quantum mechanics places the peak of the electron distribution about 1 nm inside the silicon rather than at the interface. This centroid offset adds roughly 0.3–0.4 nm of equivalent SiO2 thickness, lowering gate capacitance and drive current. Together with polysilicon gate depletion, it makes the electrical thickness (CET) larger than the physical equivalent oxide thickness (EOT), which matters more as EOT shrinks.

faq.q: What is the difference between depletion and inversion in a MOS structure?
faq.a: In depletion the gate has pushed majority carriers away, leaving fixed ionized dopants but few mobile carriers. In inversion the bending is strong enough that minority carriers gather at the surface in large numbers, forming a conductive layer of the opposite type.

faq.q: Is the inversion layer the same as the channel?
faq.a: In an enhancement-mode MOSFET, yes: the inversion layer formed under the gate is the conducting channel between source and drain. Below threshold it is too weak to carry significant current.

faq.q: Why does high-frequency C-V stay at minimum in inversion?
faq.a: Without a source and drain, inversion carriers come only from slow thermal generation, which cannot follow a signal around 1 MHz. Only the depletion edge responds, so the measured capacitance stays at its minimum.

短チャネル効果.desc: Phenomena in which, as gate length shrinks, the drain's electric field lowers the threshold voltage and increases off-state leakage current.

サブスレッショルドスイング.desc: The gate voltage needed to change drain current tenfold below threshold. Its theoretical lower limit at room temperature is about 60 mV per decade; the smaller it is, the sharper the on/off switching.

ド・モルガンの定理.desc: The rules for transforming logic expressions: NOT (A AND B) equals (NOT A) OR (NOT B), and NOT (A OR B) equals (NOT A) AND (NOT B).

真理値表.desc: A table listing the output for every combination of inputs. It is used to describe the behavior of logic circuits.

組み合わせ回路.desc: A logic circuit whose output depends only on its current inputs. Examples include adders, multiplexers and decoders.

順序回路.desc: A logic circuit that stores state in flip-flops and the like, so its output depends on both inputs and past state. Examples include counters and registers.

負帰還.desc: Returning part of the output to the input with opposite polarity. Gain drops, but it becomes stable, and distortion and bandwidth improve.

ボルテージフォロワ.desc: A unity-gain op-amp circuit with the output tied directly to the inverting input. With high input impedance and low output impedance, it is used as a buffer.

カットオフ周波数.desc: The frequency at which the output of a filter or amplifier falls 3 dB (to about 0.707 times) below the passband. For an RC circuit it is 1/(2πRC).

差動増幅回路.desc: A circuit that amplifies the difference between two inputs while rejecting components common to both, such as noise. It is used as the input stage of op-amps.

エイリアシング.desc: A phenomenon in which components above half the sampling frequency falsely appear as lower-frequency components. It is prevented with a low-pass filter before A/D conversion.

量子化誤差.desc: The error that arises when rounding a continuous analog value to a digital value with a finite number of bits. At most half of one LSB.

逐次比較型ADC.desc: An ADC that uses an internal DAC and comparator to determine one bit at a time, starting from the most significant. It balances speed, accuracy and power well.

ΔΣ型ADC.desc: An ADC that oversamples at a high rate, pushes quantization noise to high frequencies and then filters it out. Used in high-resolution applications such as audio and measurement.

1T1Cセル.desc: The DRAM memory cell that stores one bit with one transistor and one capacitor. The presence or absence of charge on the capacitor represents 0 or 1.

ビット線.desc: The wire used to read and write data in memory cells. In DRAM, the small change in bit-line potential caused by a cell's charge is amplified by a sense amplifier.

ワード線.desc: The wire connected to the gates of memory-cell transistors that selects the row to read or write.

6T SRAMセル.desc: The SRAM memory cell made of two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) and two access transistors.

不揮発性メモリ.desc: Memory that retains stored data when power is removed, such as flash memory and MRAM. DRAM and SRAM are volatile.

NOR型フラッシュメモリ.desc: Flash memory with cells connected in parallel. Random reads are fast, and it is used to store programs for microcontrollers and the like.

ウェアレベリング.desc: A technique that spreads writes so rewrites do not concentrate on particular flash blocks, extending the memory's life.

PCM(相変化メモリ).desc: Nonvolatile memory that stores information by the difference between the crystalline (low-resistance) and amorphous (high-resistance) states of a chalcogenide material.

ReRAM(抵抗変化メモリ).desc: Nonvolatile memory that applies voltage to form and break conductive paths in an oxide or similar material, storing information as differences in resistance.

FeRAM(強誘電体メモリ).desc: Nonvolatile memory that stores information in the polarization direction of a ferroelectric. Writes are fast and low-power, and it is used in IC cards and the like.

磁気トンネル接合(MTJ).desc: A structure with a thin insulating film between two magnetic layers. Resistance is low when the layers' magnetizations are parallel and high when antiparallel. It is the storage element of MRAM.

パイプライン処理.desc: A method that splits instruction processing into stages such as fetch, decode and execute, and processes several instructions at once, each offset by a stage.

ノイマン型アーキテクチャ.desc: A computer organization that keeps programs and data in the same main memory and fetches and executes instructions in sequence.

命令セットアーキテクチャ(ISA).desc: The processor specification as seen by software, including the instructions and registers it supports. Examples include x86, Arm and RISC-V.

分岐予測.desc: A technique that predicts the outcome of conditional branches before they execute, so later instructions can proceed without stalling the pipeline. A misprediction forces the work to be redone.

パワーMOSFET.desc: A MOSFET built to handle large currents and voltages. It switches quickly and is widely used in power supply circuits and the like.

オン抵抗.desc: The resistance of the current path when a power device is on. The smaller it is, the lower the conduction loss.

スイッチング損失.desc: Loss that occurs while a power device switches between on and off, when voltage and current are present at the same time. It grows with switching frequency.

CMOSイメージセンサー.desc: An image sensor made with a CMOS process that has an amplifier in each pixel. It is low-power, can integrate peripheral circuits, and dominates smartphone cameras and more.

about.h: From photon to voltage in a 4T pixel
about.p: Each pixel's photodiode absorbs light and collects electrons in proportion to the exposure; quantum efficiency for visible light is typically about 50–80%. In the common four-transistor (4T) pixel, a transfer transistor moves this charge to a small node called the floating diffusion (FD), a source-follower amplifier buffers the FD voltage onto a column line, a select transistor connects the row, and a reset transistor clears the FD. Conversion gain is q/C_FD, about 160 µV per electron for a 1 fF node. Neighboring pixels often share the FD and readout transistors to save area.

Interface states at the silicon/oxide surface generate dark current. The pinned photodiode buries the n-type collection region under a heavily doped p+ surface layer, which fills those states with holes and suppresses that current. The buried region also fully depletes, so charge transfer is complete, avoiding image lag. Readout uses correlated double sampling (CDS): the FD is sampled right after reset and again after transfer, and the difference removes kTC reset noise and amplifier offset, bringing read noise down to a few electrons or less. Column-parallel ADCs then digitize the signal on chip.

In a front-side illuminated (FSI) sensor, light must pass through gaps between metal wiring layers before reaching the photodiode, losing intensity and angle tolerance. A back-side illuminated (BSI) sensor thins the wafer to a few micrometers and receives light from the side opposite the wiring, which keeps sensitivity high for pixels around 1 µm and became standard in smartphone cameras. Stacked sensors go further, bonding the pixel wafer to a separate logic wafer that carries ADCs and image processing. Epitaxial silicon substrates are used for low-defect pixel regions.

A charge-coupled device (CCD) shifts charge packets across the chip to a single output amplifier, which needs several clock voltages and more power. A CMOS image sensor amplifies in each pixel and reads rows through column circuits, so it runs at lower power, reads out faster, and integrates timing, ADCs and processing on the same die. Row-by-row readout causes rolling-shutter distortion of fast motion, which global-shutter pixels avoid with in-pixel storage. Dual-conversion-gain pixels switch extra FD capacitance to cover both dim and bright scenes.

faq.q: What is the difference between a CMOS image sensor and a CCD?
faq.a: A CCD moves charge across the chip to one shared output amplifier, while a CMOS image sensor converts charge to voltage inside each pixel and reads it out row by row. CMOS sensors use less power and integrate ADCs and logic, which is why they dominate phones and most cameras.

faq.q: What does BSI mean in an image sensor?
faq.a: BSI stands for back-side illumination: the wafer is thinned and light enters from the back, so it reaches the photodiodes without passing through the metal wiring layers, improving sensitivity for small pixels.

faq.q: What is correlated double sampling in a CMOS image sensor?
faq.a: It reads the floating diffusion once after reset and once after charge transfer, then subtracts the two. Reset (kTC) noise and amplifier offsets appear in both samples and cancel, leaving the true signal.

量子効率.desc: The fraction of incident photons converted into signal electrons. The higher it is, the better the sensitivity.

裏面照射型(BSI).desc: An image sensor structure in which light enters from the back of the substrate, where there is no wiring. Light is not blocked by wiring, so sensitivity stays high even with small pixels.

about.p: In a front-side illuminated (FSI) CMOS image sensor, light enters from the side where transistors and wiring are built, passing through the microlens, color filter and several metal layers before reaching the photodiode. The metal blocks and reflects part of the light, and the tall optical stack loses rays arriving at oblique angles. In a backside-illuminated (BSI) sensor the wafer is flipped after front-side processing, bonded to a support wafer, and its original substrate thinned to a few µm, so light enters from the back and reaches the photodiode without crossing any wiring.

about.h: Why BSI matters for small pixels
about.p: As pixels shrink toward about 1 µm, the openings between metal lines in an FSI pixel become a small fraction of the pixel area and the stack becomes tall relative to pixel width, so sensitivity and angular response drop sharply. BSI keeps nearly the whole pixel area open to light and shortens the optical path from microlens to silicon. It also frees the wiring from optical constraints, allowing more metal layers. These advantages made BSI the standard structure for smartphone camera sensors.

Thinning must leave a uniform silicon layer a few µm thick across the wafer. The new back surface must be passivated, because defects there generate dark current; films with fixed negative charge are commonly used to accumulate holes at that surface. Thin silicon also makes optical and electrical crosstalk between neighboring pixels more likely, which deep trench isolation between pixels reduces. Red and near-infrared light has an absorption length of several µm or more in silicon, so very thin layers lose some long-wavelength response.

Because a BSI sensor already needs a bonded support wafer, that wafer can carry useful circuitry instead of being blank silicon. Stacked image sensors bond the pixel wafer to a logic wafer containing readout, analog-to-digital conversion and image processing, each made in a process suited to its function. This allows smaller chips or more processing per pixel area, and it builds directly on the wafer bonding and thinning techniques developed for BSI.

faq.q: What is the difference between BSI and FSI image sensors?
faq.a: In FSI, light passes through the wiring layers before reaching the photodiode; in BSI, the wafer is flipped and thinned so light enters from the back, where there is no wiring. BSI therefore collects more light, especially in small pixels.

faq.q: Why must the wafer be thinned in a BSI sensor?
faq.a: Light enters from the back, so it must reach the photodiodes near the front side before being absorbed. Thinning the silicon to a few µm puts the photodiodes within the light's absorption depth.

faq.q: Do BSI sensors have any disadvantages?
faq.a: They need extra steps such as wafer bonding, thinning and backside passivation, and the thin silicon increases crosstalk risk and reduces long-wavelength response. Deep trench isolation and careful surface treatment address these.

グローバルシャッター.desc: An electronic shutter method that exposes all pixels at the same time. Unlike a rolling shutter, which reads row by row, it does not distort images of moving objects.

HEMT(高電子移動度トランジスタ).desc: A transistor that uses the high-mobility two-dimensional electron gas formed at a heterojunction interface as its channel. It is used in high-frequency and high-power applications.

III-V族化合物半導体.desc: Semiconductors made of group III elements (Ga, In, Al, etc.) and group V elements (As, P, N, etc.), such as GaAs, InP and GaN.

ワイドバンドギャップ半導体.desc: Semiconductors with a larger band gap than silicon, such as SiC and GaN. Their high breakdown field makes them strong for high-voltage, high-temperature operation.

GAA(ゲートオールアラウンド).desc: A transistor structure in which the gate surrounds the channel on all sides. It controls current better than FinFET and is used in the generations after FinFET.

about.h: Why wrap the gate all the way around
about.p: Short-channel effects arise when the drain's electric field reaches into the channel and competes with the gate. The scale length λ estimates how far that influence extends; gate lengths of about 5–10 λ keep it small, and every additional gated surface shrinks λ. A planar MOSFET gates one face, a FinFET three, and a gate-all-around (GAA) transistor surrounds each channel completely. This strongest electrostatic control suppresses punch-through and leakage at shorter gate lengths, and like FinFETs, GAA devices use nearly undoped channels with threshold voltage set by the gate work function.

Production GAA devices use nanosheets: silicon plates about 5 nm thick and roughly 15–50 nm wide, typically three stacked vertically about 10 nm apart, each wrapped by gate dielectric and metal. A nanosheet resembles a FinFET fin laid on its side and stacked. A FinFET's width can only change in whole fins, but sheet width can be drawn continuously in layout, using wide sheets for high-performance cells and narrow ones for low power and SRAM. More sheets add current per footprint but complicate processing and add parasitic capacitance.

Fabrication starts with an epitaxial stack of alternating Si and SiGe layers, the SiGe containing about 25–30% germanium. The stack is patterned into fins and a dummy gate is formed. The ends of the SiGe layers are recessed and filled with a dielectric inner spacer, which reduces gate-to-source/drain capacitance and prevents shorts. After source/drain epitaxy, the dummy gate is removed and the SiGe is etched away with high selectivity, leaving the silicon sheets suspended. ALD then fills the gaps with high-k dielectric and metal gate.

Samsung announced volume production of GAA at its 3 nm node in 2022 under the name MBCFET; TSMC adopted nanosheets at its 2 nm node and Intel at 18A as RibbonFET, making GAA the successor to the FinFET. Researchers are pursuing further steps: the forksheet, which places nMOS and pMOS sheets on either side of a thin dielectric wall; the CFET, which stacks nMOS over pMOS; and two-dimensional channel materials such as MoS2 that remain semiconducting at a single layer about 0.65 nm thick.

faq.q: What is the difference between GAA and FinFET?
faq.a: A FinFET's gate covers three sides of a vertical fin, while a GAA transistor's gate surrounds stacked horizontal sheets or wires on all sides. GAA gives stronger gate control and allows the channel width to be set continuously instead of in whole fins.

faq.q: What is a nanosheet transistor?
faq.a: It is a GAA transistor whose channels are thin horizontal silicon sheets, about 5 nm thick and tens of nanometers wide, stacked about three high with the gate filling the spaces between and around them.

faq.q: Why is SiGe used when making GAA transistors?
faq.a: SiGe layers grown between the silicon channel layers act as sacrificial spacers. They can be etched away selectively later, opening gaps so the gate dielectric and metal can wrap around each silicon sheet.

ナノシート.desc: A GAA transistor structure that stacks several thin, plate-like silicon channels vertically, each surrounded by the gate. Current can be tuned by the sheet width.

about.p: A nanosheet transistor stacks typically about three horizontal silicon channels, each around 5 nm thick and from about 15 to 50 nm wide, spaced about 10 nm apart vertically. The gate dielectric and metal fill every gap, so the gate surrounds each sheet on all four sides, which is why it is called gate-all-around (GAA). It resembles a FinFET fin turned on its side and stacked. The effective channel width is the perimeter of each sheet summed over the stack, so a wider sheet carries proportionally more current.

Fabrication begins with an epitaxial stack of alternating Si and SiGe layers, the SiGe containing about 25 to 30 percent germanium. The stack is patterned like a fin and a dummy gate is formed. The ends of the SiGe layers are recessed and filled with a dielectric such as nitride, forming inner spacers that reduce gate-to-source/drain capacitance and prevent shorts. After source/drain epitaxy and removal of the dummy gate, the SiGe is etched away with high selectivity, leaving the Si sheets suspended, and ALD fills the gaps with high-k dielectric and metal gate.

In a FinFET, fin height and width are fixed by the process, so drive strength can change only by the number of fins, a constraint called width quantization. Nanosheet width can be set continuously in layout: wide sheets for high-performance logic, narrow ones for low-power cells and SRAM, which allows finer tuning of drive current and capacitance. Gating the channel from all sides also gives stronger electrostatic control and better resistance to short-channel effects, delivering more current in the same footprint. Samsung's 3 nm generation in 2022 was the first announced volume production.

Adding sheets raises current per footprint, but taller stacks make source/drain epitaxy and gate fill harder, and lower sheets see more parasitic resistance and capacitance, so about three sheets is a common compromise. At thicknesses near 5 nm, quantum confinement widens the effective band gap and shifts threshold voltage; because the shift scales inversely with thickness squared, one atomic layer of variation can move it by tens of millivolts. The thermal budget is tight too: later steps run at about 600 to 700 °C or below to avoid Si/SiGe intermixing.

faq.q: What is the difference between a nanosheet and a nanowire transistor?
faq.a: Both are gate-all-around devices. A nanowire has a narrow cross-section with width close to its thickness, while a nanosheet is much wider than it is thick, carrying more current per stacked channel and allowing width to be tuned in layout.

faq.q: What is an inner spacer in a nanosheet transistor?
faq.a: It is a dielectric plug formed between the gate and the source/drain in the gaps between sheets, made by recessing the SiGe layer ends and refilling with an insulator such as nitride. It cuts parasitic capacitance and prevents gate-to-source/drain shorts.

faq.q: Why replace FinFETs with nanosheets?
faq.a: As gate lengths shrink, a gate on three sides of a fin no longer controls the channel well enough. Wrapping the gate around each sheet improves electrostatic control, and adjustable sheet width removes the fin-count quantization of FinFET design.

CFET(相補型FET).desc: A structure that stacks nMOS and pMOS transistors vertically. It is under development because it could greatly shrink the area of CMOS circuits.

加速度センサー.desc: A sensor that detects acceleration from the movement of a small spring-supported mass. It is used for detecting smartphone orientation, in airbags and elsewhere.

ジャイロスコープ.desc: A sensor that detects rotation rate (angular velocity). MEMS versions use the Coriolis force acting on a vibrating structure.

犠牲層エッチング.desc: A typical MEMS fabrication method that etches away a temporary layer (the sacrificial layer) beneath a structure, freeing beams or membranes so they can move.

静電容量検出.desc: A method that detects displacement, pressure and the like from changes in capacitance between movable and fixed electrodes. It is widely used in MEMS sensors.

FZ法(フローティングゾーン法).desc: A method that melts a zone of a polysilicon rod and moves that molten zone along to form a single crystal. With no crucible, oxygen content is low, suiting high-resistivity wafers.

ウエハのノッチ.desc: A small cut in a wafer's edge that indicates its crystal orientation. Used on 200 mm and larger wafers; smaller wafers used an orientation flat (a straight edge) instead.

結晶方位.desc: The direction of crystal planes and axes, expressed with Miller indices such as (100). The (100) surface is standard for silicon wafers used for MOSFETs.

ゲッタリング.desc: A technique that collects and traps metal impurities in a wafer at locations away from the surface where devices are built, using oxygen precipitates and the like.

ヘテロエピタキシー.desc: Growing a single-crystal film of a material different from the substrate, such as SiGe on silicon or GaN on sapphire. Growth of the same material is homoepitaxy.

格子不整合.desc: A difference in the atomic spacing (lattice constant) between a grown film and its substrate. A large mismatch causes strain and defects such as dislocations.

選択エピタキシャル成長.desc: A method that grows crystal only where silicon is exposed, not on areas covered by insulating film. It is used for SiGe in transistor sources and drains and elsewhere.

MOCVD(有機金属気相成長).desc: A method that grows crystals using metal-organic compounds and source gases such as ammonia. It is widely used to grow compound semiconductors such as GaN and GaAs.

ドライ酸化.desc: Thermal oxidation with dry oxygen. Growth is slow, but it produces dense, high-quality oxide, used for gate oxides and the like.

ウェット酸化.desc: Thermal oxidation in an atmosphere containing water vapor. It grows faster than dry oxidation and is used to make thick oxides.

LOCOS.desc: A method that isolates devices by thickly oxidizing only areas not covered by nitride. It forms a beak-like encroachment at the edges (the bird's beak) and has been replaced by STI.

熱拡散.desc: A doping method that diffuses impurity atoms into a semiconductor at high temperature. They spread from regions of high concentration to low.

ドーズ量.desc: The number of ions implanted per unit area in ion implantation, expressed in cm⁻². It is set by beam current and implant time.

投影飛程.desc: The average depth at which implanted ions come to rest. It is deeper with higher acceleration energy and with lighter ions.

チャネリング.desc: A phenomenon in which ions pass through gaps between rows of crystal atoms and penetrate deeper than expected. It is prevented by tilting the wafer during implantation and similar measures.

PECVD(プラズマCVD).desc: CVD that decomposes source gases with plasma to deposit films. It can deposit at lower temperatures than thermal CVD and is used for insulating films in interconnect steps and the like.

ステップカバレッジ.desc: A measure of how uniformly a film covers the sidewalls and bottoms of steps and holes compared with flat areas. ALD gives excellent step coverage.

OPC(光学近接効果補正).desc: A technique that corrects mask patterns in advance, anticipating distortion of the printed pattern caused by diffraction of light and similar effects.

液浸露光.desc: Exposure with the space between the lens and the wafer filled with water. It allows a numerical aperture above 1, so ArF excimer lasers can form finer patterns.

RIE(反応性イオンエッチング).desc: Dry etching that combines reactive species in a plasma with ions accelerated by an electric field. It enables vertical, anisotropic etching.

ウェットエッチング.desc: Etching that dissolves films by immersing them in chemicals. Selectivity is high and damage low, but it generally proceeds isotropically and does not suit fine patterning.

等方性エッチング.desc: Etching that proceeds at the same rate vertically and laterally. It cuts in under the mask (undercut).

スラリー.desc: The liquid used in CMP, with fine abrasive particles dispersed in chemicals. It flattens surfaces by combining chemical action with mechanical polishing.

ディッシング.desc: A CMP phenomenon in which the center of a wide metal line is over-polished into a dish-like depression.

メガソニック洗浄.desc: A cleaning method that applies ultrasound of about 1 MHz to the cleaning solution to remove fine particles from wafer surfaces.

バリアメタル.desc: A thin metal film around copper wiring that prevents copper from diffusing into insulating films or silicon, such as Ta or TaN.

多層配線.desc: A structure that stacks many wiring layers separated by insulating films and connects them vertically with vias. Leading-edge ICs have more than ten layers.

RC遅延.desc: Signal delay determined by the product of wire resistance (R) and capacitance (C). It grows as scaling makes wires thinner, limiting performance.

特殊材料ガス.desc: High-purity gases with toxic or flammable properties used in semiconductor manufacturing, such as silane, arsine and phosphine. They are supplied under strict control.

TMAH.desc: Tetramethylammonium hydroxide, a metal-ion-free organic alkali used as a photoresist developer. Care is needed because it can cause poisoning through skin absorption.

プリカーサ(前駆体).desc: A source compound that reacts to form the desired film in CVD or ALD, such as TEOS or metal-organic compounds.

about.h: How a precursor becomes a film
about.p: In chemical vapor deposition (CVD), precursor vapor flows over a heated wafer, adsorbs on the surface and decomposes or reacts with a co-reactant, leaving a solid film while volatile byproducts are pumped away. Silane (SiH4) decomposes to silicon and hydrogen, tungsten hexafluoride (WF6) is reduced to tungsten with HF as a byproduct, and TEOS breaks down to SiO2. In atomic layer deposition (ALD) the precursor chemisorbs on surface sites until they are filled, the excess is purged, and a separate reactant such as water, ozone or ammonia completes the reaction, giving about 0.1 nm per cycle.

A useful precursor must be volatile enough to deliver as vapor; liquids such as TEOS are vaporized by bubbling a carrier gas through them or by direct liquid injection. It must survive transport without decomposing in the gas phase, yet react readily at the surface. Its ligands should leave cleanly: chlorides such as HfCl4 are thermally stable around 300 °C but can leave chlorine in the film, while metal-organics such as TEMAHf react at lower temperature but can leave carbon. Safety matters too, which is why liquid TEOS is often preferred over pyrophoric silane for oxide.

At low temperature the surface reaction is slow and sets the deposition rate, which then follows the Arrhenius law and depends exponentially on temperature, so wafer temperature uniformity controls thickness uniformity. Because precursor molecules can diffuse deep into trenches before reacting, this regime gives good step coverage. At high temperature the reaction is fast and the arrival rate of precursor limits growth, so gas-flow uniformity matters and trench openings receive more film and can pinch off. Large exposed areas consume more precursor and slow deposition, an effect known as loading.

Silicon films and epitaxy use silane, dichlorosilane (SiH2Cl2) and trichlorosilane (SiHCl3), usually diluted in hydrogen that also keeps the surface reduced and carries away chlorine as HCl. Oxide uses TEOS, tungsten plugs use WF6, and titanium nitride often uses TiCl4. High-k ALD uses HfCl4 or TEMAHf with H2O or O3, and Al2O3 uses trimethylaluminum (TMA) with water inside an ALD window of about 150 to 300 °C. Dopant gases such as phosphine and diborane are added for in-situ doping, and focused ion beam tools inject precursor gases to deposit local platinum or tungsten.

faq.q: What is the difference between a precursor and a reactant in ALD?
faq.a: The precursor carries the element that ends up in the film, such as the hafnium in HfCl4 or the aluminum in trimethylaluminum. The reactant, often water, ozone or ammonia, is dosed in a separate step to convert the adsorbed precursor layer into oxide or nitride and to restore reactive surface sites for the next cycle.

faq.q: Why is TEOS often used instead of silane for silicon oxide CVD?
faq.a: TEOS is a liquid at room temperature and is not pyrophoric, so it is safer to store and handle than silane. Its surface-driven decomposition also gives more conformal oxide with better step coverage in narrow gaps.

faq.q: Is a carrier gas the same as a precursor?
faq.a: No. A carrier gas such as hydrogen, nitrogen or argon only transports and dilutes the precursor vapor and does not supply atoms to the film, although hydrogen in silicon epitaxy also acts as a reducing agent that keeps the surface clean.

NF3(三フッ化窒素).desc: A gas used for cleaning CVD chambers and the like. Its global warming potential is high, so emission reduction is required.

リードフレーム.desc: A thin metal sheet combining the pad that holds the chip with the external terminals (leads). It is used in packages such as QFP.

アンダーフィル.desc: Resin filled into the gap between the chip and the substrate in flip-chip assembly. It spreads out stress from thermal expansion mismatch and protects the bump joints.

プローブカード.desc: A fixture that presses many needles (probes) onto chip electrodes on the wafer to connect them electrically to a tester.

ATE(自動試験装置).desc: Equipment that applies test patterns to chips, measures their outputs and automatically judges pass or fail. Also called a tester.

about.p: Automatic test equipment (ATE) applies power and signals to a device under test (DUT), measures its responses, compares them with expected values and sorts parts into pass, fail or performance bins. A test program sequences the steps. The tester has hundreds to thousands of channels; each pin's electronics can drive logic levels with programmed timing, compare outputs against expected values at strobe times, and force voltage or current while measuring the other through a per-pin parametric measurement unit. Device power supplies provide and monitor the supply rails.

ATE is used at two main points. In wafer test, also called wafer sort, a prober steps the wafer under a probe card whose needles touch each chip's pads, which are tens of micrometers across; probe marks are inspected so they do not impair later wire bonding or bumping. Failing dies are marked so they are not packaged. In final test, a handler moves packaged parts into sockets on a load board, often at hot or cold temperatures, and sorts them by result.

A typical flow starts with continuity checks for opens and shorts, then DC parametric tests such as leakage and supply current, then functional and structural tests. For digital logic, scan patterns generated by automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) detect manufacturing faults, often at speed. Memories are exercised with algorithmic patterns or built-in self-test (BIST). Analog, mixed-signal and RF parts need instruments for linearity, noise and frequency response, so tester platforms are specialized for logic and SoC, memory, mixed-signal or RF devices.

Testers are expensive, so test cost is roughly test time multiplied by the tester's cost per second. Manufacturers cut it by testing many devices in parallel (multi-site test), trimming redundant tests and adding design-for-test (DFT) features. Scan chains, compression and BIST let a modest number of tester pins and shallow pattern memory cover large chips, and reduced-pin-count test lets cheaper testers handle more sites at once.

faq.q: What does ATE stand for in semiconductors?
faq.a: ATE stands for automatic test equipment, the tester that applies test patterns to chips, measures their outputs and judges pass or fail automatically.

faq.q: What is the difference between a prober and a handler?
faq.a: Both feed devices to the ATE. A prober positions a wafer under a probe card for wafer-level test, while a handler picks up packaged chips, places them in test sockets and sorts them after final test.

faq.q: Why does design-for-test reduce ATE cost?
faq.a: Structures such as scan chains, test compression and built-in self-test let the chip test itself or be tested through few pins, shortening test time and allowing more devices to be tested in parallel on less expensive equipment.

スキャンテスト.desc: A test method that uses scan chains, formed by linking a circuit's flip-flops in series, to set and observe internal states.

エリプソメトリ.desc: A measurement method that shines polarized light on a sample and determines thin-film thickness and refractive index from the change in polarization on reflection. It is nondestructive.

about.p: Ellipsometry shines polarized light onto a sample at an oblique angle, often around 65–75° for silicon, and analyzes the polarization of the reflected beam. The light is split into p-polarized (in the plane of incidence) and s-polarized (perpendicular) components, which reflect differently from a film stack. The instrument measures two quantities: Ψ, related to the ratio of their reflection amplitudes, and Δ, their phase difference, defined by tanΨ·exp(iΔ) = rp/rs. Because it measures a ratio and a phase rather than absolute intensity, it is insensitive to source fluctuations.

about.h: From Ψ and Δ to thickness and index
about.p: Ψ and Δ do not give thickness directly. The analyst builds an optical model of the stack, for example a silicon substrate, a thin interfacial layer and an oxide film, with each layer's thickness and optical constants n and k, then adjusts the unknowns until the calculated Ψ and Δ match the measurement. Spectroscopic ellipsometry measures across many wavelengths, giving enough data to fit multilayer stacks. For films only a few nanometers thick, thickness and refractive index become strongly correlated, so the index is usually fixed at a known value.

about.h: Strengths and limits in a fab
about.p: Ellipsometry is fast, non-contact and non-destructive, with thickness repeatability better than 0.1 nm, which makes it the workhorse for monitoring gate oxides, nitrides and other thin films. Its accuracy is only as good as the model: interface layers, surface roughness, absorbing films and unknown composition all complicate the fit. The beam spot is relatively large, so measurements on product wafers are made on dedicated test pads, typically in the scribe lines, rather than on dense circuit patterns.

Oxide interference colors give only a rough estimate of thickness. Spectral reflectometry measures reflected intensity versus wavelength; it is simpler and works well for thicker films, but carries less information than ellipsometry's phase data for very thin layers. X-ray reflectivity and cross-sectional TEM serve as references, the latter destructive. Ellipsometry measures film thickness and optical constants only; sheet resistance needs a four-point probe, and surface metal contamination needs a method such as TXRF.

faq.q: What does ellipsometry measure?
faq.a: It measures how reflection changes the polarization of light, expressed as the amplitude ratio Ψ and phase difference Δ. Fitting these to an optical model yields film thickness and refractive index.

faq.q: What is the difference between ellipsometry and reflectometry?
faq.a: Reflectometry measures only the intensity of reflected light, while ellipsometry also measures the phase difference between two polarizations. The extra phase information makes ellipsometry more sensitive for very thin films.

faq.q: Can ellipsometry measure films only a few nanometers thick?
faq.a: Yes, with sub-0.1 nm repeatability, which is why it is used for gate dielectrics. For such thin films, though, the refractive index is usually fixed in the model because it cannot be separated reliably from thickness.

四探針法.desc: A method that passes current through the outer two of four collinear needles and measures voltage across the inner two to find the sheet resistance of wafers and thin films.

TEM(透過電子顕微鏡).desc: A microscope that observes thinned samples by passing an electron beam through them. With atomic-level resolution, it reveals cross-sectional structures and crystal defects.

キラー欠陥.desc: A defect that makes a chip fail, such as particles or pattern anomalies of a size and location that cause shorts or opens in wiring.

ポアソン歩留まりモデル.desc: A model that assumes defects are randomly distributed and expresses yield as Y = exp(−D×A), where D is defect density and A is chip area.

SPC(統計的工程管理).desc: A method of maintaining quality by monitoring process data with control charts and the like and detecting anomalies statistically.

工程能力指数(Cpk).desc: An index of how much margin a process's variation and mean offset leave relative to the specification limits. A common benchmark is 1.33 or higher.

TDDB(経時絶縁破壊).desc: A phenomenon in which an insulating film under sustained voltage eventually breaks down even below its breakdown voltage. It is used to evaluate the lifetime of gate oxides and the like.

NBTI.desc: A degradation phenomenon in which the magnitude of a pMOS threshold voltage gradually increases under negative gate voltage at high temperature.

MTTF(平均故障時間).desc: The average time until a non-repairable product fails. It is used as an indicator of product lifetime.

RTL(レジスタ転送レベル).desc: A design abstraction that describes circuits by how data moves and is processed between registers. It is written in Verilog or VHDL and serves as the input to logic synthesis.

配置配線.desc: The design step that arranges cells on the chip (placement) from the netlist produced by logic synthesis and determines the wiring between them (routing).

DRC(デザインルールチェック).desc: Verification that checks whether a layout follows the geometric rules required for manufacturing, such as line widths and spacings.

ISO 14644-1.desc: The international standard that defines cleanroom cleanliness classes by the number of airborne particles. The smaller the number, the cleaner.

ULPAフィルタ.desc: A high-performance air filter that captures even finer particles than a HEPA filter. It is used in the ceilings of high-cleanliness cleanrooms.

ダウンフロー.desc: A cleanroom airflow method that sends clean air in one direction from the entire ceiling to the floor, quickly carrying generated particles away under the floor.

分子状汚染(AMC).desc: Gaseous contaminants in the air such as acids, alkalis and organics. Particle filters cannot remove them, so chemical filters are used.

パーフルオロカーボン.desc: Also called PFCs. Fluorinated gases such as CF4 and C2F6 used in etching and chamber cleaning. Their greenhouse effect is very large.

GHS.desc: The internationally harmonized system that communicates chemical hazards with pictograms and precautionary statements.

除害装置.desc: Equipment that removes hazardous substances from tool exhaust gas by combustion, adsorption, water scrubbing and the like.

RoHS指令.desc: The EU regulation restricting the use of specific hazardous substances such as lead and mercury in electrical and electronic equipment.

IDM(垂直統合型デバイスメーカー).desc: A semiconductor company that does everything in-house, from design through front-end and back-end manufacturing to sales.

OSAT.desc: A company that provides back-end services such as semiconductor assembly and testing under contract.

about.p: An OSAT (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test) company performs the back-end steps that turn finished wafers into tested, shippable chips. Typical services include wafer probing, backgrinding to thin the wafer, dicing, die attach, wire bonding or flip-chip bumping, molding, marking, and final electrical test. The front end, building transistors and interconnect on the wafer, is done by an integrated device manufacturer (IDM) or a foundry; the OSAT receives the processed wafers and returns packaged, tested parts to the chip company.

about.h: Place in the industry's division of labor
about.p: The modern supply chain splits work among fabless design companies, foundries for wafer fabrication, and OSATs for packaging and test. A fabless company may never own a factory: it sends designs to a foundry and has the resulting wafers assembled and tested by an OSAT. IDMs often keep some back-end work in house but outsource part of it for capacity or cost. Back-end work is more labor- and floor-space-intensive than wafer fabrication, and major OSAT sites are concentrated in Taiwan, China and Southeast Asia.
