As scaling slows, more performance comes from packaging: flip-chip bumps, copper pillars, fan-out wafer-level packaging, silicon interposers and chiplets stacked or placed side by side. These steps use wafer-level processes such as lithography, plating and redistribution layers, so OSATs have invested in fab-like equipment, while foundries have started offering their own advanced packaging. The simple split of front end at the foundry and back end at the OSAT therefore no longer holds for the most advanced products.

faq.q: What does OSAT stand for?
faq.a: OSAT stands for outsourced semiconductor assembly and test. It refers to companies that package and test chips under contract for other semiconductor companies.

faq.q: What is the difference between an OSAT and a foundry?
faq.a: A foundry manufactures the wafers, building transistors and wiring in the front-end process. An OSAT takes finished wafers and does the back-end work of cutting, packaging and testing the chips.

faq.q: Do fabless companies need OSATs?
faq.a: Usually yes. A fabless company owns no fabrication or assembly lines, so it relies on a foundry for wafers and on an OSAT, or a foundry offering packaging, for assembly and test.

ムーアの法則.desc: The empirical rule that the number of transistors on an integrated circuit doubles about every two years. It has served as a target for semiconductor scaling.

ハイブリッドボンディング.desc: A technique that directly bonds copper electrodes and dielectric surfaces without bumps, providing huge numbers of connections at extremely fine pitch.

シリコンインターポーザ.desc: A silicon intermediate substrate that holds chips side by side and connects them densely with fine wiring. It is used to connect GPUs and HBM, among other things.

有効質量.desc: An apparent mass used to treat electrons and holes in a crystal as if they were free particles responding to external forces. It is set by the curvature of the band; a smaller effective mass tends to give higher mobility.

縮退半導体.desc: A semiconductor doped so heavily that the Fermi level lies inside the conduction or valence band. It behaves almost like a metal and is used in tunnel diodes and low-resistance contacts.

間接遷移型.desc: A band structure in which the bottom of the conduction band and the top of the valence band occur at different momenta. Transitions need a phonon, so light emission is inefficient. Silicon and germanium are typical examples.

SRH再結合(ショックレー・リード・ホール再結合).desc: Recombination of electrons and holes through deep levels (traps) in the band gap. It mainly determines minority-carrier lifetime in silicon and is accelerated by metal contamination and crystal defects.

オージェ再結合.desc: Recombination in which the released energy is given to another carrier instead of being emitted as light. It becomes significant at high carrier densities and affects lifetime in heavily doped layers and efficiency loss in LEDs.

擬フェルミ準位.desc: Separate Fermi levels for electrons and holes, used to describe a semiconductor driven out of equilibrium by light or current injection. The larger the split between them, the more excess carriers there are.

拡散長.desc: The average distance minority carriers diffuse before recombining, given by L = √(Dτ) from the diffusion coefficient D and lifetime τ. It strongly affects the efficiency of solar cells and photodetectors.

アインシュタインの関係式.desc: The relation D = μkT/q that links the diffusion coefficient D and mobility μ of carriers. It shows that materials with higher mobility also allow faster diffusion.

電子親和力.desc: The energy difference between the vacuum level and the bottom of the conduction band of a semiconductor. It is used to estimate band offsets at heterojunctions and barrier heights at metal contacts.

仕事関数.desc: The energy difference between the vacuum level and the Fermi level: the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from a material. It affects the threshold voltage of metal gates and the height of Schottky barriers.

真性キャリア密度.desc: The density of thermally generated electrons and holes in an undoped semiconductor, written ni. For silicon it is about 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ at room temperature and rises steeply with temperature. In equilibrium, n × p = ni².

ショットキーバリアダイオード.desc: A diode that uses a metal-semiconductor junction (Schottky junction). It has a low forward voltage and switches fast because there is no minority-carrier storage.

接合容量(空乏層容量).desc: Capacitance arising because the depletion layer of a PN junction acts like a parallel-plate capacitor. It decreases as reverse bias widens the depletion layer; varactor diodes use this property.

拡散容量.desc: Capacitance in a forward-biased PN junction caused by injected minority carriers stored in the neutral regions. It grows in proportion to forward current and limits high-speed operation.

逆回復時間.desc: The time during which reverse current keeps flowing after a conducting diode is reverse-biased, until the stored minority carriers are removed. It causes switching loss and noise.

伝導度変調.desc: A large drop in the resistance of a lightly doped layer when many minority carriers are injected into it. PIN diodes and IGBTs use it to combine high breakdown voltage with low on-state voltage.

トンネルダイオード(エサキダイオード).desc: A diode with very heavily doped p and n sides that shows negative resistance in forward bias due to tunneling. It was discovered by Leo Esaki in 1957.

理想係数.desc: The factor n in the diode equation I ∝ exp(qV/nkT). It is close to 1 when diffusion current dominates and close to 2 when recombination in the depletion layer dominates, so it indicates junction quality.

オーミック接触.desc: A metal-semiconductor contact with low resistance in both directions and a linear current-voltage relation. It is made by heavily doping the semiconductor surface so carriers can tunnel through the barrier.

飽和領域.desc: The state of a bipolar transistor in which both the base-emitter and base-collector junctions are forward-biased. The collector-emitter voltage falls to about 0.1-0.3 V, corresponding to a switch in the on state.

遮断領域.desc: The state of a bipolar transistor in which both junctions are reverse-biased and almost no collector current flows. It corresponds to a switch in the off state.

about.p: A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) has four operating regions set by its two junctions. In the forward-active region the base-emitter junction is forward biased and the base-collector junction reverse biased; in saturation both are forward biased; in cutoff both are reverse biased. In practice a silicon transistor is effectively in cutoff whenever VBE is below about 0.5 V, because forward current is then negligible. Only junction leakage, on the order of nanoamperes, reaches the collector, so the collector-emitter path behaves like an open switch.

about.h: Cutoff as the off state of a switch
about.p: In switching circuits a BJT alternates between cutoff (off) and saturation (on). In cutoff almost no collector current flows, so there is no drop across the load resistor and VCE rises to nearly the supply voltage; power dissipation is close to zero. If the base is left floating, collector-base leakage flows into the base and is amplified by the current gain, so the transistor may not turn off fully, especially when hot, since leakage rises steeply with temperature. A resistor between base and emitter diverts this leakage and guarantees cutoff.

Switching speed depends on how fast the transistor crosses between regions. Turning on from cutoff requires charging the junction capacitances until VBE reaches about 0.6–0.7 V before collector current rises, a delay time. Turning off from saturation is slower, because excess minority charge stored in the base must be removed before the transistor can return to cutoff (the storage time). Circuits that keep the transistor out of deep saturation, such as Schottky-clamped transistors, shorten this turn-off delay.

For a MOSFET, the comparable off state is VGS below the threshold voltage, although subthreshold current still flows and is usually larger than BJT cutoff leakage in scaled devices. Note that the word saturation means different things for the two devices: BJT saturation is the fully on switch state, whereas MOSFET saturation corresponds to the BJT's active region. The cutoff region is also unrelated to the cutoff frequency (fT), which is the frequency at which current gain falls to one.

faq.q: What are the conditions for a BJT to be in the cutoff region?
faq.a: Both the base-emitter and base-collector junctions are reverse biased, or in practice VBE is below about 0.5 V for silicon. Collector current is then limited to leakage of around nanoamperes.

faq.q: Why put a resistor between base and emitter?
faq.a: With a floating base, collector-base leakage flows through the base-emitter junction and is amplified by the current gain, so the transistor may conduct slightly. The resistor shunts that leakage away so the transistor stays firmly in cutoff.

faq.q: Is the cutoff region related to the cutoff frequency?
faq.a: No. The cutoff region is a DC bias state where the transistor is off, while the cutoff frequency (fT) is the frequency at which the transistor's small-signal current gain drops to one.

カレントミラー回路.desc: A circuit that uses two matched transistors to copy the current flowing in one into the other (or at a fixed ratio). It is widely used for bias current sources and active loads in analog ICs.

トランジション周波数.desc: The frequency at which the common-emitter current gain falls to 1, written fT. It is a key indicator of a transistor's high-frequency performance.

エミッタフォロワ.desc: A common-collector amplifier. Its voltage gain is about 1, but its high input impedance and low output impedance make it a buffer that drives the next stage without loading the signal.

ダーリントン接続.desc: A connection that feeds the emitter current of one transistor into the base of a second. The overall current gain is roughly the product of the two, so a small base current can control a large current.

クロスオーバーひずみ.desc: Distortion in a class-B push-pull amplifier near 0 V, where neither transistor conducts during the handover between positive and negative half-cycles. Class-AB biasing with a small idle current reduces it.

ミラー効果.desc: The effect by which a capacitance between the input and output of an inverting amplifier appears (1 + gain) times larger from the input. It degrades the high-frequency response of common-emitter and common-source stages.

チャネル長変調.desc: In a saturated MOSFET, raising the drain voltage moves the pinch-off point toward the source, shortening the effective channel and slightly increasing drain current. It makes the output resistance finite.

速度飽和.desc: Under strong electric fields, carrier drift velocity stops increasing in proportion to the field and levels off at about 1×10⁷ cm/s. In short-channel MOSFETs it makes drain current smaller than the square law predicts.

相互コンダクタンス.desc: The ratio of the change in drain current to the change in gate voltage, written gm. It expresses a transistor's amplifying ability; amplifier gain is roughly gm times the load resistance.

DIBL.desc: Short for drain-induced barrier lowering. In short-channel MOSFETs, a higher drain voltage lowers the potential barrier at the source, reducing the threshold voltage and increasing off-state leakage.

GIDL(ゲート誘起ドレインリーク).desc: Off-state leakage caused by band-to-band tunneling in the strong field where the gate overlaps the drain. It is a concern for data retention in DRAM, among others.

パンチスルー.desc: A condition in which the source and drain depletion regions merge and current flows that the gate cannot control. It occurs when the channel is too short or the substrate doping is too low.

about.h: How punch-through develops in a MOSFET
about.p: When drain voltage is applied, the drain-to-body junction is reverse biased and its depletion region spreads toward the source. Depletion width grows roughly with the square root of voltage divided by doping, so a short channel and lightly doped substrate let it reach the source-side depletion region. Once the two merge below the surface, the drain itself pulls down the potential barrier that normally holds back source carriers. Current then flows deep in the substrate, where the gate field is weak, so the transistor cannot be switched off and drain current climbs steeply with drain voltage.

about.h: Punch-through vs. DIBL and avalanche breakdown
about.p: Punch-through is the extreme case of drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL). With moderate DIBL, the drain only partly lowers the source barrier, so threshold voltage falls as drain voltage rises and the subthreshold swing worsens. In punch-through the barrier in the subsurface region effectively disappears and gate control is lost. It is a purely electrostatic effect and needs no impact ionization, unlike avalanche breakdown, where carriers gain enough energy in a high field to generate new electron-hole pairs.

about.h: How process and structure suppress it
about.p: The usual cure is more doping exactly where the depletion regions would meet, without raising doping at the channel surface, which would increase threshold voltage and cut mobility. Halo (pocket) implants, tilted about 20–45°, place channel-type dopant under the source/drain edges. Retrograde wells use implants of hundreds of keV to MeV to put peak doping deep below the surface. Bulk FinFETs add a heavily doped punch-through stopper at the fin base, which the gate cannot control. SOI substrates and gate-all-around (GAA) structures remove the uncontrolled path altogether.

Bipolar transistors suffer a similar failure. A thin base reduces recombination and raises current gain and speed, but at high collector-base reverse voltage the collector depletion region can spread across the whole base and reach the emitter depletion region. The base potential barrier then collapses and collector current rises uncontrollably, which caps the usable breakdown voltage. Base width and base doping are therefore chosen together, trading current gain and high-frequency performance against punch-through voltage.

faq.q: What is the difference between punch-through and avalanche breakdown?
faq.a: Punch-through happens when the drain and source depletion regions merge and the source barrier collapses, which is purely electrostatic. Avalanche breakdown happens when carriers in a high field create new electron-hole pairs by impact ionization, multiplying the current.

faq.q: How do halo implants prevent punch-through?
faq.a: Halo implants add extra dopant of the substrate type locally under the edges of the source and drain. This narrows the drain depletion region near the channel ends, so it cannot reach the source, while leaving the rest of the channel lightly doped.

faq.q: Why do bulk FinFETs need a punch-through stopper?
faq.a: The gate wraps only the upper part of the fin, so the lower part near the substrate offers a leakage path the gate cannot shut off. A heavily doped layer of the opposite type at the fin base blocks this path.

フラットバンド電圧.desc: The gate voltage at which the bands at the semiconductor surface of a MOS structure are flat. It is set by the work-function difference between gate and substrate and by charges in the oxide, and is one component of the threshold voltage.

LDD構造.desc: Short for lightly doped drain. The drain is made lightly doped only at its edge next to the gate, relaxing the electric field and suppressing hot-carrier degradation.

基板バイアス効果.desc: An increase in threshold voltage when reverse bias is applied between source and substrate (body), because the depletion charge grows. Also called the substrate bias effect; it is sometimes used to tune the threshold.

貫通電流.desc: Current that flows from supply to ground in a CMOS gate during the brief time while the input switches and both the pMOS and nMOS are on. Also called crowbar current, it adds to power consumption.

トランスミッションゲート.desc: An analog switch made of an nMOS and a pMOS connected in parallel. The nMOS passes 0 well and the pMOS passes 1 well, so both values pass without voltage loss.

メタステーブル.desc: A state in which a flip-flop's output stays between 0 and 1 for a while when setup or hold time is violated. Asynchronous signals are passed through two flip-flops (a synchronizer) to guard against it.

グレイコード.desc: A code in which successive values differ in only one bit. It prevents read errors in rotary encoders and when passing counter values between different clock domains.

2の補数.desc: The usual binary representation of negative integers. Inverting all bits and adding 1 negates a number. n bits cover −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1, and the same adder can be used for subtraction.

カルノー図.desc: A diagram that arranges a truth table so that adjacent cells differ in one bit. Grouping neighboring 1s lets you simplify a logic expression visually.

マルチプレクサ.desc: A circuit that selects one of several inputs according to select signals and passes it to the output. The reverse, routing one input to one of several outputs, is a demultiplexer.

about.p: A 2:1 multiplexer (mux) outputs Y = S'·A + S·B: input A when the select signal S is 0 and input B when S is 1. With n select bits a mux chooses among 2ⁿ inputs, so an 8:1 mux needs three select lines. In CMOS, muxes are built from AND-OR or NAND-NAND logic, from transmission gates, or as trees of 2:1 muxes for wide inputs. A mux is also a universal logic element: tying its data inputs to the constants of a truth table makes a 2ⁿ:1 mux implement any n-input Boolean function.

Processor datapaths are full of muxes: they select ALU operands from registers or immediates, forward results through bypass paths to avoid pipeline stalls, choose the next program counter and switch shared buses. FPGA logic blocks implement arbitrary functions with lookup tables (LUTs), which are small memories read out through a mux tree. In design for testability, scan flip-flops add a mux at the data input so the flip-flops can be chained into shift registers in test mode. On boards, analog multiplexers share one ADC among several sensors, and I2C multiplexers separate devices with identical addresses.

In Verilog or VHDL, a conditional assignment, if statement or case statement usually synthesizes to a multiplexer. A long if/else-if chain implies priority, giving a series of 2:1 muxes with long delay, while a case statement on mutually exclusive values tends to become a single wide parallel mux, although modern synthesis tools often optimize either form. A common pitfall is leaving some branch without an assignment in combinational logic, which infers a latch to hold the old value instead of a pure mux.

A demultiplexer does the reverse of a multiplexer: it routes one input to one of 2ⁿ outputs chosen by the select bits. A decoder converts an n-bit code into 2ⁿ one-hot lines and is in effect a demultiplexer with its data input held at 1; decoders drive the select logic of large muxes and memory word lines. In communications, multiplexing more generally means sharing one channel among several signals by time, frequency or code.

faq.q: How many select lines does an 8-to-1 multiplexer need?
faq.a: Three, because 2³ = 8. In general a mux with 2ⁿ data inputs needs n select lines.

faq.q: What is the difference between a multiplexer and a demultiplexer?
faq.a: A multiplexer selects one of several inputs and passes it to a single output. A demultiplexer takes a single input and steers it to one of several outputs.

faq.q: How can a multiplexer implement any logic function?
faq.a: Connect the select lines to the function's input variables and tie each data input to 0 or 1 according to the truth table. The mux then outputs the correct table entry for every input combination, which is how FPGA lookup tables work.

デコーダ.desc: A circuit that activates exactly one of 2ⁿ outputs according to an n-bit input. It is used to select the row addressed in a memory. The reverse function is an encoder.

シフトレジスタ.desc: A chain of flip-flops that moves data one bit to the next stage on each clock. It is used for serial-parallel conversion and as the scan chain in scan testing.

全加算器.desc: A circuit that adds two bits plus a carry-in from the lower digit and outputs a sum and a carry-out. A version without carry-in is a half adder. Chaining full adders makes a multi-bit adder.

セットアップ時間.desc: The minimum time before the active clock edge during which a flip-flop's data input must be stable. Paths that cannot meet it limit the maximum operating frequency.

ホールド時間.desc: The minimum time after the active clock edge during which a flip-flop's data input must stay unchanged. Violations are not fixed by lowering the clock frequency, so delay is added to the path.

クロックスキュー.desc: The difference in arrival time of the same clock signal at different flip-flops. Because it changes setup and hold margins, clock tree synthesis keeps it small.

グリッチ.desc: An unwanted momentary pulse on an output, caused for example by differing delays along signal paths. In combinational logic it is also called a hazard; in DACs it appears when the code changes.

トライステートバッファ.desc: A buffer that can output 0, 1 or a disconnected high-impedance state. It prevents output conflicts when several circuits share one bus.

仮想短絡(イマジナリーショート).desc: The property of an ideal op-amp with negative feedback that its two input voltages become nearly equal. Although no current flows between them, they can be treated as shorted, which makes gain calculations simple.

スルーレート.desc: The maximum rate at which an op-amp's output voltage can change, expressed in V/µs. If it is insufficient for large, high-frequency signals, the waveform distorts.

利得帯域幅積(GBW).desc: The product of an op-amp's gain and bandwidth, which stays roughly constant. With a GBW of 1 MHz, for example, a gain-of-10 circuit has a bandwidth of about 100 kHz.

CMRR(同相信号除去比).desc: The ratio of differential gain to common-mode gain in a differential amplifier. The larger it is, the better the circuit rejects noise that appears equally on both inputs.

PSRR(電源電圧変動除去比).desc: A measure of how little supply-voltage variation reaches a circuit's output. The larger it is, the more immune the circuit is to supply noise.

位相余裕(フェーズマージン).desc: How far the phase lag is from 180° at the frequency where the feedback loop gain is 1 (0 dB). A small margin causes ringing, and zero or negative margin causes oscillation; 45-60° or more is a common target.

計装アンプ(インスツルメンテーションアンプ).desc: A differential amplifier, typically built from three op-amps, with high input impedance and high CMRR. It amplifies small differential signals from sensors with high accuracy.

トランスインピーダンスアンプ.desc: An amplifier that converts an input current to a voltage. The current enters the op-amp's inverting input and a feedback resistor turns it into a voltage. It is used to read photodiode signals.

バンドギャップ基準電圧回路.desc: A circuit that adds a diode voltage that falls with temperature to a voltage that rises with temperature, producing a reference of about 1.2 V that barely depends on temperature. It is widely used in ADCs and power ICs.

PLL(位相同期回路).desc: A circuit that detects the phase difference from a reference clock and controls an oscillator to produce a clock locked to the reference, for example at an integer multiple of its frequency. It is used to generate CPU clocks and synthesize radio frequencies.

シュミットトリガ.desc: A circuit whose switching threshold differs for rising and falling inputs (hysteresis). Its output does not chatter even with slowly changing or noisy signals.

1/f雑音(フリッカ雑音).desc: Noise that grows larger at lower frequencies. In MOSFETs it comes from traps at the gate-oxide interface capturing and releasing carriers, and it matters in low-frequency analog circuits.

熱雑音(ジョンソン雑音).desc: Noise caused by the thermal motion of electrons in a resistor. Its mean-square voltage is 4kTRΔf, proportional to temperature, resistance and bandwidth.

LDO.desc: Short for low-dropout regulator: a linear regulator that works with only a small difference between input and output voltage. It is low-noise, but the voltage difference times the current is lost as heat.

コンパレータ.desc: A circuit that compares two input voltages and outputs the result as a binary high or low. It is also a basic building block of ADCs.

時定数.desc: A quantity describing how fast a circuit such as an RC network responds to a step; for an RC circuit τ = RC. The response reaches about 63% of its final value after τ and has nearly settled after about 5τ.

ENOB(有効ビット数).desc: The real performance of an ADC, including noise and distortion (SINAD), expressed as the bit count of an ideal ADC. A 12-bit ADC with an ENOB of around 10 bits is not unusual.

DNL(微分非直線性).desc: The error in each code step width of an ADC relative to the ideal 1 LSB. When it reaches −1 LSB, a missing code occurs.

INL(積分非直線性).desc: The maximum deviation of an ADC's or DAC's actual transfer characteristic from the ideal straight line. It corresponds to the accumulated DNL.

ミッシングコード.desc: A defect in which an ADC never outputs a particular code no matter how the input varies. It occurs when DNL reaches −1 LSB.

フラッシュ型ADC.desc: The fastest type of ADC, which compares the input against many comparators at once. N bits need 2ᴺ − 1 comparators, so the circuit grows rapidly with resolution.

パイプライン型ADC.desc: An ADC that splits conversion into stages, each resolving a few bits and passing the residue to the next, like an assembly line. It combines high speed with medium to high resolution.

サンプルホールド回路.desc: A circuit that captures (samples) the input voltage at an instant and holds it constant until AD conversion finishes. It is built from a switch and a capacitor.

R-2Rラダー型DAC.desc: A DAC built from a ladder of only two resistor values, R and 2R. It needs few resistor types, and the resistor ratio does not grow as bits are added.

オーバーサンプリング.desc: Sampling at a rate well above what the signal requires (twice its bandwidth). It spreads quantization noise over a wider band and reduces noise in the signal band; it is the basis of delta-sigma ADCs.

ノイズシェーピング.desc: A technique that uses a feedback loop to push quantization noise toward high frequencies, lowering noise in the signal band. Delta-sigma ADCs combine it with oversampling to achieve high resolution.

ナイキスト周波数.desc: Half the sampling frequency. Components above it are folded back to lower frequencies when sampled (aliasing).

ジッタ.desc: Small fluctuations in the timing of clock or signal edges from their ideal positions. When sampling high-frequency signals, even slight jitter causes large voltage errors.

プリチャージ.desc: Charging the bit lines to a set potential (half the supply voltage in DRAM, for example) before a read. In DRAM it also means closing the open row to prepare for activating the next one.

ロウハンマー.desc: A DRAM phenomenon in which repeatedly activating the same row in a short time drains charge from cells in neighboring rows and flips their data. Because it can be exploited in attacks, countermeasures are built into DRAMs and memory controllers.

DDR SDRAM.desc: Synchronous DRAM that transfers data on both the rising and falling clock edges. Successive generations such as DDR4 and DDR5 have raised the data rate. It is the standard main memory of PCs and servers.

LPDDR.desc: Short for low-power DDR: a DRAM standard for smartphones and laptops with lower supply voltages and enhanced power-saving features.

CASレイテンシ.desc: The number of clock cycles in DRAM from a read command (specifying the column address) until data appears at the output, abbreviated CL. Smaller values mean a faster response.

バンク.desc: One of several independently operating sections inside a DRAM. Overlapping activation and access across different banks raises effective performance.

ECC(誤り訂正符号).desc: A scheme that adds redundant bits to data so that bit errors can be detected and corrected on readout. It is used in server memory, flash memory and inside DDR5 chips, among others.

冗長救済.desc: Replacing rows or columns that contain defective memory cells with spare rows or columns prepared in advance. The defect locations are found by testing and the switch is made with fuses or similar. It greatly improves yield.

メモリウォール.desc: The problem that memory bandwidth and latency improve more slowly than processor performance, limiting overall performance. HBM, larger caches and advanced packaging are used to address it.

DIMM.desc: A memory module that mounts several DRAM chips on a small board so it can be plugged into a slot in a PC or server.

3D NAND.desc: NAND flash in which memory cells are stacked vertically in many layers to increase capacity. It was introduced to get past the limits of planar scaling, and layer counts now exceed 200.

フローティングゲート.desc: An electrode in a flash memory cell that is completely surrounded by insulator. Storing electrons on it shifts the transistor's threshold voltage, so data is kept even without power.

電荷トラップ型セル.desc: A flash memory cell that stores electrons in traps within an insulating film such as silicon nitride instead of in a floating gate. It is mainly used in 3D NAND.

FNトンネル電流(ファウラー・ノルドハイム).desc: Current that flows when a strong electric field lets electrons tunnel through the triangular barrier of a thin insulator. It is used to program and erase NAND flash.

ガベージコレクション.desc: In an SSD, moving the still-valid data out of blocks that contain invalid data and then erasing those blocks to create free space.

TRIM.desc: A command by which the operating system tells an SSD which areas belong to deleted files. Knowing which data is no longer needed makes garbage collection more efficient.

リードディスターブ.desc: In NAND flash, the gradual shift in threshold voltage of unread cells caused by the weak voltage applied to them when the same block is read many times.

書き込み増幅(ライトアンプリフィケーション).desc: The amount of data actually written to flash exceeding what the host wrote, because of garbage collection and similar operations. The larger it is, the shorter the SSD's life.

SLC(シングルレベルセル).desc: A flash format that stores one bit per cell. With only two threshold-voltage states it is faster and more durable than multi-level formats.

TLC(トリプルレベルセル).desc: A flash format that stores three bits per cell, distinguishing eight threshold-voltage states. It lowers cost per bit but reduces endurance. Four bits per cell is QLC.

NVMe.desc: An interface standard for fast access to SSDs connected over PCI Express. It processes many commands in parallel and has lower latency than SATA, which was designed for HDDs.

about.h: Why SSDs needed a new interface
about.p: SATA SSDs use AHCI, a host interface designed for hard disks: one command queue holding up to 32 commands, behind a link that tops out around 600 MB/s. Flash memory can service many requests in parallel, so this became the bottleneck. NVMe (NVM Express) is a protocol designed for non-volatile memory attached directly to PCI Express. It supports up to 64K I/O queues, each up to 64K commands deep, uses a compact command set, and lets each CPU core own its own queues, cutting software overhead and lock contention.

NVMe queues are rings in host memory. To issue a read or write, the driver places a 64-byte command in a submission queue and writes the new tail position to a doorbell register on the device. The controller fetches commands by DMA, moves the data directly to or from host memory, and writes a 16-byte entry to the paired completion queue, typically signaling the host with an MSI-X interrupt. The host then updates the completion queue's head doorbell. Host and device advance independently, so many transfers are in flight at once.

Because NVMe rides on PCIe, its bandwidth follows the link generation and lane count: about 7 GB/s for PCIe 4.0 x4 drives and over 10 GB/s with PCIe 5.0 x4. Protocol latency is a few microseconds, small compared with flash read times of tens of microseconds. NVMe drives come as compact M.2 cards, 2.5-inch U.2 drives and add-in cards. Note that M.2 is only a connector: an M.2 slot may carry SATA or PCIe, so an M.2 SSD is not necessarily NVMe. NVMe over Fabrics extends the protocol across networks.

Besides reads and writes, NVMe defines administrative commands for creating queues, identifying the controller, managing namespaces and updating firmware. The Deallocate operation, part of the Dataset Management command, is the NVMe equivalent of ATA TRIM: it tells the SSD which logical blocks no longer hold useful data, so garbage collection can erase them without copying. This reduces write amplification, which improves sustained write performance and extends flash endurance.

faq.q: What does NVMe stand for?
faq.a: NVMe stands for Non-Volatile Memory Express, also written NVM Express. It is a host interface and command protocol for accessing SSDs and other non-volatile memory over PCI Express.

faq.q: What is the difference between an NVMe SSD and a SATA SSD?
faq.a: A SATA SSD uses the AHCI protocol with a single 32-command queue and a link limited to about 600 MB/s. An NVMe SSD connects over PCIe with thousands of parallel queues, giving several to more than ten gigabytes per second and lower software latency.

faq.q: Does NVMe support TRIM?
faq.a: Yes. NVMe provides the same function through the Deallocate attribute of the Dataset Management command, which operating systems issue when files are deleted.

STT-MRAM.desc: MRAM that writes by flipping the magnetization of the MTJ's free layer using the spin-transfer torque of a spin-polarized current. It is in volume production as embedded non-volatile memory.

SOT-MRAM.desc: MRAM that flips magnetization by spin-orbit torque from a current in a heavy-metal layer. The write and read current paths are separate, giving fast, durable writes.

カルコゲナイド.desc: A compound containing group 16 elements such as sulfur, selenium or tellurium. It is used as the recording material of phase-change memory (such as GST) and in selectors (OTS) that switch on abruptly above a threshold voltage.

フォーミング.desc: An initialization step for ReRAM in which a relatively high voltage is first applied after fabrication to create the conductive filament that later switches resistance.

クロスポイント型メモリ.desc: Memory with a storage element at each intersection of row and column lines. It is very dense, but a selector is placed in series with each element to stop current sneaking through unselected cells.

ストレージクラスメモリ.desc: Non-volatile memory intended to bridge the gap in speed, capacity and cost between DRAM and NAND flash. Products based on 3D XPoint were the best-known example.

3D XPoint.desc: Cross-point non-volatile memory jointly developed by Intel and Micron. It stacked phase-change material with OTS selectors and was sold as Optane, but the business was wound down in 2022.

FeFET(強誘電体トランジスタ).desc: A transistor with a ferroelectric gate insulator. Its threshold voltage depends on the polarization direction, so a single transistor can store data non-volatilely and be read non-destructively.

TMR比.desc: In an MTJ, the difference between the resistances in the parallel and antiparallel states divided by the parallel-state resistance. The larger it is, the easier it is to tell 0 from 1; MgO barriers give large values.

インメモリコンピューティング.desc: Performing computations such as multiply-accumulate inside the memory array to cut data movement between memory and processor. Research is under way on using resistive elements and the like for AI inference.

スーパースカラ.desc: A processor design that issues and executes several instructions per clock cycle. It has multiple execution units and processes independent instructions in parallel.

アウトオブオーダー実行.desc: Executing instructions as soon as their dependencies allow, in a different order from the program, to improve performance. Results are committed in program order through a reorder buffer.

TLB(変換索引バッファ).desc: A small cache that holds recent virtual-to-physical address translations. It avoids walking the page tables in memory on every access, speeding up address translation.

SIMD.desc: Short for single instruction, multiple data: one instruction performs the same operation on several data elements at once. It speeds up image processing and AI calculations.

DMA(ダイレクトメモリアクセス).desc: A mechanism that transfers data directly between peripherals and memory without going through the CPU, so the CPU can do other work during large transfers.

割り込み.desc: A CPU mechanism that temporarily suspends the current task to handle a request, for example from an external device, and then returns to the original task.

about.h: What happens when an interrupt is taken
about.p: When a device, timer or other source raises an interrupt and it is enabled, the CPU saves the address of the next instruction together with state such as the privilege mode and interrupt-enable bit in dedicated registers. It obtains a vector number for the cause, reads the handler's start address from the interrupt vector table set up by the OS, and jumps there. The handler saves the registers it uses, services the device, clears the interrupt source, restores state, and returns with a special instruction such as RISC-V mret or sret, which restores the mode and return address atomically.

Interrupts are asynchronous: a timer tick or network packet arrives regardless of which instruction is running. Exceptions such as page faults, division by zero or a deliberate system call (RISC-V ecall) are synchronous, caused by a specific instruction. Polling, in which the CPU repeatedly reads device status, is the alternative to interrupts. Interrupts are better when events are rare or the CPU should sleep, but each costs state saving and a jump, so at very high event rates, as in fast networking, batched polling can be more efficient.

An interrupt controller arbitrates simultaneous requests, often with a priority encoder, and with nesting a higher-priority interrupt can preempt a lower-priority handler, as in the Arm Cortex-M NVIC. Software can mask interrupts, but a non-maskable interrupt (NMI) is reserved for serious events such as uncorrectable memory errors or watchdog timeouts. Worst-case interrupt latency is set mostly by the longest section that runs with interrupts disabled, so operating systems split handling into a short urgent part and deferred work done later with interrupts enabled. PCI Express devices signal interrupts by memory writes (MSI) instead of dedicated wires.

Handlers should be short: no printf or waiting loops, just moving data to a buffer or setting a flag for the main loop. Variables shared with a handler must be declared volatile, or the compiler may read them only once. Read-modify-write updates like reg |= mask can lose a bit changed by a handler in between, and an 8-bit microcontroller reading a 32-bit counter can see half-updated bytes; disabling interrupts briefly fixes both. A periodic timer interrupt, for example 16 MHz divided by 16 counting to 1000 for 1 ms, provides the system tick.

faq.q: What is the difference between an interrupt and an exception?
faq.a: An interrupt is asynchronous and comes from outside the instruction stream, such as a timer or I/O device. An exception is synchronous, triggered by executing a particular instruction, such as a page fault, illegal instruction or system call.

faq.q: What is an interrupt vector table?
faq.a: It is a table, set up by the OS or firmware, that maps each interrupt or exception number to the start address of its handler. The CPU uses it to jump to the right routine for each cause.

faq.q: Why should an interrupt handler be kept short?
faq.a: While a handler runs, interrupts of the same or lower priority are usually held off and the main program is stalled, so a long handler increases latency for everything else. Heavy work is deferred to a task or main loop that runs with interrupts enabled.

キャッシュコヒーレンシ.desc: In a multicore CPU, the mechanism that keeps copies of the same address in different cores' caches consistent, for example by invalidating other copies when one core writes.

DVFS(動的電圧・周波数制御).desc: Changing operating frequency and supply voltage dynamically according to load. Since dynamic power scales with the square of voltage, lowering voltage during light loads saves a lot of power.

TDP(熱設計電力).desc: A guide to the heat a CPU or similar chip generates under a typical heavy load. Cooling systems are designed around it.

IPC.desc: Short for instructions per cycle: the number of instructions executed per clock. It expresses design efficiency; performance is roughly IPC times clock frequency. Its reciprocal is CPI.

アムダールの法則.desc: The law that when only part of a program is parallelized, overall speedup is limited by the part that cannot be. For example, parallelizing 90% gives at most a 10x speedup.

仮想記憶.desc: A system in which the OS and hardware map the addresses a program uses (virtual addresses) to physical memory addresses. Each program gets a large, independent address space.

GPU.desc: Short for graphics processing unit: a processor with many simple execution units that processes large amounts of data in parallel. Besides graphics, it is widely used for AI training and inference.

NPU(ニューラルプロセッシングユニット).desc: A dedicated circuit for running neural-network inference quickly and at low power. It is built into the SoCs of smartphones and PCs.

マイコン(マイクロコントローラ).desc: A small computer that integrates a CPU, memory and peripherals such as timers and ADCs on one chip. It is embedded in appliances, cars and other equipment to control them. Also called an MCU.

SMT(同時マルチスレッディング).desc: A technique in which one CPU core processes instructions from several threads at once, making better use of its execution units. Intel calls it Hyper-Threading.

about.p: A modern out-of-order core can issue several instructions per cycle, but a single thread rarely keeps all its execution units busy because of dependencies, branch mispredictions and cache misses. Simultaneous multithreading (SMT) gives the core a separate architectural state, such as program counter and architectural registers, for each hardware thread, while the threads share execution units, caches, branch predictors and internal buffers. In the same cycle, instructions from different threads can be issued to different units. The operating system sees each hardware thread as a logical processor, typically two per core.

Because the threads compete for the same execution resources, SMT does not double performance the way a second core can. Typical gains range from about 0 to 30 percent. Workloads that stall often, such as those waiting on memory, benefit most: while one thread waits for a cache miss, the other keeps the units busy. Workloads that already saturate the floating-point units or memory bandwidth gain little, and contention in shared caches can even make individual threads slower, which matters for latency-sensitive applications.

about.h: SMT versus other kinds of multithreading
about.p: Coarse-grained multithreading switches to another thread only on a long stall such as a cache miss. Fine-grained multithreading interleaves threads cycle by cycle but issues from only one thread per cycle, an approach common in GPUs and some network processors. SMT goes further by issuing from multiple threads in the same cycle, which suits wide superscalar cores. Multicore, by contrast, duplicates the entire core. Intel brands its two-way SMT as Hyper-Threading, and some server processors support four or eight threads per core.

Two SMT threads share the L1 caches, branch predictor, execution ports and buffers at very fine granularity, so one thread can infer what the other is doing by measuring its own timing. Several side-channel vulnerabilities depend on exactly this arrangement. Systems that run untrusted code from different customers on the same hardware therefore may disable SMT or use core scheduling, which only places threads from the same trust domain on sibling logical processors. Both reduce throughput, so the decision weighs performance against isolation.

faq.q: Is Hyper-Threading the same as SMT?
faq.a: Yes. Hyper-Threading is Intel's brand name for its implementation of simultaneous multithreading, in which each physical core appears to the operating system as two logical processors.

faq.q: Does SMT double CPU performance?
faq.a: No. The two threads share one core's execution units and caches, so typical throughput gains are about 0 to 30 percent depending on the workload, far less than adding a second core.

faq.q: Why do some systems disable SMT?
faq.a: Threads on the same core share caches and execution resources closely enough for one to observe the other through timing side channels. Disabling SMT, or scheduling only mutually trusted threads together, removes that exposure at some cost in throughput.

シストリックアレイ.desc: An arrangement of many multiply-accumulate units in a grid that computes matrix products by passing data to neighboring units step by step. It is used in AI accelerators.

スーパージャンクションMOSFET.desc: A power MOSFET whose drift layer has alternating p-type and n-type pillars. It allows higher drift-layer doping without losing breakdown voltage, achieving on-resistance below the conventional silicon limit.

ボディダイオード.desc: A parasitic diode formed between source and drain by the structure of a power MOSFET. It can serve as the freewheeling diode in an inverter, but its reverse recovery needs attention.

ゲートドライバ.desc: A circuit that receives control signals and drives a power device's gate with the right voltage and enough current. Many include isolation or level shifting to drive high-side switches.

ノーマリーオフ.desc: The property of passing no current when the gate voltage is 0 V. It is required of power devices for safety, since current stops even if the drive circuit fails.

DC-DCコンバータ.desc: A circuit that converts one DC voltage into another. Using switches, inductors and capacitors, buck types lower the voltage and boost types raise it.

デッドタイム.desc: A short interval during which both the upper and lower switches of an inverter are off while switching between them. It prevents both from being on at once and shorting the supply.

スナバ回路.desc: A network such as a resistor and capacitor placed across a power device to suppress the voltage spikes (surges) and ringing that occur during switching.

テール電流.desc: Current that keeps flowing like a tail as an IGBT turns off, because stored minority carriers prevent it from dropping to zero immediately. It causes turn-off loss.

短絡耐量.desc: The time a power device can survive a short circuit, such as both inverter switches turning on at once, without being destroyed. Protection circuits must cut the current within this time.

ソフトスイッチング.desc: Turning a switch on or off when the voltage across it or current through it is nearly zero, as in zero-voltage switching (ZVS). It reduces switching loss and noise.

GaAs(ガリウムヒ素).desc: A III-V compound semiconductor of gallium and arsenic with a direct band gap of about 1.42 eV. Its high electron mobility makes it useful for high-frequency transistors and infrared LEDs and lasers.

InP(リン化インジウム).desc: A compound semiconductor of indium and phosphorus. As a substrate for lattice-matched layers such as InGaAs, it is used for fiber-optic lasers and photodetectors and for high-speed transistors.

Ga2O3(酸化ガリウム).desc: An oxide semiconductor with a band gap of about 4.5-4.9 eV, even wider than SiC or GaN. Its crystals can be grown from the melt, and it is being researched as a next-generation power semiconductor material.

混晶半導体.desc: A semiconductor crystal that mixes several elements, such as AlGaAs or InGaN. Changing the composition tunes the band gap and lattice constant continuously.

量子井戸.desc: A structure in which a thin layer, a few nanometers thick, with a small band gap is sandwiched between layers with a larger band gap. It confines carriers to promote recombination and is used as the active layer of LEDs and lasers.

VCSEL(垂直共振器面発光レーザー).desc: A semiconductor laser that emits light perpendicular to the substrate. It can be tested on the wafer and easily arranged in 2D arrays, so it is used in data links and as the light source for face recognition.

2次元電子ガス(2DEG).desc: A dense sheet of electrons confined at a heterojunction interface such as AlGaN/GaN. With little impurity scattering and high mobility, it serves as the channel of a HEMT.

MMIC.desc: Short for monolithic microwave integrated circuit: a high-frequency IC that integrates transistors together with passive components such as inductors and capacitors on a substrate such as GaAs.

ベガード則.desc: The empirical rule that the lattice constant of an alloy varies almost linearly with composition. It is used to find the composition that lattice-matches a given substrate.

効率ドループ.desc: The drop in luminous efficiency of InGaN LEDs as current increases. Auger recombination is thought to be one cause.

ウルツ鉱型構造.desc: The hexagonal crystal structure of GaN, ZnO and others. It has polarization along certain crystal directions, which creates the 2DEG in GaN HEMTs.

CCDイメージセンサ.desc: An image sensor that shifts pixel charges along like a bucket brigade and converts them to voltage at an output stage. It offered low noise and high image quality but used more power, and CMOS sensors have replaced it in most uses.

ベイヤー配列.desc: A color filter arrangement of red, green, green and blue over each 2×2 block of pixels, with two greens because the eye is most sensitive to green. Missing colors at each pixel are interpolated from neighbors (demosaicing).

マイクロレンズ.desc: A tiny lens placed over each pixel of an image sensor. It gathers light and directs it efficiently onto the photodiode, raising sensitivity.

ローリングシャッター.desc: A readout method that exposes and reads pixel rows one after another. It is simple, but fast-moving subjects appear skewed. Exposing all pixels at once is a global shutter.

暗電流.desc: Current that flows in a photodiode even without light, caused for example by thermal generation of carriers. It rises with temperature and appears as noise in dark images.

相関二重サンプリング(CDS).desc: Taking the difference between a pixel's voltage just after reset and its voltage when the signal is read. It removes reset noise and per-pixel offsets.

埋め込みフォトダイオード(ピンドフォトダイオード).desc: A photodiode with a heavily doped p+ layer at the surface that keeps the collection region away from the interface. It suppresses dark current from interface states and allows complete charge transfer; it is standard in CMOS image sensors.

固定パターンノイズ.desc: Noise that appears in the same place every time, caused by variations between pixels or readout circuits. It is removed by correlated double sampling or calibration.

ショットノイズ.desc: Noise from statistical fluctuation in the number of photons or electrons. Its size is proportional to √N for a signal of N electrons, so it is relatively larger when light is scarce.

飽和電子数(フルウェル容量).desc: The maximum number of electrons one image-sensor pixel can hold. The larger it is, the brighter the scene can be before highlights clip, widening dynamic range.

ToF(Time of Flight).desc: Measuring distance from the time light takes to travel to an object and back. ToF sensors are used in face recognition, robotics and automotive LiDAR.

SPAD(単一光子アバランシェダイオード).desc: A photodetector biased above breakdown so that even a single photon triggers a large avalanche pulse. It is used for ranging, such as in LiDAR.

積層型CMOSイメージセンサ.desc: An image sensor whose pixel array and signal-processing circuitry are made on separate chips and bonded together. Each can use the most suitable process, making the chip smaller and processing faster.

インゴット.desc: A cylindrical single-crystal block grown by the CZ method or similar, before it is cut into wafers. The ends are removed and the outside is ground to a uniform diameter before slicing.

SOIウエハ.desc: A wafer with a thin silicon layer on a buried oxide (BOX) layer over a silicon substrate. It is made, for example, by bonding a hydrogen-implanted wafer and splitting it. Its low parasitic capacitance suits FD-SOI devices and MEMS.

シーメンス法.desc: A method that reduces trichlorosilane with hydrogen to deposit high-purity polycrystalline silicon on heated silicon rods. It is the main way to make raw silicon for semiconductors.

偏析係数.desc: The ratio of impurity concentration in the crystal to that in the melt during solidification. For most impurities it is below 1, so they concentrate in the melt and the later part of a CZ crystal has higher impurity levels.

ネッキング.desc: Growing a thin neck just after the seed at the start of CZ pulling. It lets dislocations created by thermal shock when the seed touches the melt escape, giving a dislocation-free crystal.

MCZ法(磁場印加CZ法).desc: A CZ variant that applies a magnetic field to the crucible to suppress melt convection. It makes the oxygen concentration in the crystal easier to control and is used for large-diameter crystals.

酸素析出物(BMD).desc: Tiny defects formed inside a CZ silicon wafer when its oxygen precipitates during heat treatment. Also called BMDs (bulk micro defects), they serve as gettering sites that capture metal impurities.

DZ(無欠陥層).desc: A layer near the wafer surface with few defects such as oxygen precipitates, made by out-diffusing oxygen during heat treatment. Devices are built in this layer while precipitates deeper inside provide gettering.

スリップ.desc: A defect in which crystal planes shift and dislocations form under stress from temperature differences or the wafer's own weight during high-temperature processing of large wafers. It can cause problems such as overlay errors.

サーマルドナー.desc: Oxygen clusters that act as donors when CZ silicon is heated around 450°C. Because they change the wafer's resistivity, they are annihilated by a higher-temperature treatment.

モニターウエハ.desc: A wafer run through a process separately from products to check equipment or measure film thickness and particles. Also called a test wafer, it is often stripped, repolished and reused as a reclaimed wafer.

Deal-Groveモデル.desc: A model of thermal oxidation in which the oxidant diffuses through the oxide and reacts with silicon at the Si/SiO2 interface. Thickness grows linearly with time for thin oxides and with the square root of time for thick ones.

STI(シャロートレンチ分離).desc: Isolating devices by etching shallow trenches in silicon, filling them with insulator and planarizing by CMP. It has no bird's beak like LOCOS and is the standard isolation for fine-pitch ICs.

about.p: A thin pad oxide and a silicon nitride layer are deposited, then lithography and etching open trenches about 200 to 300 nm deep into the silicon. A thin liner oxide is grown, often by thermal or ISSG oxidation, to repair etch damage and round the trench corners. The trench is filled with CVD oxide and annealed to densify it. Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) removes the excess oxide and stops on the nitride, often using ceria slurries with oxide-to-nitride selectivity of tens to over 100. Finally the nitride is stripped in hot phosphoric acid at about 160 °C.

In local oxidation of silicon (LOCOS), nitride masks the active areas while exposed silicon is thermally oxidized, but oxidant diffuses sideways under the nitride edge and grows a bird's beak that can encroach about half the oxide thickness on each side. That eats into active area, limits how close devices can be placed and leaves surface steps. STI isolates with an etched and filled trench, so the surface stays flat and isolation width is set by lithography. It replaced LOCOS around the 0.25 µm generation and is used today to isolate FinFET fins as well.

Ordinary CVD tends to pinch off at the trench opening and trap a void. From about the 0.25 µm to 65 nm generations, high-density plasma CVD filled STI by sputtering the corners while depositing; narrower trenches, down to around 10 nm, use flowable CVD or spin-on dielectrics that fill from the bottom and are then converted to oxide. Corners matter as well: a sharp top corner concentrates the gate field and creates a parasitic edge transistor, and an oxide divot from later wet cleans makes this worse, so corner rounding and recess control are tuned carefully.

The oxide in STI trenches stresses the neighboring silicon, and the amount depends on how far a transistor sits from the trench edge, so drive current can vary with active-area size and layout. Circuit models and design rules account for this. Trench etch must also avoid microtrenching at the bottom corners, which can create later filling or field concentration problems. In FinFET flows, the STI oxide is recessed after CMP to expose the upper part of each fin, and the recess depth sets the active fin height.

faq.q: What is the difference between STI and LOCOS?
faq.a: LOCOS grows thick thermal oxide in unmasked regions and suffers bird's-beak encroachment and surface steps. STI etches trenches, fills them with oxide and planarizes by CMP, giving flat surfaces and much narrower isolation.

faq.q: Why is it called shallow trench isolation?
faq.a: Its trenches are only a few hundred nanometers deep, shallow compared with the deep trench isolation, several micrometers deep, used in some bipolar, power, image sensor and older DRAM technologies.

faq.q: Why is ceria slurry used in STI CMP?
faq.a: Ceria removes silicon oxide efficiently, and with suitable additives it barely polishes silicon nitride. The high oxide-to-nitride selectivity lets polishing stop reliably on the nitride layer.

バーズビーク.desc: In LOCOS, the beak-shaped encroachment of oxide under the edge of the nitride mask. Because it wastes active area, it led to the switch to STI at finer geometries.

フォーミングガスアニール.desc: Heat treatment in a mixture of hydrogen and nitrogen (forming gas). Hydrogen terminates dangling bonds at the Si/SiO2 interface, reducing interface states.

界面準位.desc: Energy levels within the band gap at a semiconductor-insulator interface, created by broken bonds and similar defects. They trap and release carriers, causing threshold shifts, lower mobility and noise.

RTP(急速熱処理).desc: Heating single wafers to high temperature for a few seconds, typically with lamps. It allows annealing and thin oxide growth while limiting unwanted dopant diffusion.

可動イオン.desc: Ions such as sodium and potassium that can move within the gate oxide. They drift with field and temperature and shift the threshold voltage. Because they can come from sources such as human sweat, they are tightly controlled.

ドライブイン.desc: In thermal diffusion, the high-temperature step after a fixed amount of dopant has been introduced at the surface (predeposition), which pushes the dopant deeper.

酸化増速拡散(OED).desc: Faster diffusion of boron and phosphorus during oxidation than without it, caused by silicon interstitials injected into the silicon by the oxidation.

酸窒化膜(SiON).desc: Gate oxide with nitrogen incorporated. It blocks boron penetration from the gate electrode and has a slightly higher permittivity, so it was used as the gate insulator before high-k films.

過渡増速拡散(TED).desc: A temporary speed-up of boron and other dopant diffusion early in post-implant annealing, caused by excess silicon interstitials from the implant. It hinders the formation of shallow junctions.

プリアモルファス化注入(PAI).desc: Implanting germanium or similar first to make the surface amorphous, so that the following implant does not channel and a shallow junction results.

ハロー注入(ポケット注入).desc: Angled implantation of dopant of the same type as the channel near the source and drain edges. It limits the spread of the drain depletion region and suppresses short-channel effects.

レトログレードウェル.desc: A well whose doping is higher deeper below the surface, made by high-energy implantation. It suppresses punch-through and latch-up while keeping the channel doping at the surface low.

固溶度.desc: The maximum concentration of an impurity that can dissolve in a crystal at a given temperature. It sets the upper limit of electrically active dopant concentration.

スパイクアニール.desc: An anneal that ramps the wafer quickly to a high temperature and cools it again with almost no hold time. It activates dopants while limiting diffusion, for shallow junctions.

レーザーアニール.desc: Heating only the near-surface region of a wafer for an extremely short time with laser light. It achieves high activation with almost no diffusion.

ファラデーカップ.desc: A device that collects an ion beam and measures the resulting current. In ion implanters it is used to determine the implanted dose.

プラズマドーピング.desc: Implanting low-energy ions by exposing the wafer directly to a plasma containing the dopant. It delivers high doses quickly and dopes 3D structures such as fins fairly uniformly.

シャドウイング.desc: When implanting at a tilt, the effect of tall patterns such as resist casting shadows so that some areas receive no implant.

LPCVD(減圧CVD).desc: Thermal CVD performed under reduced pressure. Faster gas diffusion gives good thickness uniformity and step coverage, and many wafers can be processed at once in a vertical furnace. It is used for polysilicon and nitride films.

TEOS.desc: Short for tetraethoxysilane, a liquid organosilicon compound widely used as the source for CVD silicon oxide. It gives oxide films with good step coverage.

電解めっき.desc: Depositing metal by passing current through a plating bath with the wafer as the cathode. It fills copper interconnect trenches, with additives making the fill proceed from the bottom up.

マグネトロンスパッタリング.desc: Sputtering with magnets behind the target that trap electrons near it and raise plasma density. It increases deposition rate and is the mainstream sputtering method today.

反応性スパッタリング.desc: Sputtering a metal target in an atmosphere containing a reactive gas such as nitrogen or oxygen to form nitride or oxide films. It is used for films such as titanium nitride (TiN).

真空蒸着.desc: Forming a film by heating a material in vacuum until it evaporates and condenses on the substrate. Electron-beam heating handles high-melting-point materials, but step coverage is poor.

HDP-CVD(高密度プラズマCVD).desc: CVD using a high-density plasma that deposits while ion sputtering trims film at the trench openings. It has been used to fill narrow trenches with insulator without voids.

静電チャック.desc: A mechanism that holds the wafer to its stage by electrostatic force. It works in vacuum and allows backside gas for temperature control; it is widely used in deposition and etch tools.

スピンコート.desc: Dispensing a liquid at the center of the wafer and spinning it at high speed so centrifugal force spreads a thin, uniform film. It is used for photoresist and spin-on dielectrics.

領域選択成膜.desc: Growing a film only in certain places by exploiting differences in the underlying materials. Because it can save lithography and etch steps, it is being researched and introduced for advanced interconnects.

ArFエキシマレーザー.desc: A laser using argon and fluorine that emits 193 nm ultraviolet light. Combined with immersion, ArF immersion lithography is a leading-edge technique alongside EUV. The 248 nm version is the KrF excimer laser.

about.h: How an ArF laser produces 193 nm light
about.p: The laser chamber holds a gas mixture of a small amount of argon and fluorine diluted in neon as a buffer gas. A fast electrical discharge excites the mixture and forms ArF molecules that are bound only in the excited state, an excimer or excited dimer. When the molecule emits a 193 nm photon it drops to a repulsive ground state and immediately falls apart, so the lower laser level is effectively always empty and population inversion is easy to achieve. The laser is pulsed, with lithography lasers running at repetition rates of several kHz.

about.h: Why lithography needs a narrow line
about.p: Few materials are transparent at 193 nm, so projection lenses are built from fused silica with some calcium fluoride elements. With so little choice of glass, chromatic aberration cannot be corrected the way it is in visible optics, and the laser output must instead be line-narrowed to a bandwidth of well under a picometer. Lithography lasers also stabilize pulse energy and wavelength from pulse to pulse, and the fluorine-based gas fill degrades over time and is periodically refreshed. Photoresists had to change as well, because phenolic KrF resists absorb too strongly at 193 nm.

Resolution follows the Rayleigh relation R = k1·λ/NA. Dry ArF scanners reach a numerical aperture (NA) of about 0.93. ArF immersion fills the gap between the final lens and the wafer with water, whose refractive index at 193 nm is about 1.44, allowing NA up to 1.35. With k1 near its practical limit, single exposures resolve roughly 38 to 40 nm half-pitch. Smaller pitches are made with multiple patterning, such as litho-etch-litho-etch or self-aligned double and quadruple patterning, which is how ArF immersion reached nodes far below its single-exposure limit.

The KrF excimer laser uses krypton and fluorine to emit 248 nm and serves less critical layers where cost matters more than resolution. EUV lithography at 13.5 nm does not use an excimer laser at all: its light comes from a tin plasma, and its optics are reflective mirrors. Even in leading-edge chips patterned with EUV for the tightest layers, many other layers are still exposed with ArF immersion, which has higher throughput and a mature infrastructure.

faq.q: What wavelength does an ArF excimer laser emit?
faq.a: It emits deep-ultraviolet light at 193 nm. The KrF excimer laser, the previous lithography generation, emits at 248 nm.

faq.q: What is the difference between dry ArF and ArF immersion lithography?
faq.a: Dry ArF has air between the lens and the wafer, limiting the numerical aperture to about 0.93. Immersion fills that gap with water, raising NA to about 1.35 so that features roughly 30 percent smaller can be resolved at the same wavelength.

faq.q: Why is it called an excimer laser?
faq.a: Excimer is short for excited dimer, a molecule such as ArF that is bound only in its excited state. Because it dissociates as soon as it emits, the lower laser level stays empty, making efficient ultraviolet lasing possible.

化学増幅型レジスト.desc: A resist in which acid generated by exposure catalyzes a chain of reactions during the post-exposure bake (PEB). It needs little exposure dose and is widely used from KrF onward, but is sensitive to basic contamination.

ポジ型フォトレジスト.desc: A photoresist whose exposed areas dissolve and are removed during development. One whose exposed areas remain is a negative resist.

位相シフトマスク.desc: A photomask that shifts the phase of light passing through neighboring openings, using interference to improve image contrast and resolution.

マルチパターニング.desc: Forming patterns with a pitch too fine for a single exposure by splitting them across several exposures or process steps. Splitting into two is double patterning.

ペリクル.desc: A thin membrane stretched a short distance above a photomask. It keeps particles off the mask surface, and particles landing on the pellicle are out of focus and do not print.

about.p: A photomask, or reticle, is imaged onto every exposure field of every wafer it prints. A single particle on its patterned surface therefore becomes a repeating defect that can kill the same die location across thousands of wafers. Masks are expensive, and cleaning them repeatedly risks damaging the pattern. The pellicle solves this by keeping particles off the patterned surface entirely, so that contamination arriving during handling, storage and exposure lands somewhere harmless.

The pellicle is a thin transparent membrane, under 1 µm thick for deep-ultraviolet tools, stretched on a frame about 6 mm from the patterned surface. The projection lens is focused on the pattern, and its depth of focus at the mask side is a tiny fraction of a millimeter. A particle on the pellicle is therefore millimeters out of focus; its image is so blurred that it only slightly dims a wide area instead of printing as a sharp defect. The membrane must transmit the exposure light with minimal loss and stay stable under prolonged irradiation.

Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light at 13.5 nm is strongly absorbed by every material, so an EUV pellicle must be only tens of nanometers thick, made from materials such as polysilicon or carbon nanotube films, and still transmits only around 90% per pass. Because EUV masks are reflective, light crosses the pellicle twice, compounding the loss. The membrane also absorbs part of the high source power and heats up, so it must survive high temperatures while remaining mechanically intact across the full mask area.

The pellicle protects the mask, not the wafer. In ArF immersion lithography, a topcoat over the photoresist keeps immersion water from leaching resist components, and a bottom antireflective coating (BARC) under the resist controls reflections; neither has anything to do with mask contamination. A pellicle also cannot fix defects already present in the mask pattern or particles trapped under it during mounting, so masks are inspected before the pellicle is attached.

faq.q: What is a pellicle in lithography?
faq.a: A pellicle is a thin transparent membrane mounted on a frame a few millimeters above a photomask's pattern. Particles land on the membrane instead of the mask, where they are out of focus and do not print.

faq.q: Why is an EUV pellicle hard to make?
faq.a: All materials absorb EUV strongly, so the membrane must be only tens of nanometers thick yet span the whole mask, survive heating from absorbed power, and still transmit around 90% of the light on each pass.

faq.q: Does a pellicle prevent all mask defects?
faq.a: No. It only keeps new particles off the patterned surface after mounting; pattern defects, or particles trapped underneath when the pellicle is attached, still print.

フォトマスク(レチクル).desc: The master pattern used for exposure, typically a light-blocking pattern on a quartz substrate (reflective for EUV). For reduction scanners it is made four times larger than the pattern on the wafer.

about.p: Mask making starts from a mask blank: a low-defect, very flat quartz plate 6 inches square and about 6 mm thick, coated with a chromium or MoSi absorber film and resist. An electron-beam writer exposes the pattern directly into the resist. Single-beam writers can take over ten hours for a complex mask, so advanced masks with heavy optical proximity correction (OPC) or curvilinear shapes use multi-beam writers with hundreds of thousands of beamlets. After development and etching, the mask is measured, inspected for defects, repaired where possible and fitted with a pellicle.

Scanners project the mask through reduction optics, so mask features are four times larger than on the wafer, which makes them easier to write and makes small mask errors shrink on the wafer. One exposure covers a field of about 26 mm by 33 mm, roughly 858 mm², on the wafer. This reticle limit caps the size of a single die, which is why very large processors approach it and why larger systems use chiplets. Silicon interposers bigger than one field are made by stitching wiring across adjacent exposures. High-NA EUV fields are half the standard size.

A binary mask simply blocks light with chromium. An attenuated phase-shift mask uses a partially transmitting MoSi film that also shifts the light phase by 180 degrees, sharpening the image at feature edges. Because EUV light at 13.5 nm is absorbed by almost every material, EUV masks are reflective: a multilayer stack of molybdenum and silicon acts as a mirror, and a patterned absorber on top defines dark regions. EUV blanks must be nearly free of defects, since a buried flaw in the multilayer cannot be removed later.

Any defect on a mask prints in every field of every wafer exposed with it, appearing on wafer maps as a failure at the same position in each shot. A pellicle, a transparent membrane under 1 µm thick stretched on a frame about 6 mm above the patterned surface, keeps particles away from the focal plane so they are blurred and do not print. EUV pellicles must be only tens of nanometers thick, made of materials such as polysilicon or carbon nanotubes, to transmit around 90 percent of the light and survive heating.

faq.q: What is the difference between a photomask and a reticle?
faq.a: Historically a photomask carried the pattern for an entire wafer at 1:1, while a reticle carried one or a few dies for a stepper that repeats it across the wafer. Today the terms are used almost interchangeably for the master plate used in scanners.

faq.q: Why are photomask patterns four times larger than on the wafer?
faq.a: Scanners use 4x reduction projection optics. Larger features are easier to write and inspect on the mask, and errors in mask dimensions are reduced by the same factor when printed.

faq.q: What is a pellicle on a photomask?
faq.a: It is a thin transparent membrane mounted a few millimeters above the mask pattern. Particles that land on it are out of focus during exposure and therefore do not print on the wafer.

スキャナー.desc: An exposure tool that moves the mask and wafer in sync under a slit of light. It is the mainstream production lithography tool and generally projects the mask pattern at 1/4 size.

焦点深度(DOF).desc: The range of focus over which a pattern prints with acceptable quality. Raising the numerical aperture improves resolution but reduces DOF, which makes wafer planarity important.

オーバーレイ(重ね合わせ精度).desc: How accurately a new pattern is placed relative to the patterns made in earlier steps. Misalignment causes defects such as missed contacts, so it is controlled at the nanometer level.

ラインエッジラフネス(LER).desc: Nanometer-scale roughness along the edges of fine resist lines. It causes line-width variation (LWR) and leads to variation in transistor characteristics.

プロセスウィンドウ.desc: The range of exposure dose and focus over which pattern dimensions stay within tolerance. The wider it is, the more robust manufacturing is to variation.

High-NA EUV.desc: Next-generation EUV lithography that raises the projection optics' numerical aperture from 0.33 to 0.55 to improve resolution.

反射防止膜(BARC).desc: A layer coated under the resist that suppresses standing waves in the resist and dimension variation over topography caused by light reflected from the substrate.

ナノインプリントリソグラフィ.desc: Transferring patterns by pressing a mold with fine features into resist on the wafer. It can make fine patterns without expensive optics.

プラズマ.desc: A state in which a gas is ionized into a mixture of electrons, ions and radicals (reactive neutrals). It is used in many processes, including dry etching, plasma CVD and ashing.

ラジカル.desc: A neutral atom or molecule with an unpaired electron that is highly reactive chemically. Plasmas contain far more radicals than ions, and they drive chemical etching and deposition.

ドライエッチング.desc: Removing material with plasma or gas instead of liquid chemicals. Combining ion bombardment allows anisotropic etching, which is essential for fine patterns.

about.h: What does the etching in a plasma
about.p: Etch plasmas are weakly ionized, typically about 0.01% or less, and contain electrons, positive ions, highly reactive radicals and neutral molecules. Radicals supply the chemistry and ions supply directional energy. Etching works only if the reaction product is volatile: silicon leaves as SiF4, SiCl4 or SiBr4, silicon dioxide etched with fluorocarbon gases such as CF4 or C4F8 leaves as SiF4 plus CO or CO2, and GaN etched with Cl2 and BCl3 leaves as GaCl3. Copper chlorides are not volatile at normal process temperatures, which is why copper lines are formed by damascene instead.

Ions and radicals together etch much faster than either alone; in a classic experiment, XeF2 gas plus an argon ion beam etched silicon about ten times faster than the sum of the two separately. Because ions arrive vertically, feature bottoms etch quickly while sidewalls do not. In addition, polymer from fluorocarbon gases or HBr-derived byproducts coats the sidewalls and blocks lateral attack, while ion bombardment clears it from the bottom. Too much passivation tapers the profile and too little causes bowing, so chemistry, bias and temperature are balanced.

Key figures are etch rate, uniformity, profile and selectivity; Cl2 and HBr etch polysilicon with selectivity above 100 to thin gate oxide. Endpoint is detected by optical emission spectroscopy (OES), watching emission lines that change when the film clears, such as CO at 483 nm dropping at the end of an oxide etch; interferometry helps when the open area is too small for a clear signal. Typical defects include microtrenching at feature corners and sidewall residues, which are removed by ashing and wet cleans to avoid corrosion and high contact resistance.

Wet etching dissolves films in liquid, usually isotropically, undercutting the mask by roughly the film thickness, but it is cheap, can process many wafers at once and gives high selectivity. Dry etching, including reactive ion etching (RIE) and high-density ICP etching, transfers mask patterns with little dimensional loss and is essential below a few micrometers. Fabs therefore use dry etching for patterning and wet processes for blanket film removal and cleaning. Many etch gases, especially fluorocarbons, have very high global warming potentials, so exhaust passes through abatement systems.

faq.q: What is the difference between dry etching and wet etching?
faq.a: Dry etching removes material with plasma or reactive gas and, with ion bombardment, can etch vertically for fine patterns. Wet etching uses liquid chemicals, is usually isotropic and undercuts the mask, but is simple, high-throughput and highly selective.

faq.q: Why can copper not be patterned by dry etching?
faq.a: Copper chlorides and fluorides do not evaporate below several hundred degrees Celsius, so reaction products stay on the surface instead of being pumped away. Copper wiring is therefore made by etching trenches in the dielectric, filling them with copper and polishing off the excess.

faq.q: How is the endpoint of a dry etch detected?
faq.a: Most tools monitor the plasma's optical emission at wavelengths tied to reaction products, which change sharply when the film clears and the underlayer is exposed. Laser or broadband interferometry of film thickness is used when the exposed area is small.

アッシング.desc: Removing photoresist that is no longer needed after etching or implantation by oxidizing it to ash, typically with an oxygen plasma.

終点検出.desc: Detecting the moment when the target film has been fully etched, commonly by monitoring changes in the plasma's emission spectrum.

アスペクト比.desc: The ratio of a hole's or trench's depth to its width. Higher ratios make etching and deposition harder; memory holes in 3D NAND reach several tens or more.

about.p: Aspect ratio is depth divided by width. A hole 100 nm across and 1 µm deep has an aspect ratio of 10. Memory holes in 3D NAND, about 100 nm wide and several µm deep, reach 50 to 100, and DRAM capacitor holes are also extremely tall and narrow. The same idea applies to lines: a copper interconnect's thickness-to-width ratio is often around 2. Aspect ratio should not be confused with selectivity, which is the ratio of etch rates of two materials, or with the overall shape of a die.

about.h: Why deep, narrow features are hard to etch
about.p: As aspect ratio rises, fewer reactive radicals reach the bottom because they react with or stick to the walls along the way, ions are deflected by charge built up on insulating sidewalls, and reaction products escape slowly.
