The etch rate therefore falls with depth, an effect called aspect-ratio-dependent etching (ARDE) or microloading, so narrow holes end up shallower than wide ones etched at the same time. Deep etches also suffer bowing, twisting and tapered bottoms, which is why high-aspect-ratio etching is one of the hardest steps in memory fabrication.

Physical vapor deposition (PVD) atoms travel in nearly straight lines, so sidewalls and bottoms of deep features are shadowed and receive little film. CVD under surface-reaction-limited conditions coats much more uniformly, and ALD can coat features with aspect ratios of several tens because each step is self-limiting. Filling a gap completely is harder than lining it: film builds up at the opening and pinches off, trapping a void. High-density plasma CVD, which sputters back the corners, and flowable CVD, which fills from the bottom, were developed for this.

Tall, thin structures can be pulled together during drying by the surface tension of liquid between them, and the force grows with aspect ratio and with narrower gaps. Low-surface-tension rinses such as IPA, hydrophobic surface treatments and supercritical CO2 drying reduce pattern collapse. In interconnects, raising aspect ratio lowers resistance but increases sidewall capacitance to neighbors, so it is balanced per metal level. In DRAM, capacitor aspect ratio is approaching practical limits, one motivation for stacking cells in 3D DRAM.

faq.q: How is aspect ratio calculated in semiconductor etching?
faq.a: Divide the depth of the hole or trench by its width or opening diameter. For example, a trench 50 nm wide and 500 nm deep has an aspect ratio of 10.

faq.q: What is ARDE in plasma etching?
faq.a: Aspect-ratio-dependent etching (ARDE) is the slowing of etch rate as features become narrower and deeper, because fewer radicals and ions reach the bottom and products escape more slowly. It makes narrow features shallower than wide ones etched at the same time.

faq.q: Why do high-aspect-ratio patterns collapse?
faq.a: When rinse liquid dries between tall, narrow structures, capillary forces from surface tension pull neighboring structures together. Higher aspect ratio and narrower spacing increase the risk.

ARDE(アスペクト比依存エッチング).desc: The slowdown of etch rate in narrower, deeper features because ions and radicals reach the bottom less easily. Also called the microloading effect.

ハードマスク.desc: A durable mask of nitride, carbon, metal or similar used when photoresist alone cannot survive the etch, for example in deep-hole etching.

about.p: Resist for fine patterns is thin, often around 100 nm, partly because tall narrow resist lines collapse. Etching consumes the mask too, and selectivity, the target etch rate divided by the mask etch rate, sets how much is lost: at 100 nm/min for oxide and 20 nm/min for the mask, selectivity is 5, so etching 500 nm of oxide consumes 100 nm of mask, and with overetch and edge erosion about 150–200 nm is needed. A hard mask, an inorganic or carbon film that resists the main etch far better, removes this limit.

about.h: How a hard mask is used
about.p: The film stack is deposited first, then lithography patterns the resist. A short etch transfers the pattern into the hard mask, the resist can be stripped, and the hard mask defines the main etch. Multilayer schemes chain this idea: in a tri-layer stack, resist patterns a thin silicon-containing antireflective layer, which in turn masks an oxygen-based etch of a thick carbon layer, because oxygen plasma removes carbon but barely attacks silicon-containing films. The thick carbon then masks the target film.

The hard mask must resist the chemistry that etches the target. Silicon nitride, oxide or oxynitride mask silicon and polysilicon etches; amorphous carbon or polysilicon masks oxide etches with fluorocarbon gases; titanium nitride has been used as a metal hard mask for trenches in low-k dielectrics. For the very deep, high-aspect-ratio holes of 3D NAND, amorphous-carbon hard masks several micrometers thick are used, so their deposition, etch and removal are major process steps. Carbon is easy to strip by oxygen ashing, while metal masks need wet removal.

Hard masks also define geometry beyond simple etch resistance. In self-aligned double or quadruple patterning, spacers deposited on mandrels and then etched back become the hard mask that sets line width. In self-aligned via schemes, the hard mask used to pattern wiring trenches is kept, or materially distinct caps are placed over lines, so a via etch stays confined within the target line's width even with a few nanometers of misalignment, avoiding shorts to neighboring lines at tight pitches.

faq.q: What is the difference between a hard mask and a photoresist mask?
faq.a: Photoresist is a light-sensitive polymer patterned directly by lithography but erodes quickly in plasma. A hard mask is a durable film such as nitride, oxide, carbon or metal that is patterned using the resist and then survives long, aggressive etches.

faq.q: Why is amorphous carbon used as a hard mask?
faq.a: Amorphous carbon etches very slowly in the fluorocarbon plasmas used for oxide and nitride, so a thick layer can last through deep etches, and it is removed easily afterward by oxygen ashing without damaging the patterned film.

faq.q: How thick should an etch mask be?
faq.a: Divide the target etch depth by the selectivity to estimate mask consumption, then add margin for overetch and corner erosion. For 500 nm of oxide at selectivity 5, about 100 nm is consumed, so roughly 150–200 nm is a safe thickness.

オーバーエッチング.desc: Continuing to etch for a set time after endpoint so the film is removed everywhere on the wafer. It is done under conditions with high selectivity to the underlying layer.

ICP(誘導結合プラズマ).desc: A method that generates a high-density plasma with RF current in a coil. It makes it easy to control plasma density and the energy of ions reaching the wafer independently.

about.p: An inductively coupled plasma (ICP) source drives RF current, commonly at 13.56 MHz, through a flat spiral or cylindrical coil placed outside a dielectric window of quartz or ceramic. The coil's oscillating magnetic field induces a circulating electric field inside the chamber, which accelerates electrons and keeps the gas ionized. Because power is transferred to the electrons inductively instead of through a high-voltage sheath at an electrode, the discharge reaches densities of about 10¹¹–10¹² cm⁻³ while operating at low pressures of a few pascals or less.

about.h: Separate knobs for density and ion energy
about.p: An ICP etcher uses two RF supplies. Source power to the coil sets plasma density, and therefore the flux of ions and radicals. A separate bias supply on the wafer chuck sets the DC self-bias and therefore the energy of ions striking the wafer. Engineers can etch fast with low ion energy to protect the underlayer and limit damage, or raise bias for more vertical profiles. Low pressure gives a long mean free path, so ions cross the sheath with few collisions and arrive nearly perpendicular, which supports anisotropic etching.

In a capacitively coupled plasma (CCP), RF power is applied between parallel-plate electrodes, so the same power that sustains the plasma also sets the sheath voltage; density and ion energy rise together. CCP densities are typically around 10⁹–10¹⁰ cm⁻³ with higher ion energies, and CCP tools, often with two frequencies to partly decouple the two, are widely used for oxide and nitride etching with fluorocarbon gases. ICP tools are favored for silicon, polysilicon gates, metals and compound semiconductors, where high radical flux and modest ion energy are wanted.

In fabs, ICP etchers handle shallow trench isolation, gate and fin etching, and metal lines. For GaN, chlorine-based ICP plasmas (Cl2, BCl3) etch LED and laser mesas and HEMT gate recesses at low ion energy to keep damage from degrading devices. High-density plasma CVD for gap fill also uses inductive sources. Outside processing, the same principle appears in ICP-MS, where an atmospheric-pressure argon plasma ionizes samples for trace-metal analysis, for example of droplets collected from wafer surfaces by vapor phase decomposition (VPD).

faq.q: What is the difference between ICP and CCP etching?
faq.a: ICP sustains the plasma with an inductive coil and biases the wafer with a separate RF supply, so plasma density and ion energy can be set independently and density is high. CCP drives parallel-plate electrodes, so density and ion energy are coupled and density is lower, which suits energetic dielectric etching.

faq.q: What plasma density does an ICP etcher reach?
faq.a: Typical ICP etch plasmas reach about 10¹¹–10¹² cm⁻³ at pressures of a few pascals or below, roughly one to two orders of magnitude denser than a conventional capacitively coupled plasma.

faq.q: Is the ICP in ICP-MS the same as in ICP etching?
faq.a: Both use an inductively coupled plasma, but ICP-MS runs an atmospheric-pressure argon plasma to ionize a liquid sample for mass spectrometry, while an ICP etcher runs a low-pressure reactive plasma to remove material from a wafer.

ALE(原子層エッチング).desc: Etching by alternating surface modification and removal so that each cycle removes about one atomic layer. It gives extremely precise control of etch depth.

about.p: Atomic layer etching (ALE) divides etching into separate, self-limiting half-steps. In a typical plasma ALE of silicon, chlorine is first introduced and adsorbs on the surface until it saturates, converting only the top layer into a weakly bonded chlorinated layer. After a purge, low-energy argon ions are applied with energy high enough to remove the modified layer but below the threshold for sputtering the unmodified silicon. Another purge follows and the cycle repeats. Each cycle removes a fixed amount, typically about 0.1–0.5 nm.

Because each step stops by itself, the etched depth is set by counting cycles rather than by timing a continuous etch. Removal per cycle is nearly the same in dense and isolated features, surfaces stay smooth, and the low ion energy causes little lattice damage. This makes ALE suited to steps that must stop within a few nanometers or etch films only a few atomic layers thick. The drawback is speed: gas switching and purges make each cycle slow, so ALE is usually reserved for the final, critical part of an etch.

Plasma ALE, which uses ions in the removal step, is directional and can etch the bottom of a feature without attacking its sidewalls. Thermal ALE instead uses purely chemical reactions, for example fluorinating a metal oxide surface and then removing the fluoride with a ligand-exchange precursor, so it etches isotropically. Thermal ALE is useful where a precise, uniform lateral recess is needed inside three-dimensional structures that ions cannot reach directly.

ALE is the etching counterpart of atomic layer deposition (ALD), which builds films by alternating self-limiting precursor exposures. Both trade speed for atomic-scale control and uniformity. As transistor structures move to gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheets with layers only a few nanometers thick, ALE is entering use in gate-region processing and other steps where overetch must be minimal, and it is also studied for low-damage recess etching in compound-semiconductor devices.

faq.q: What is the difference between ALE and ALD?
faq.a: Both rely on alternating self-limiting surface reactions, but ALD adds material a fraction of a nanometer per cycle while ALE removes it. They are often described as mirror-image processes.

faq.q: How much material does one ALE cycle remove?
faq.a: Typically about 0.1–0.5 nm per cycle, roughly one atomic layer or less, depending on the material and chemistry. Total depth is set by the number of cycles.

faq.q: Why is atomic layer etching not used for every etch step?
faq.a: Each cycle needs separate modification, purge and removal steps, so the net etch rate is far lower than continuous plasma etching. It is used where precision and low damage justify the lower throughput.

アンテナ効果.desc: Damage to a gate oxide when a connected conductor, such as a long wire, collects charge like an antenna during plasma processing. Design rules limit the area ratio of such wires to prevent it.

バッファードフッ酸(BHF).desc: Hydrofluoric acid buffered with ammonium fluoride. It is used for wet etching of SiO2 with a stable etch rate and little damage to resist.

シーズニング.desc: Running dummy wafers before product to stabilize the condition of an etch (or similar) chamber's walls, since wall changes alter process results.

セルフバイアス.desc: The negative DC potential that the wafer electrode naturally acquires in a capacitively coupled plasma. It accelerates positive ions toward the wafer, aiding anisotropic etching.

SC-1(APM).desc: A mixture of ammonia, hydrogen peroxide and water used first in RCA cleaning. It removes particles and organics while lightly etching the surface.

SC-2(HPM).desc: A mixture of hydrochloric acid, hydrogen peroxide and water used after SC-1 in RCA cleaning to remove metal contamination.

SPM(硫酸過水).desc: A mixture of sulfuric acid and hydrogen peroxide. Its strong oxidizing power removes organics such as resist.

希フッ酸(DHF).desc: Hydrofluoric acid diluted with water. It removes native oxide from silicon and leaves a hydrophobic, hydrogen-terminated surface.

自然酸化膜.desc: A thin oxide about 1 nm thick that forms naturally when silicon is exposed to air or water. Because it raises contact resistance and disturbs epitaxial growth, it is removed right before such steps.

パッドコンディショニング.desc: Abrading the surface of a CMP polishing pad with a diamond tool to restore its texture and slurry-holding ability, stabilizing the removal rate. Also called dressing.

エロージョン.desc: In CMP, excessive polishing of an entire region of dense lines, insulator included, so it ends up lower than its surroundings. Along with dishing of wide lines, it is a typical CMP defect.

プレストンの式.desc: The empirical rule that the CMP removal rate is proportional to the product of polishing pressure and the relative speed between pad and wafer.

セリア(酸化セリウム).desc: An abrasive used in CMP slurries. It reacts chemically with oxide and gives high selectivity to nitride, so it is used for STI CMP.

パターン倒壊.desc: A defect in which tall, fine patterns topple or stick together during cleaning and drying because of the surface tension of liquid left between them.

枚葉式洗浄.desc: A cleaning method that processes one wafer at a time. It minimizes cross-contamination and allows per-wafer control. Immersing many wafers in a tank at once is batch cleaning.

MBE(分子線エピタキシー).desc: Epitaxial growth in ultra-high vacuum by supplying source materials to the substrate as molecular beams. It controls thickness and composition at the atomic-layer level and is used in compound-semiconductor research and quantum structures.

オートドーピング.desc: Unintended incorporation into a growing epitaxial layer of dopant from the substrate or elsewhere via the gas phase. It is a problem when growing lightly doped layers on heavily doped substrates.

臨界膜厚.desc: The maximum thickness to which a lattice-mismatched layer can be grown while staying strained without forming dislocations. Beyond it, misfit dislocations appear.

ミスフィット転位.desc: A dislocation at the interface between crystals with different lattice constants that relieves strain. It forms when the grown layer exceeds the critical thickness.

貫通転位.desc: A dislocation that runs up through the grown layer to the surface. GaN on sapphire or silicon has high densities (about 10⁸-10⁹ cm⁻²), which degrade device performance and reliability.

積層欠陥.desc: A planar defect in which the stacking order of atomic planes is disrupted. It is a concern in epitaxial layers, thermal oxidation (OSF) and SiC crystals.

横方向エピタキシャル成長(ELO).desc: Growing crystal from mask openings and letting it spread sideways over the mask. Dislocations from below do not propagate into the overgrown regions, reducing dislocations in materials such as GaN.

超格子.desc: A periodic structure of alternating layers of different materials, each a few nanometers thick. It shows electronic properties absent in bulk crystals and is used in lasers, buffer layers and more.

SiGe(シリコンゲルマニウム).desc: An alloy of silicon and germanium with a larger lattice constant than silicon. Grown epitaxially, it is used to strain channels, as the base of HBTs and as the sacrificial layer in GAA transistors.

ひずみシリコン.desc: Silicon whose band structure is modified by strain to raise carrier mobility. Tensile strain helps nMOS and compressive strain helps pMOS; it is applied with SiGe source/drain regions, nitride films and the like.

HVPE(ハイドライド気相成長).desc: Vapor-phase growth using gallium chloride, formed by reacting HCl with gallium, together with ammonia. Its very high growth rate is used to grow thick GaN crystals for free-standing substrates.

ステップフロー成長.desc: A growth mode in which the crystal extends sideways from atomic steps on a slightly off-axis substrate. In SiC it is used so the layer inherits the substrate's polytype.

4H-SiC.desc: The SiC polytype mainly used for power devices. It has a wide band gap of about 3.3 eV and relatively high electron mobility.

ビア.desc: A conductor that electrically connects the wiring layers above and below it in a multilevel interconnect. It is made by filling a hole in the insulator with metal.

コンタクト.desc: The connection between a transistor's source, drain or gate and the lowest wiring layer. It is made by filling a contact hole in the insulator with tungsten or similar metal.

シリサイド.desc: A compound of silicon and a metal, such as NiSi or TiSi2. It is formed on source, drain and gate surfaces to reduce resistance and contact resistance.

デュアルダマシン法.desc: Forming both the trench for a wire and the hole for a via in the insulator, filling them with copper together and finishing with a single CMP step. It reduces process steps.

シード層.desc: A thin copper film deposited by sputtering or similar before copper electroplating. It provides the conductive path for the plating current.

エアギャップ.desc: Leaving part of the insulator between wires as empty space. Since air has a relative permittivity of about 1, it greatly reduces capacitance between wires.

IRドロップ.desc: The drop in supply voltage reaching a circuit because current (I) flows through the resistance (R) of the power wiring. It increases delay and can cause malfunctions.

クロストーク.desc: Noise that appears on one wire when the signal on a neighboring wire changes, mainly through capacitive coupling. Wider spacing and shield wires reduce it.

パッシベーション膜.desc: A film formed as the topmost layer of a chip to protect the circuitry from moisture, contamination and mechanical damage. Silicon nitride and polyimide are typical materials.

裏面電源供給.desc: Placing the power wiring on the back of the wafer so the front-side wiring can be used for signals. It reduces voltage drop and routing congestion.

MOL(ミドル・オブ・ライン).desc: The contacts and local interconnects that link transistors (FEOL) to the multilevel wiring (BEOL). With scaling, their resistance has grown and now limits performance.

表皮効果.desc: The concentration of high-frequency current near the surface of a conductor, which raises its effective resistance. The higher the frequency, the thinner the surface layer carrying the current.

ブラックの式.desc: An empirical formula for interconnect lifetime under electromigration in terms of current density and temperature. Lifetime is inversely proportional to a power of current density and falls exponentially as temperature rises.

ダイシング.desc: Cutting a wafer into individual chips (dies). Besides sawing with a rotating blade, there are methods such as stealth dicing, which forms a modified layer inside the wafer with a laser.

ダイボンディング.desc: Attaching and fixing a diced chip at its position on a lead frame or package substrate, using adhesive, solder or sintered material.

バックグラインド.desc: Grinding the back of a wafer before dicing to thin it for packaging. Chips for stacking are thinned to a few tens of micrometers.

WLP(ウエハレベルパッケージ).desc: A package in which redistribution wiring and external terminals are formed while the chips are still in wafer form, before dicing. The result is a small package about the size of the chip.

CSP(チップサイズパッケージ).desc: A general term for packages shrunk to nearly the size of the chip. They are widely used in compact devices such as smartphones.

リフローはんだ付け.desc: Printing solder paste on a circuit board, placing components and heating everything in an oven to melt the solder. It is the standard method for surface mounting.

熱抵抗.desc: A measure of how hard it is for heat to flow, in °C/W. Multiplying dissipated power by thermal resistance gives the temperature rise. Junction-to-ambient thermal resistance is written θJA.

ウエハテスト(プローブテスト).desc: Checking the electrical characteristics of each chip on the wafer by touching probes to its pads before dicing. It finds bad chips before assembly so they are not packaged needlessly.

BIST(組み込み自己テスト).desc: Test circuitry built into the chip so that it generates test patterns and checks results by itself. It is widely used, for example, to test memories.

ATPG(自動テストパターン生成).desc: Automatically generating test patterns that detect faults from a circuit's netlist. It is used together with scan design.

縮退故障.desc: The basic fault model in logic testing, which assumes a signal line is stuck at 0 or 1.

故障検出率(フォールトカバレッジ).desc: The fraction of modeled faults that a set of test patterns can detect. The higher it is, the less likely defective chips are to escape.

IDDQテスト.desc: A test that measures the supply current of a CMOS circuit at rest and flags defects such as bridging faults when it is abnormally high.

KGD(ノウングッドダイ).desc: A chip confirmed to be good before packaging. It matters when several chips go into one package, because a single bad chip ruins the whole module.

パレート図.desc: A chart that lists items such as defect types as bars in descending order of count, with a line for the cumulative share. It shows which items to tackle first.

管理図.desc: A chart that plots process measurements over time against a center line and control limits (usually ±3σ) to judge whether the process is stable. Points outside the limits or runs on one side signal problems.

特性要因図.desc: A diagram that organizes the causes affecting a problem (the effect) in the shape of a fish skeleton. Also called a fishbone diagram.

about.p: The problem being studied, called the effect, is written at the head on the right side, and a horizontal spine runs to it. Major bones branch off the spine for categories of causes, classically the 4Ms: man (people), machine, material and method. Many teams add measurement and environment to make 5M+E or 6M. Each major bone carries smaller bones for more specific causes, and those can branch further, so the diagram shows a hierarchy from broad category to concrete, checkable cause. It is also called an Ishikawa diagram after the quality engineer Kaoru Ishikawa.

Start by stating the effect narrowly and measurably, for example a rise in particle defects after a particular etch step rather than simply low yield. The team then brainstorms causes under each category, asking why repeatedly to move from vague items to specific ones, and avoids judging ideas while the diagram is being filled. Once the list is reasonably exhaustive, the most plausible causes are marked and each is checked against data, such as tool logs, inspection results or a designed experiment. The diagram generates hypotheses; it does not prove which cause is responsible.

Suppose wafer edge yield has dropped on one product. Under machine the team might list chamber wall flaking, a worn edge ring or a change in maintenance interval. Under material: a new photoresist lot or incoming wafer flatness. Under method: a recent recipe change or different chamber seasoning. Under measurement: a changed inspection threshold. Under man: a manual handling step done differently by shifts. Wafer maps, tool history and lot genealogy are then used to narrow the list to the cause that actually matches the failure pattern.

about.h: Place among the seven QC tools
about.p: The cause-and-effect diagram is one of the seven basic quality control tools, together with the check sheet, Pareto chart, histogram, scatter diagram, control chart and stratification (some lists use a flowchart or graph instead). The tools complement each other: a Pareto chart ranks defect types by count to pick which effect to attack, the fishbone lists candidate causes, a scatter diagram tests whether a suspected cause correlates with the result, and a histogram shows the distribution, where two peaks often mean data from two tools or materials are mixed and should be stratified.

faq.q: Why is it called a fishbone diagram?
faq.a: The effect sits at the head on the right, the main line forms the spine, and the cause categories branch off at an angle like ribs, so the finished drawing looks like a fish skeleton.

faq.q: What are the 4Ms in a cause-and-effect diagram?
faq.a: They are man (people), machine, material and method, the standard categories for the major bones. Measurement and environment are often added, giving 5M+E.

faq.q: What is the difference between a fishbone diagram and a Pareto chart?
faq.a: A Pareto chart ranks problems or defect categories by frequency to show which few matter most. A fishbone diagram takes one chosen problem and organizes its possible causes so they can be investigated.

FMEA(故障モード影響解析).desc: A method that lists the possible failure modes of a product or process, evaluates their effects and severity, and plans countermeasures in advance.

APC(先進的プロセス制御).desc: Automatically adjusting the process settings for the next lot or wafer based on earlier measurements, as in run-to-run control. It reduces variation.

システマティック不良.desc: A defect that occurs repeatedly at particular patterns or locations because of interactions between design and process. It is distinguished from random defects caused by chance particles.

アレニウスモデル.desc: A model in which reaction or degradation rates vary with temperature as exp(−Ea/kT). It is used to estimate lifetime at operating temperature from accelerated tests at higher temperatures.

FIT.desc: A unit of failure rate: 1 FIT is one failure per billion (10⁹) device-hours. It is used for parts with very low failure rates, such as semiconductors.

ワイブル分布.desc: A probability distribution widely used to analyze lifetime data. Its shape parameter can represent early-failure, random-failure and wear-out behavior.

ホットキャリア注入(HCI).desc: Degradation in which carriers accelerated by the strong field near the drain are injected into the gate insulator, shifting the threshold voltage and reducing drive current.

ラッチアップ.desc: A condition in which a parasitic thyristor structure in a CMOS circuit turns on and a large current keeps flowing between supply and ground. It is prevented by well-contact placement, guard rings and similar measures.

ESD(静電気放電).desc: A sudden discharge of static electricity from a charged person or object. Applied to an IC pin it can destroy gate oxides and other structures, so I/O pins have protection circuits.

ソフトエラー.desc: A temporary flip of data stored in memory or flip-flops caused by neutrons from cosmic rays, alpha particles and the like. The device is not damaged, so rewriting restores correct operation.

ネットリスト.desc: Data describing the elements (cells) of a circuit and how they are connected. It is the output of logic synthesis and the input to place-and-route and timing analysis.

about.p: A netlist lists instances, the cells or transistors in a circuit, and nets, the electrical connections between their pins, plus the ports that connect the circuit to the outside. It is pure connectivity: it says that the output pin of one NAND gate drives the inputs of two flip-flops, but nothing about where those cells sit or how the wires are drawn. A gate-level netlist references cells from a standard-cell library and is usually written as structural Verilog, while a transistor-level SPICE netlist lists individual MOSFETs, resistors and capacitors with their parameters for circuit simulation.

about.h: Where netlists appear in the design flow
about.p: Logic synthesis converts register-transfer level (RTL) code into a gate-level netlist that meets timing, area and power constraints. Place-and-route reads that netlist, then adds buffers and a synthesized clock tree, producing an updated post-layout netlist. Parasitic resistance and capacitance extracted from the layout are attached for static timing analysis. Formal equivalence checking compares the netlist against the RTL, automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) works on the netlist to target faults such as stuck-at faults, and layout-versus-schematic (LVS) checking compares a netlist extracted from the layout with the reference netlist.

RTL simulation is fast but abstract, so some bugs only appear after synthesis. Simulating the gate-level netlist exercises the actual gates and flip-flops, exposing reset and initialization problems that X-optimism hides in RTL, and cases where the synthesized logic differs from the designer's intent. When gate and wire delays from the layout are back-annotated in SDF (Standard Delay Format), timing-related problems also show up. Because gate-level simulation is far slower than RTL simulation, it is usually run on a limited set of tests.

The netlist and the layout describe the same chip in different ways. The netlist captures what is connected to what, while layout data in GDSII or OASIS format holds the polygons on each mask layer that will actually be printed on the wafer. Verification ties them together: LVS proves that the drawn shapes implement exactly the connections in the netlist, and design rule checking (DRC) separately confirms that the shapes obey manufacturing rules. Only layout data goes to mask making after tape-out.

faq.q: What is the difference between RTL and a netlist?
faq.a: RTL describes behavior as registers and the logic operations between them in a language like Verilog or VHDL. A netlist is the structural result after synthesis, listing specific library cells and the wires connecting them.

faq.q: What is a SPICE netlist?
faq.a: It is a transistor-level netlist in the input format of SPICE circuit simulators, listing devices such as MOSFETs, resistors and capacitors with their node connections and model parameters, used for analog and cell-level simulation.

faq.q: Does a netlist contain physical layout information?
faq.a: No. A netlist contains only components and connectivity. Cell positions and wire shapes live in the layout database and in GDSII or OASIS files, although parasitics extracted from the layout can be attached to the netlist for timing analysis.

スタンダードセル.desc: A pre-designed, pre-verified building block such as a logic gate or flip-flop. Cells share a common height so automatic place-and-route can line them up to build large circuits.

PDK(プロセスデザインキット).desc: The set of design data a foundry gives to designers, including design rules, device models, cell libraries and verification rule decks.

テープアウト.desc: Handing over the finished, verified layout data to manufacturing for mask making. The name comes from the days when data was delivered on magnetic tape.

SPICE.desc: A circuit simulator that calculates voltages and currents in transistor-level circuits in detail using device models. It is used for analog design and cell characterization.

高位合成(HLS).desc: Automatically generating RTL from an algorithm written in C, C++ or similar. It is used in developing FPGAs and accelerators.

クロックゲーティング.desc: A low-power design technique that stops the clock to idle circuit blocks, avoiding wasted switching power.

FPGA.desc: A chip whose logic configuration the user can rewrite after manufacture. It is used for prototypes, low-volume products and ASIC verification.

about.p: A field-programmable gate array (FPGA) is a grid of configurable logic blocks joined by programmable interconnect. Each logic block contains lookup tables (LUTs), small memories whose stored bits define a truth table and whose inputs drive multiplexers that select the output, so a k-input LUT can implement any function of k inputs. Flip-flops store state. Modern devices also include hard blocks such as block RAM, DSP multiply-accumulate units, clock managers, high-speed serial transceivers and sometimes processor cores. In most FPGAs the configuration lives in SRAM cells and is loaded from external flash at power-up.

Designs are written in a hardware description language such as Verilog or VHDL. Synthesis maps the logic onto LUTs, flip-flops and hard blocks, recognizing standard coding patterns: a register array written and read synchronously with the clock is inferred as block RAM, while an asynchronous read may become flip-flops or distributed memory. Place-and-route then assigns resources and wires, static timing analysis checks clock frequency, and the result is a bitstream loaded into the device. Processing blocks are often linked with standard on-chip interfaces such as AXI4-Stream.

An FPGA needs no masks or fabrication lead time and can be reprogrammed in the field, so bugs and new features can be handled after shipment. The price is overhead: the configurable routing and LUTs make the same function slower, more power-hungry and much larger in area than in an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), and the unit price is higher. ASICs win at high volume once their large up-front engineering and mask costs are spread across many units; FPGAs win for prototypes, low volumes and fast-changing requirements.

FPGAs appear in communications equipment, test and measurement instruments, video and signal-processing pipelines, industrial control and data-center accelerators. They are also central to verifying large SoCs: mapping the design onto FPGAs (FPGA prototyping) runs it orders of magnitude faster than software simulation, so real operating systems and applications can run before silicon exists. Hardware emulators serve the same purpose with better visibility into internal signals, while FPGA prototypes generally run faster.

faq.q: What does FPGA stand for?
faq.a: FPGA stands for field-programmable gate array: a chip whose logic and wiring can be configured by the user after manufacture, in the field, rather than fixed during fabrication.

faq.q: What is the difference between an FPGA and a microcontroller?
faq.a: A microcontroller has a fixed processor that executes software instructions one after another. An FPGA has no fixed function; its hardware itself is configured, so many operations can run in parallel every clock cycle, at the cost of a harder design flow.

faq.q: Does an FPGA keep its configuration when power is off?
faq.a: Most FPGAs store their configuration in SRAM and lose it at power-off, reloading a bitstream from an external flash memory at each power-up. Some families use on-chip flash or one-time antifuses and are non-volatile.

LVS.desc: Short for layout versus schematic: checking that the connectivity extracted from the layout matches the schematic or netlist. It is always run before tape-out, along with DRC.

ミニエンバイロメント.desc: Keeping only the small space around the wafers highly clean. Sealed carriers such as FOUPs combined with EFEMs on the tools lower the cleanliness required of the room as a whole, reducing cost.

OHT(天井走行式無人搬送車).desc: Vehicles that run along ceiling rails and automatically carry FOUPs between tools. They are the backbone of automated transport in 300 mm fabs.

FFU(ファンフィルタユニット).desc: A unit combining a fan with a high-efficiency filter. Arrays of them in the cleanroom ceiling blow clean air downward.

EFEM.desc: Short for equipment front end module: the unit at the front of a tool that opens FOUPs and transfers wafers into the tool in a clean environment. It includes load ports and a transfer robot.

about.p: An EFEM (equipment front end module) is the enclosed section at the front of a process or metrology tool. It contains load ports where FOUPs (front-opening unified pods) are docked, a mechanism that unlatches and removes the FOUP door, an atmospheric wafer-handling robot, and usually an aligner that finds the wafer notch before processing. Sensors map which FOUP slots hold wafers. A fan filter unit (FFU) on top blows HEPA- or ULPA-filtered air downward and keeps the enclosure at slight positive pressure, so room air does not leak in.

Instead of keeping an entire cleanroom at the cleanest level, modern fabs isolate wafers in small clean volumes: the sealed FOUP during transport and storage, and the EFEM during transfer into the tool. Wafers move from FOUP to tool without ever being exposed to the room, so the surrounding cleanroom can be held to a less strict class at lower cost. In the 200 mm era, SMIF pods served this role by lowering a cassette into the tool; 300 mm FOUPs open from the front and dock directly to EFEM load ports.

The EFEM operates at atmospheric pressure. For vacuum tools such as etchers and CVD systems, its robot places wafers into a load lock, which is pumped down before a vacuum robot moves them to the process chambers; finished wafers return the same way. Overhead hoist transport (OHT) vehicles deliver FOUPs to the load ports automatically. Load-port dimensions and handoff signaling follow SEMI standards, so FOUPs and transport systems from different suppliers work with many tools.

Particles are not the only concern. Moisture and oxygen can grow native oxide on exposed silicon or metal, and outgassing from just-processed wafers can contaminate others in the same FOUP. Some EFEMs therefore use a nitrogen-filled enclosure rather than filtered air, and load ports can purge FOUPs with nitrogen, limiting oxidation and cross-contamination between process steps.

faq.q: What does EFEM stand for?
faq.a: EFEM stands for equipment front end module: the front section of a semiconductor tool that opens FOUPs and transfers wafers into the tool in a clean environment.

faq.q: What is the difference between an EFEM and a load lock?
faq.a: An EFEM is an atmospheric, filtered-air enclosure with load ports and a robot that unloads FOUPs. A load lock is a small chamber that cycles between atmospheric pressure and vacuum so wafers can pass from the EFEM into a vacuum process tool.

faq.q: How is an EFEM different from an FFU?
faq.a: An FFU is a fan and filter unit that supplies clean air, used across cleanroom ceilings and on top of EFEMs. The EFEM is the complete wafer-transfer module, which includes an FFU to keep its interior clean.

HEPAフィルタ.desc: A high-efficiency air filter that captures at least 99.97% of 0.3 µm particles. Filters that capture even finer particles are ULPA filters.

局所排気装置.desc: Equipment that draws in gases and mists at their source, such as tools handling chemicals, and exhausts them. It keeps workers from inhaling hazardous substances.

爆発下限界(LEL).desc: The lowest concentration in air at which a flammable gas can burn or explode. Gas detectors are often set to alarm at a percentage of this level.

酸素欠乏(酸欠).desc: A condition in which the oxygen concentration in air falls below 18%. It tends to occur where large amounts of nitrogen are used or in confined spaces, and can cause unconsciousness within a few breaths.

リスクアセスメント.desc: Identifying the hazards of tasks or chemicals, estimating the size of the risks and deciding countermeasures in order of priority.

ロックアウト・タグアウト(LOTO).desc: A procedure that isolates energy sources such as power and gas before maintenance and fits locks and tags so no one can accidentally restore them during the work.

シリコンサイクル.desc: The recurring boom-and-bust pattern of the semiconductor market driven by supply and demand. One cause is that fabs take years to build, so supply lags changes in demand.

SoC(システムオンチップ).desc: An IC that integrates the functions a system needs, such as CPU, GPU, memory controller and communications, on one chip. The heart of a smartphone is a typical example.

about.p: A typical smartphone system on chip (SoC) contains several CPU cores, a GPU, often a neural processing unit and image signal processor, on-chip SRAM caches, a memory controller with its DRAM interface, display and camera interfaces, high-speed I/O, security blocks and power management logic, and in some designs a cellular modem. Main DRAM normally stays on separate chips, often stacked on top of the SoC package. Blocks inside communicate over an on-chip interconnect; Arm's AMBA AXI family, including AXI4-Lite for register access and AXI4-Stream for data flows, is a widely used standard that lets IP from different vendors connect.

Signals that stay on one die avoid package pins, board traces and the large drivers needed to switch them, so an SoC is smaller, faster and uses less power than the same functions spread over several chips, and the board needs fewer parts. The costs are real, however. Large dies have lower yield because each defect kills more area, the die cannot exceed the lithography field of about 26 mm by 33 mm, and functions that need different processes, such as DRAM, analog or RF, are hard to build optimally on the same logic process.

about.h: Power and security inside an SoC
about.p: Because blocks differ in speed requirements and activity, an SoC is split into power domains. Each can run at its own voltage and frequency through dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) or be switched off entirely, while a small always-on domain handles wake-up. Signals crossing domains need level shifters and isolation cells. An external power management IC (PMIC) generates the many supply rails from the battery under SoC control. For security, mechanisms such as Arm TrustZone tag every bus access as secure or normal, creating a protected environment within the same chip.

An SoC puts the system on one die. A system in package (SiP) instead places several dies and passive components in one package, which makes it easy to combine chips made in different processes and to reuse existing parts, at some cost in interconnect density and power. Chiplet designs split what would be a very large SoC into several dies connected at high density in an advanced package, improving yield and allowing systems larger than one reticle field. Many companies that design SoCs are fabless and have them manufactured by foundries.

faq.q: What is the difference between an SoC and a SiP?
faq.a: An SoC integrates the system's functions on a single silicon die, while a SiP houses multiple separate dies and components in one package. SoCs give the lowest power and latency; SiPs make it easier to mix chips from different processes.

faq.q: Is a microcontroller an SoC?
faq.a: In a broad sense yes, since a microcontroller integrates a CPU, flash, SRAM and peripherals on one chip. The term SoC is usually reserved for larger application processors that run a full operating system with external DRAM.

faq.q: Why is DRAM usually not on the same die as the SoC?
faq.a: Commodity DRAM uses a specialized process optimized for dense capacitor cells, which is incompatible with a high-performance logic process. Smartphones therefore stack separate DRAM chips on or next to the SoC package instead.

ASIC(特定用途向けIC).desc: An IC designed specifically for one application or customer. It beats general-purpose chips on performance and power, but high development costs suit it to high-volume uses.

about.p: An application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) carries large one-time costs, called non-recurring engineering (NRE): architecture and logic design, verification, licensed IP blocks, physical design, and a mask set that can cost millions to tens of millions of dollars at advanced nodes, plus months of fabrication lead time. In return, the chip contains only the needed functions, so each unit is small, fast, power-efficient and cheap to make. ASICs therefore pay off when volume is high enough to spread the NRE, or when no off-the-shelf part meets the performance or power target.

Most digital ASICs follow a standard-cell flow. Engineers write register-transfer level (RTL) code in Verilog or VHDL, verify it by simulation and, for large designs, emulation or FPGA prototyping, then synthesize it into gates from the foundry's cell library, with memories mapped to memory macros. Place-and-route builds the physical layout, static timing analysis and physical verification (DRC and LVS) confirm it, and the final layout is taped out to make masks. Full-custom design is used for the most performance-critical analog or memory blocks.

An FPGA implements logic in reprogrammable fabric, with no masks or fab wait, so it suits prototypes, low volumes and changing requirements; the same function as an ASIC is faster, smaller and lower power. An application-specific standard product (ASSP) is also dedicated to one application, but is sold as a catalog part to many customers, whereas an ASIC is typically built for one product or company. General-purpose CPUs and GPUs trade efficiency for flexibility through software.

ASICs appear wherever volume or efficiency justifies custom silicon: networking switches, storage controllers, consumer electronics, automotive systems, cryptocurrency mining and AI accelerators. Many are mixed-signal. A MEMS microphone, for example, pairs its capacitive sensing element with a small readout ASIC in the same package that converts the tiny capacitance change into an electrical signal. In these sensor uses, the ASIC is often designed jointly with the sensor itself.

faq.q: What does ASIC stand for?
faq.a: ASIC stands for application-specific integrated circuit, a chip designed for one particular product or use rather than as a general-purpose part.

faq.q: What is the difference between an ASIC and an FPGA?
faq.a: An ASIC's logic is fixed in silicon at manufacture, giving the best speed, power and unit cost but high up-front cost and long lead time. An FPGA can be reconfigured after manufacture with no mask cost, but is slower, larger and more power-hungry for the same function.

faq.q: What is the difference between an ASIC and an ASSP?
faq.a: Both target a specific application, but an ASIC is usually designed for a single customer or product, while an ASSP is a standard product a chip vendor sells to many customers.

MPW(マルチプロジェクトウエハ).desc: Prototyping several customers' designs together on one wafer (one mask set). Sharing the expensive mask cost makes it popular with universities and startups.

about.p: A foundry or aggregator announces runs on a given process at scheduled dates. Each participant submits a finished layout for a die area of agreed size by the deadline. The designs are tiled together on a shared reticle, one mask set is made, and the wafers are processed as a single lot. Afterwards the wafers are diced and each participant receives its own dies, often a few dozen, sometimes packaged. Mask and wafer costs are split among the participants, usually in proportion to silicon area, which is why the scheme is also called a shuttle.

A full mask set at an advanced node can cost tens of millions of dollars, and even mature nodes cost far more than a small team can spend on a first prototype. Sharing that cost lets universities, research groups and startups fabricate real chips for a small fraction of the price. Established companies use MPWs too, for test chips that characterize new circuits, validate IP blocks or check a new process before committing to a dedicated tape-out.

An MPW serves prototyping and evaluation, not production. Each participant gets only a limited number of dies, because neighboring designs share the wafer and dicing one design out can sacrifice its neighbors. Runs follow the foundry's calendar, so a missed deadline means waiting for the next shuttle, and die size, process options and turnaround are fixed by the organizer. Wafer-level testing and yield data are also limited compared with a dedicated lot.

Once a prototype works, the design moves to its own mask set for engineering lots and then volume production. For low-volume products, a multi-layer reticle, which places several mask layers on one reticle, can cut mask cost further at the expense of scanner throughput. For digital logic alone, an FPGA can validate function without any fabrication, but analog, RF and process-specific behavior can only be confirmed on real silicon, which is what an MPW run provides.

faq.q: What does MPW stand for?
faq.a: MPW stands for multi-project wafer: a fabrication run in which designs from several customers share one mask set and one set of wafers.

faq.q: Why do startups and universities use MPW runs?
faq.a: Because mask and wafer costs are divided among all participants, an MPW lets a small team obtain real prototype chips at a fraction of the cost of a dedicated mask set.

faq.q: Can an MPW be used for volume production?
faq.a: No. Each participant receives only a limited number of dies on a fixed schedule, so MPWs are used for prototypes and test chips; production requires a dedicated mask set.

デナードスケーリング.desc: The rule that shrinking transistor dimensions and supply voltage by the same factor gives faster, denser circuits at constant power density. It broke down in the mid-2000s when voltages could no longer be lowered easily.

ディスクリート半導体.desc: The category of semiconductor products that perform one function as a single device, such as diodes, individual transistors and power MOSFETs, as opposed to integrated circuits.

2.5D実装.desc: Placing several chips side by side on an intermediate substrate such as a silicon interposer and connecting them with dense, fine wiring. It is used, for example, to connect GPUs and HBM.

3D実装.desc: Stacking chips vertically and connecting them with TSVs or hybrid bonding. Shorter connections improve speed and power, but heat removal becomes a challenge.

再配線層(RDL).desc: A wiring layer formed on a chip or wafer surface to route pads out to the positions of the external terminals. It is used in fan-out packages and interposers.

マイクロバンプ.desc: A bump far smaller than an ordinary solder ball, used to connect TSV-stacked chips or chips to an interposer. The pitch is a few tens of micrometers.

UCIe.desc: Short for Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express: an industry-standard die-to-die interface intended to let chiplets from different companies connect to each other.

CoWoS.desc: TSMC's 2.5D packaging technology, which places logic chips and HBM side by side on a silicon interposer. It is widely used for AI GPUs and similar products.

FD-SOI(完全空乏型SOI).desc: Building transistors in a very thin silicon layer on buried oxide so the channel is fully depleted. The channel can be lightly doped, and body bias can tune the threshold voltage easily.

EOT(等価酸化膜厚).desc: The thickness of SiO2 that would give the same gate capacitance as a gate insulator such as a high-k film. A physically thick film can have a small EOT, giving high capacitance while limiting tunneling current.

ランダムドーパントゆらぎ(RDF).desc: Threshold-voltage variation in small transistors caused by statistical variation in the number and position of dopant atoms in the channel. FinFETs and FD-SOI, which allow lightly doped channels, reduce it.

SADP(自己整合ダブルパターニング).desc: Forming spacers on the sidewalls of a core pattern, removing the core and using the spacers as the mask to make a pitch half of what lithography alone allows. Doing it twice is SAQP.

ゲートラスト(リプレースメントメタルゲート).desc: Building the transistor first with a dummy gate, then removing it after high-temperature steps such as source/drain activation and replacing it with a high-k dielectric and metal gate.

DTCO(設計・技術協調最適化).desc: Optimizing cell area and performance by considering circuit design and process technology together, as scaling becomes harder.

ピエゾ抵抗効果.desc: The change in a material's electrical resistivity under mechanical stress. It is especially large in silicon and is used in semiconductor pressure sensors and similar devices.

ホール素子.desc: A sensor that detects magnetic fields using the Hall effect: a magnetic field applied to a current-carrying semiconductor produces a voltage perpendicular to both. It is used, for example, to sense motor rotation.

コリオリ力.desc: An apparent force acting perpendicular to the motion of an object moving in a rotating frame. Vibratory MEMS gyroscopes detect angular rate from the displacement it causes.

ボッシュプロセス(Deep RIE).desc: A dry-etching technique that alternates short etch and sidewall-passivation steps to cut deep, vertical holes and trenches in silicon. It is used for MEMS and TSVs.

スティクション.desc: The sticking of tiny moving MEMS parts to the substrate through surface tension or surface adhesion, so they no longer move. It often happens during drying after sacrificial-layer removal.

陽極接合.desc: Joining silicon to sodium-containing glass by heating them together while applying a voltage. It is used, for example, to seal MEMS devices.

シラン(SiH4).desc: A gas compound of silicon and hydrogen used as the source for CVD of polysilicon, silicon oxide and silicon nitride. It ignites spontaneously in air, so it is handled under strict control.

about.p: Silane (SiH4, monosilane) decomposes on heating to deposit silicon: SiH4 → Si + 2H2. In LPCVD at about 600–650 °C it forms polysilicon for gates, resistors and MEMS layers; below about 580 °C the film is amorphous, and annealing that amorphous film near 600 °C grows larger grains than direct poly deposition. For epitaxy, silane works at roughly 600–900 °C, lower than dichlorosilane or trichlorosilane. Disilane (Si2H6) and trisilane decompose even more readily for low-temperature growth, and silane mixed with germane (GeH4) grows SiGe.

Silane also supplies silicon for dielectrics. In plasma-enhanced CVD (PECVD) at about 300–400 °C, silane with nitrous oxide (N2O) deposits silicon oxide or tunable-index oxynitride (SiON), and silane with ammonia deposits silicon nitride containing about 10–30% hydrogen, used as final passivation and as a copper cap. Higher-quality LPCVD nitride uses dichlorosilane and ammonia at 700–800 °C instead. Silane is also used to nucleate tungsten CVD before WF6 is reduced with hydrogen, and with a hydrocarbon such as propane for SiC epitaxy.

Silane is pyrophoric: it can ignite spontaneously on contact with air, burning to a white silica powder. The worse hazard is that a high-concentration leak may not ignite at once, allowing a gas cloud to accumulate and then ignite explosively. Its lower explosive limit is about 1.4% in air. Fabs therefore store cylinders in exhausted gas cabinets, deliver it through lines with leak detectors, flow-limiting devices and automatic emergency shutoff valves, and purge lines with inert gas before any maintenance.

Chlorinated sources such as dichlorosilane and trichlorosilane need higher temperatures, but the HCl they release suppresses nucleation on oxide, favoring selective epitaxy, and trichlorosilane at about 1100–1150 °C grows thick layers at several µm per minute. Silane deposits at lower temperatures without chlorine, but grows less selectively and can form particles by gas-phase reaction. For oxide, liquid TEOS is a safer alternative that gives more conformal step coverage than silane-based oxide.

faq.q: Why is silane dangerous?
faq.a: Silane is pyrophoric and can ignite spontaneously in air. A large leak may also build up before igniting, causing an explosion, so it is handled in exhausted cabinets with leak detection and automatic shutoff.

faq.q: At what temperature does silane deposit polysilicon?
faq.a: LPCVD polysilicon is typically deposited from silane at about 600–650 °C. Below roughly 580 °C the film comes out amorphous instead of polycrystalline.

faq.q: What is the difference between silane and disilane?
faq.a: Disilane (Si2H6) contains a Si–Si bond that breaks more easily than the bonds in monosilane (SiH4), so it decomposes and deposits silicon at lower temperatures, which helps keep dopant profiles sharp in low-temperature epitaxy.

ホスフィン(PH3).desc: A gas compound of phosphorus and hydrogen used to introduce n-type dopant (phosphorus) into silicon. It is extremely toxic.

about.p: Phosphine (PH3) supplies phosphorus, the most common n-type dopant for silicon. In ion implantation it is cracked and ionized in the ion source, and the mass analyzer selects P⁺ ions. In CVD and epitaxy it is flowed alongside the silicon source for in-situ doping, producing conductive polysilicon for electrodes or phosphorus-doped silicon (Si:P) source/drain regions with concentrations on the order of 10²¹ cm⁻³. It is also used to deposit phosphosilicate glass, and in compound semiconductor growth it is the phosphorus source for materials such as indium phosphide.

Only tiny amounts of dopant are needed, so pure phosphine would require flows too small for a mass flow controller to meter accurately. Diluting it to a few percent or to ppm levels in hydrogen or nitrogen lets the required dose be delivered at controllable flows. Dilution also lowers the concentration released in a leak, reducing both toxic and fire risk. For implanters, phosphine is often stored adsorbed on a porous solid in sub-atmospheric containers, which tend to draw air in rather than leak gas out if a valve or fitting fails.

Phosphine is extremely toxic, with occupational exposure limits around 0.05 ppm, and it is also flammable. Fabs therefore keep cylinders in exhausted gas cabinets, run it through double-contained lines, and install continuous leak detectors tied to emergency shutoff valves. Exhaust from process tools passes through abatement systems that burn, scrub or adsorb unreacted hydride before release. Sub-atmospheric adsorbent sources reduce the chance of a large release, but they do not change the toxicity of the gas, so detection and exhaust are still required.

Arsine (AsH3) is the other hydride n-type source; arsenic is heavier and diffuses more slowly than phosphorus, which suits shallow junctions. Phosphorus oxychloride (POCl3) is a liquid source used in furnace diffusion, where it forms phosphorus-rich glass on the wafer surface and is still common for crystalline silicon solar cell emitters. For the p-type dopant boron, diborane (B2H6) is the usual in-situ doping gas and boron trifluoride (BF3) the usual implant source gas.

faq.q: Why is phosphine so dangerous?
faq.a: It is highly toxic at very low concentrations, with exposure limits around 0.05 ppm, and it is flammable. A leak can harm people before it is noticed, so it is handled only with gas cabinets, leak detectors, automatic shutoff and exhaust abatement.

faq.q: Is phosphine an n-type or p-type dopant source?
faq.a: It is an n-type source: phosphorus has five valence electrons, one more than silicon, so each substitutional phosphorus atom donates an electron. The common p-type counterparts are diborane and boron trifluoride.

faq.q: What is the difference between phosphine and POCl3 doping?
faq.a: Phosphine is a gas used in ion implanters and for in-situ doping during CVD or epitaxy. POCl3 is a liquid source used in diffusion furnaces, where it forms a phosphorus glass on the wafer from which phosphorus diffuses into the silicon.

アルシン(AsH3).desc: A gas compound of arsenic and hydrogen used to introduce n-type dopant (arsenic) and to grow compound semiconductors such as GaAs. It is extremely toxic.

マスフローコントローラ(MFC).desc: A device in deposition and etch tools that precisely measures the mass flow of a gas and holds it at a set value.

SEM(走査電子顕微鏡).desc: A microscope that scans a finely focused electron beam over a sample and detects secondary electrons and other signals to image the surface. It resolves features of a few nanometers, far beyond optical microscopes.

AFM(原子間力顕微鏡).desc: A microscope that traces a sharp tip over a sample and measures fine surface topography from the forces between tip and surface. It is used, for example, to evaluate surface roughness.

EDX(エネルギー分散型X線分光).desc: An analysis method that measures the energies of characteristic X-rays emitted under an electron beam to identify which elements are present and how much. It is used with SEM or TEM.

XPS(X線光電子分光法).desc: An analysis method that determines the elements in the top few nanometers of a surface and their chemical bonding states from the energies of photoelectrons emitted under X-ray irradiation.

TXRF(全反射蛍光X線分析).desc: An analysis method that shines X-rays at a grazing angle so they totally reflect, then sensitively measures the fluorescent X-rays from trace metal contamination on the wafer surface.

FIB(集束イオンビーム).desc: An instrument that mills or deposits material with a finely focused ion beam. It is used for cross-sectioning tiny areas, preparing thin TEM samples and editing circuits.

XRD(X線回折).desc: An analysis method that shines X-rays on a crystal and uses the angles and intensities of the diffracted beams to determine crystal structure, lattice constant, film strain and crystal quality.

欠陥検査装置.desc: Equipment that finds particles and pattern defects on wafers, for example by detecting scattered light or by comparing images of neighboring dies.

時間的局所性.desc: The tendency to access the same data or instructions again soon after a first access, as with variables reused inside a loop. One of the reasons caches work.

空間的局所性.desc: The tendency to access addresses near one just accessed, as when reading an array in order. It is why caches fetch data a whole cache line at a time.

ダイレクトマップ方式.desc: A cache organization in which each address can be placed in exactly one location. It is simple with short hit time, but prone to conflict misses when addresses compete for the same slot.

セットアソシアティブ方式.desc: A cache organization in which data can go in any of several locations (ways) within the one set selected by the address. An n-way cache compares n tags in parallel on each access.

フルアソシアティブ方式.desc: A cache organization in which any data can be placed in any location. It has no conflict misses but must compare against every tag, so it suits small structures such as TLBs rather than large caches.

キャッシュライン.desc: The unit in which data moves between a cache and the level below, also called a cache block. Many CPUs use 64 bytes, and the low address bits give the position (offset) within the line.

ライトスルー方式.desc: A write policy that writes to the level below (such as main memory) at the same time as the cache. The lower level stays up to date, but write traffic is heavy, so it is paired with a write buffer.

ライトアロケート.desc: A policy that, on a write miss, first brings the line into the cache and then writes it. Usually paired with write-back; writing directly to the lower level without fetching is called no-write-allocate.

初期参照ミス.desc: A cache miss that inevitably occurs on the first access to data. A larger cache does not reduce it, but larger lines or prefetching can.

容量ミス.desc: A cache miss caused by the working set being larger than the cache. It occurs even in a fully associative cache and is reduced by a larger cache or by improving data reuse.

競合ミス.desc: A cache miss caused when several blocks compete for the same set and evict each other even though capacity remains. Higher associativity or shifting data placement reduces it.

LRU(Least Recently Used).desc: A cache replacement policy that evicts the least recently used data. It exploits temporal locality well, but exact tracking is costly with many ways, so approximations are used.

プリフェッチ.desc: Loading data into the cache before it is requested because it is likely to be needed soon. Hardware prefetchers detect access patterns, and software prefetching uses explicit instructions.

平均メモリアクセス時間(AMAT).desc: The average time per memory access, computed as hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. A basic metric for comparing cache designs.

ミスペナルティ.desc: The extra time needed to fetch data from the next level when a cache miss occurs, determined by the lower level's access time and the line transfer time.

ループブロッキング.desc: An optimization that processes large arrays in small blocks that fit in the cache so loaded data is reused many times before eviction. Very effective for matrix multiplication.

ノンブロッキングキャッシュ.desc: A cache that keeps servicing other accesses while a miss is outstanding. It can handle multiple misses at once, overlapping and hiding memory latency.

特権モード.desc: A CPU operating mode reserved for the OS kernel, in which dangerous operations such as setting page tables and controlling I/O are allowed. It is distinguished from user mode, where applications run.

システムコール.desc: The mechanism by which applications ask the OS for services such as file I/O or memory allocation. A dedicated instruction raises an exception that switches to privileged mode and invokes the kernel.

割り込みハンドラ.desc: The routine a CPU runs when an interrupt or exception occurs. It saves the interrupted state, handles the cause and returns. Handlers should be kept as short as possible.

割り込みベクタテーブル.desc: A table listing, for each type of interrupt or exception, the start address of its handler. The CPU indexes it by the cause number to find where to begin handling.

ページテーブル.desc: A table recording the mapping from virtual page numbers to physical page numbers. The OS builds one per process, and the CPU's MMU walks it to translate addresses. Each entry also holds protection bits.

ページフォルト.desc: An exception raised when an accessed page is not mapped to physical memory or the access type is not permitted. The OS either supplies the page and retries the instruction or treats it as an illegal access.

デマンドページング.desc: Loading a program's pages into physical memory only when first accessed and a page fault occurs, rather than all at once. It speeds startup and saves memory for unused parts.

コピーオンライト.desc: Sharing duplicated memory with the original at first and copying a page only when either side tries to write it. It speeds process creation and saves memory.

スラッシング.desc: A state in which physical memory is so short that pages are constantly evicted and reloaded, and little useful work gets done. It is relieved by running fewer processes or adding memory.

コンテキストスイッチ.desc: Switching the process or thread running on a CPU. Registers, the program counter and other state are saved and restored, and switching processes also switches address spaces.

ASID(アドレス空間識別子).desc: A number tagged onto each TLB entry indicating which process's address space the translation belongs to. The TLB need not be flushed on a process switch, reducing TLB misses afterward.

TLBシュートダウン.desc: On a multiprocessor, the procedure for making other cores discard stale translations from their TLBs after a page table is modified. It uses inter-processor interrupts or instructions that broadcast the invalidation to all cores, and is costly.

メモリマップドI/O.desc: Assigning peripheral registers to specific addresses in the same address space as memory and accessing them with ordinary load and store instructions. That region is configured as uncached.

デバイスドライバ.desc: An OS component that operates a specific peripheral. It handles the device's registers and interrupts and lets applications use the device through a common interface.

IOMMU.desc: A unit that translates and protects the addresses peripherals use for DMA. It keeps devices from writing to unauthorized memory and is also used when assigning devices to virtual machines.

ハイパーバイザ.desc: Software that runs multiple virtual machines on one computer, allocating CPU, memory and devices to each guest OS and isolating them from one another. Also called a virtual machine monitor.

入れ子ページング.desc: Hardware that walks two levels of page tables in succession, one managed by the guest OS and one by the hypervisor. It reduces hypervisor intervention and speeds up virtualization.

NMI(マスク不可能割り込み).desc: An interrupt that is always accepted regardless of interrupt masking. It is used to report uncorrectable memory errors, serious hardware faults and watchdog events.

字句解析.desc: The first compiler phase, which splits the characters of source code into tokens such as identifiers, numbers, operators and keywords. Whitespace and comments are removed here.

構文解析.desc: The compiler phase that checks whether the token sequence follows the language grammar and builds the program's structure as a tree. Grammar errors are detected here.

抽象構文木(AST).desc: A tree representing program structure with operations and statements as nodes. Meaningless details such as parentheses and separators are omitted, and operator precedence is expressed by the tree's shape.

中間表現.desc: A form of the program inside a compiler that depends on neither the source language nor the target CPU. Most optimizations operate on it, separating language-specific front ends from CPU-specific back ends.

SSA形式.desc: An IR form in which variables are renamed so each is assigned exactly once, with φ functions selecting values at join points. Clear definition-use relationships make optimization easier.

基本ブロック.desc: A sequence of instructions with no branch entering or leaving in the middle, always executed from start to end. Basic blocks are the nodes of a control-flow graph and units of local optimization.

制御フローグラフ.desc: A graph representing a program's execution flow, with basic blocks as nodes and branches between them as edges. It is used to detect loops and analyze data flow.

定数畳み込み.desc: An optimization that evaluates expressions whose values are known at compile time and replaces them with the resulting constant, such as turning 3 * 4 into 12. It removes run-time computation.

共通部分式の削除.desc: An optimization that computes a repeatedly evaluated expression once and reuses the result, after confirming its operands do not change in between.

インライン展開.desc: Replacing a function call with the body of the called function. It removes call overhead and enables further optimizations but enlarges the code.

ループ展開.desc: Replicating a loop body several times to reduce the number of iterations. It cuts branch and counter overhead and gives more freedom to reorder instructions, at the cost of larger code.

ベクトル化.desc: Transforming a loop that performs the same computation on each element so that SIMD instructions process several elements at once. It requires no data dependence between iterations.

強度低減.desc: Replacing expensive operations such as multiplication with cheaper ones such as addition or shifts, for example adding 4 each iteration instead of computing i * 4 every time.

レジスタ割り当て.desc: Assigning program variables and temporaries to the CPU's limited registers, ensuring values in use at the same time get different registers, often via coloring an interference graph.

スピル.desc: Saving some values to memory (the stack) during register allocation when more values are live than there are registers. The extra stores and reloads slow the code.

命令スケジューリング.desc: Reordering instructions without changing results so that latencies of operations and memory accesses are filled with independent instructions.

LLVM.desc: A compiler infrastructure built around a common intermediate representation (LLVM IR), combining language front ends, optimization passes and CPU back ends. It is used for many languages and CPUs.

JITコンパイル.desc: Compiling frequently executed parts of a program to machine code while it runs, enabling optimizations based on run-time information. Used in runtimes for Java, JavaScript and others.

固定小数点.desc: Representing fractions with ordinary integer bit patterns and an agreed binary-point position. Integer arithmetic circuits suffice, giving small, low-power hardware, but the range is narrow. Formats are often named by fraction bits, as in Q15.

IEEE 754.desc: The international standard defining floating-point formats and arithmetic, including single (32-bit) and double (64-bit) precision, rounding, and special values such as infinity and NaN, so results agree across computers.

仮数.desc: The bits of a floating-point number holding its significant digits. For normalized numbers the leading 1 is implied, so single precision stores 23 bits but has 24 bits of precision.

指数部.desc: The bits of a floating-point number giving the power of two. To represent negative exponents, the true exponent plus a bias (127 for single precision) is stored.

非正規化数.desc: A floating-point number whose exponent field is all zeros, without an implied leading 1, representing values smaller than the smallest normal number. It fills the gap to zero gradually (gradual underflow), so x − y = 0 implies x = y.

NaN.desc: Short for Not a Number, a floating-point special value produced by operations with no numeric result, such as 0 ÷ 0 or the square root of a negative number. It has an all-ones exponent and a nonzero significand, and compares unequal even to itself.

最近接偶数丸め.desc: Rounding to the nearest representable value and, on an exact tie, to the one whose last bit is even (0). It is the IEEE 754 default and keeps rounding errors from accumulating in one direction.

桁落ち.desc: Loss of significant digits when subtracting two nearly equal numbers, as their leading digits cancel and the relative weight of existing rounding error grows. It is avoided by rearranging formulas.

情報落ち.desc: Loss of the smaller operand's low-order digits when adding numbers of very different magnitude, because they do not fit in the significand. It matters when summing many small values.

マシンイプシロン.desc: The difference between 1 and the next larger representable floating-point number, a measure of relative precision: 2⁻²³ (about 1.19 × 10⁻⁷) in single precision and 2⁻⁵² (about 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶) in double.

FMA(融合積和演算).desc: An operation computing a × b + c in one instruction, rounding only once at the end without rounding the intermediate product. It is faster and more accurate than separate multiply and add and is heavily used in matrix computation.

bfloat16.desc: A 16-bit floating-point format with 1 sign, 8 exponent and 7 significand bits. Sharing FP32's exponent width gives it a wide range, so despite low precision it is used for AI training. FP16, with 5 exponent and 10 significand bits, is more precise but has a narrow range.

FP8.desc: 8-bit floating-point formats: E4M3 (4 exponent, 3 significand bits) and E5M2 (5 exponent, 2 significand bits), chosen to trade precision against range. Used to make AI training and inference faster and more power-efficient.

INT8.desc: An 8-bit signed integer (−128 to 127). In AI inference, quantizing weights and activations to INT8 with a scale factor greatly cuts computation and memory and allows fast processing on small integer circuits.

桁上げ先見加算器.desc: An adder that computes carries in parallel from each bit's generate signal g = a·b and propagate signal p = a ⊕ b, without waiting for carries to ripple. Delay stays small even for wide operands.

about.p: For each bit with inputs a and b, the generate signal g = a·b is 1 when the bit produces a carry regardless of the carry coming in, and the propagate signal p = a ⊕ b is 1 when an incoming carry will pass through. The carry out is c(i+1) = g(i) + p(i)·c(i), and the sum is s(i) = p(i) ⊕ c(i). Expanding the recurrence gives c1 = g0 + p0·c0 and c2 = g1 + p1·g0 + p1·p0·c0, so every carry can be written in two-level logic using only the g and p signals and the input carry c0.

In a ripple-carry adder, each full adder must wait for the carry from the bit below. In the worst case, such as adding 1 to a word of all ones, the carry travels through every bit, so delay grows linearly with width; a 64-bit ripple-carry adder is far too slow for a processor clocked at gigahertz rates. A carry-lookahead adder (CLA) computes the carries directly from the inputs in parallel, and with hierarchical lookahead its delay grows only with the logarithm of the width.

Fully expanded carry equations quickly need gates with too many inputs, so practical designs use blocks of about 4 bits. Each block produces a group generate, G = g3 + p3·g2 + p3·p2·g1 + p3·p2·p1·g0, and a group propagate, P = p3·p2·p1·p0. A second-level lookahead unit treats these exactly like single-bit g and p signals to compute the carries into each block, and a third level extends the scheme to 64 bits. Parallel prefix adders such as Kogge-Stone and Brent-Kung generalize the same idea, trading wiring and area for logic depth.

Fast adders sit in ALUs, address generators and floating-point units, and in the last stage of multipliers. A multiplier first reduces its many partial products with carry-save adders, which are independent full adders that turn three numbers into two with only one full-adder delay and no carry propagation. Only the final two numbers need a carry-propagating addition, which is done once by a carry-lookahead or prefix adder. Other compromises, such as carry-select and carry-skip adders, sit between ripple-carry and full lookahead in speed and area.

faq.q: Why is a carry-lookahead adder faster than a ripple-carry adder?
faq.a: A ripple-carry adder waits for the carry to pass through every bit in turn, so delay grows linearly with width. A carry-lookahead adder computes all carries in parallel from generate and propagate signals, so delay grows roughly with the logarithm of the width.

faq.q: Can the propagate signal use OR instead of XOR?
faq.a: Yes, for the carry chain: p = a + b gives the same carries because when both inputs are 1 the generate term already produces the carry. The sum bit still needs a ⊕ b, so many designs compute XOR for p and use it for both.

faq.q: What is group generate and group propagate?
faq.a: They summarize a block of bits: group generate is 1 if the block produces a carry out by itself, and group propagate is 1 if a carry entering the block will pass all the way through. Higher lookahead levels use them to compute block carries quickly.

桁上げ保存加算器.desc: An adder that reduces three numbers to two, a sum and a carry, without propagating carries. Made of independent full adders per bit, its delay is constant, so multipliers use it to add many partial products.

ウォレスツリー.desc: A multiplier structure that reduces many partial products in parallel with a tree of carry-save adders. Its depth grows only logarithmically with width, so it is used in fast multipliers; a final adder sums the last two numbers.

ブースのアルゴリズム.desc: A multiplication method that recodes the multiplier's bits, for example in pairs, into signed digits to reduce the number of partial products. Radix-4 Booth encoding roughly halves them.

飽和演算.desc: Arithmetic that clamps results exceeding the representable range to the maximum or minimum instead of wrapping around. Used in audio and image signal processing to avoid large errors.

算術シフト.desc: A right shift of a signed integer that copies the sign bit into the vacated high bits. Shifting a negative number right by one divides by 2, rounding toward negative infinity. Filling with zeros is a logical shift.

ロード・ストア・アーキテクチャ.desc: An ISA style in which only load and store instructions access memory and arithmetic works only on registers. Used by RISC-V and Arm, it gives instructions a uniform shape that is easy to pipeline.

アドレッシングモード.desc: The way an instruction specifies the address of data or a jump target. Examples include immediate, register, base register plus offset and PC-relative.

PC相対アドレッシング.desc: Specifying a branch target or data address as a distance from the current instruction's address (PC). The distance is unchanged wherever the program is loaded, so it underpins position-independent code.
