即値.desc: A constant embedded directly in an instruction. In RISC-V addi it is a 12-bit signed integer that is sign-extended before use.

符号拡張.desc: Widening a signed integer to more bits by copying its top (sign) bit into all the new upper bits, which preserves its value. Filling the upper bits with zeros is zero extension.

疑似命令.desc: Something written like an instruction in assembly that the assembler replaces with one or more real instructions, such as RISC-V nop, mv, li, j and ret.

アセンブラ.desc: Software that converts a program written in assembly language into machine instruction bit patterns. It turns labels into addresses and expands pseudo-instructions into real instructions.

呼び出し規約.desc: The agreement on how arguments and return values are passed in registers or on the stack, and who saves which registers, when calling a function. It is a key part of the ABI.

スタックフレーム.desc: The area reserved on the stack each time a function is called. It holds the return address, saved registers and local variables and is freed when the function returns.

スタックポインタ.desc: The register that points to the current top of the stack; sp (x2) in RISC-V. In many ISAs the stack grows toward lower addresses.

フレームポインタ.desc: A register that keeps pointing at the stack position on function entry; s0 (fp) in RISC-V. Locals can be addressed at fixed offsets, and the call chain is easy to walk.

呼び出し先保存レジスタ.desc: A register guaranteed to keep its value across a call; if the called function uses it, the function saves and restores it. In RISC-V these are s0-s11.

呼び出し元保存レジスタ.desc: A register the called function may overwrite freely; if the caller needs its value after the call, the caller saves it. In RISC-V these include t0-t6 and a0-a7.

リターンアドレス.desc: The address to go back to when a function finishes. In RISC-V, jal puts the next instruction's address in ra (x1); in x86, call pushes it on the stack.

葉関数.desc: A function that calls no other functions. Its return address is never overwritten, so it need not be saved, and it often needs no stack frame at all.

ABI(アプリケーションバイナリインターフェース).desc: The machine-level agreement that lets compiled programs and libraries work together, covering the calling convention, data type sizes and alignment, how system calls are made and more.

マイクロオペレーション.desc: A simple internal operation into which a CPU decodes an instruction, also written μop. x86 CPUs split complex instructions into μops and execute them with RISC-like fast techniques.

圧縮命令.desc: An instruction that encodes a common operation in fewer bits than usual. The RISC-V C extension adds 16-bit instructions and cuts code size by roughly 25-30%.

分岐遅延スロット.desc: An ISA rule that the instruction right after a branch always executes, taken or not. Found in older ISAs such as MIPS, it exposed a pipeline detail in the ISA and later became a burden.

条件コード.desc: Flags such as zero, negative, carry and overflow that record the outcome of a compare or arithmetic operation. Conditional branches in x86 and Arm test them; RISC-V has none.

オブジェクトファイル.desc: The file a compiler produces from one source file. It contains machine code, initial data, a symbol table and relocation entries, but addresses in other files are unresolved, so it cannot run until linked.

リンカ.desc: Software that combines object files and libraries, performs symbol resolution and relocation, and produces an executable or shared library.

ローダ.desc: The OS function that reads an executable into memory, maps its parts with the right permissions, sets up arguments on the stack and starts the program.

シンボル解決.desc: The linker step that matches each function or variable name referenced in a file with its definition. No definition gives an undefined-reference error; more than one gives a multiple-definition error.

再配置.desc: Rewriting placeholder addresses in instructions and data with correct values once final addresses are decided. The linker does it, and with dynamic linking part of it is done at run time by the dynamic linker.

シンボルテーブル.desc: The list of function and variable names, with their addresses and attributes, contained in object files and executables. Used for linking and debugging; strip can remove it.

ELF.desc: The file format used for object files, executables and shared libraries on Linux and other UNIX-like systems and in embedded devices.

BSSセクション.desc: The area for global and static variables with no initializer (or zero). Only its size is recorded in the file and it is zero-filled at load time, so it does not enlarge the executable.

ヒープ.desc: The area from which a running program obtains memory of any size with malloc and the like and returns it with free. Repeated allocation and release can cause fragmentation.

静的リンク.desc: Linking that copies the code of the libraries used into the executable. It runs without the libraries present, but the file is larger and library fixes require rebuilding.

動的リンク.desc: Linking that loads and binds shared libraries at run time. Libraries can be shared between processes and fixed by replacement, but a compatible library must be present on the system.

共有ライブラリ.desc: A library loaded at run time by dynamic linking: .so on Linux, .dll on Windows. Built as position-independent code, its code pages can be shared by many processes.

静的ライブラリ.desc: An archive bundling many object files (.a on Linux). During static linking, the linker extracts only the objects it needs into the executable.

位置独立コード.desc: Machine code that runs without modification at any load address, also called PIC. It uses PC-relative references and the GOT and is used for shared libraries and PIEs.

GOT(グローバルオフセットテーブル).desc: A table of the actual addresses of external variables and functions, filled in by the dynamic linker at run time. Position-independent code refers to them through it, so code pages need no patching.

PLT(プロシージャリンケージテーブル).desc: A table of small stubs used to call shared-library functions. With lazy binding, the dynamic linker resolves the address on the first call and writes it into the GOT.

動的リンカ.desc: Software that, when a dynamically linked program starts, finds and loads shared libraries, applies relocations and binds symbols before starting the program, such as ld.so on Linux.

ASLR.desc: A countermeasure that changes the addresses of the stack, heap, shared libraries and executable every run so attackers cannot easily predict them.

PIE(位置独立実行ファイル).desc: An executable whose main program is also built as position-independent code. It runs at any address, so ASLR can randomize the main program's code too.

エントリポイント.desc: The address where a program begins execution, recorded in the ELF header. In C it is usually start-up code such as _start, which initializes and then calls main.

名前修飾.desc: A C++ compiler's encoding of argument types and namespaces into a function's symbol name, so the linker can tell overloaded functions apart.

弱いシンボル.desc: A fallback definition replaced by any ordinary (strong) definition with the same name. Embedded code uses it for default interrupt handlers and similar.

リンカスクリプト.desc: A file telling the linker at which memory addresses to place each section. Embedded development uses it to lay out flash and RAM and to fix the interrupt vector address.

断片化.desc: The condition in which repeated allocation and release split free memory into small pieces, so a large contiguous block cannot be allocated even though the total is sufficient.

MESIプロトコル.desc: A coherence protocol that tracks each cache line in one of four states: Modified, Exclusive, Shared or Invalid. On a write it invalidates other cores' copies.

スヌーピング.desc: A coherence approach in which each cache watches other cores' reads and writes on a shared bus or similar and updates its own line states. It suits small core counts.

ディレクトリ方式.desc: A coherence approach that records in a table which cores hold each line and notifies only those cores. Used in systems with many cores.

偽共有.desc: A slowdown in which threads update different variables that happen to share a cache line, so the line bounces between cores.

データ競合.desc: A situation in which threads access the same variable concurrently without synchronization and at least one access is a write. Results vary between runs; in C and C++ it is undefined behavior.

アトミック命令.desc: An instruction that performs a memory read and write as one operation no other core can interrupt, such as CAS, fetch-and-add and LR/SC.

コンペア・アンド・スワップ.desc: An atomic instruction that writes a new value only if memory still holds an expected value. Wrapped in a retry loop, it enables lock-free updates.

LR/SC.desc: A pair of instructions, also called LL/SC: if another core writes the address after the load-reserved, the store-conditional fails, enabling atomic updates.

ABA問題.desc: The problem that when a value changes from A to B and back to A, a CAS comparing only values fails to notice and succeeds. Lock-free data structures must guard against it.

about.p: Compare-and-swap (CAS) writes a new value only if a location still holds an expected value, and it compares values, not history. Consider a lock-free stack whose head points to node A, with A's next pointer pointing to B. Thread 1 reads head = A and next = B, then is preempted. Thread 2 pops A, pops B, and pushes A back, or pushes a new node that happens to reuse A's address. Thread 1 resumes, its CAS(head, A, B) succeeds because head is still A, and head now points to B, a node that is no longer in the stack.

about.h: Why memory reuse makes it likely
about.p: The problem is most common in languages with manual memory management. When a node is freed, the allocator readily hands the same address to the next allocation, so a pointer value can return to A even though it refers to a different node. In garbage-collected languages a node cannot be reclaimed while a thread still holds a reference to it, which largely removes the address-reuse form of ABA, although the logical form can still occur if the same node is deliberately reinserted.

The classic fix pairs the pointer with a modification counter and compares both in one atomic operation, using a double-width CAS or spare pointer bits; every update increments the counter, so A with tag 5 differs from A with tag 7. Load-linked/store-conditional (LL/SC, called LR/SC in RISC-V) fails if the location was written at all since the load, even when the value is the same. Safe memory reclamation schemes, such as hazard pointers and epoch-based reclamation, prevent a node from being freed and reused while any thread may still access it.

A lock-free algorithm guarantees that some thread always makes progress even if others stall, because a CAS fails only when another thread's update succeeded. That progress guarantee says nothing about correctness, and ABA is the classic way a seemingly correct CAS loop corrupts a data structure. It is hard to catch in testing because it needs a specific interleaving plus memory reuse, so lock-free code should be designed with an explicit ABA strategy from the start.

faq.q: What is the ABA problem in simple terms?
faq.a: A thread sees value A, another thread changes it to B and back to A, and the first thread's compare-and-swap succeeds as if nothing had happened. The value matches, but the state behind it has changed.

faq.q: How does LL/SC avoid the ABA problem?
faq.a: Store-conditional succeeds only if no write has occurred to the location since the matching load-linked, regardless of the value written. A change from A to B and back to A therefore still makes the store fail.

faq.q: Does a version counter fully solve ABA?
faq.a: In practice yes, as long as the counter is wide enough that it cannot wrap around to the same value while a thread is stalled. A very narrow counter can in principle wrap and reintroduce the problem.

スピンロック.desc: A lock that waits by repeatedly checking the lock variable in a loop. Fast for short waits, but it keeps using the CPU while waiting.

ミューテックス.desc: A lock that only one thread can hold at a time. Typically a thread that cannot get it sleeps and yields the CPU, and the OS wakes it when the lock is released.

デッドロック.desc: A state in which threads each hold a resource while waiting for one held by another, so none can proceed. Fixing a global lock order prevents it.

メモリ一貫性モデル.desc: The contract specifying in what order a core's reads and writes to multiple addresses may be observed by other cores. Examples include sequential consistency, x86 TSO and the weak models of Arm and RISC-V.

逐次一貫性.desc: The most intuitive memory consistency model: all cores' operations appear in one order in which each core's operations keep their program order.

TSO(トータルストアオーダー).desc: The x86 memory consistency model. It allows only a later read of a different address to overtake an earlier write, reflecting the presence of a store buffer.

ストアバッファ.desc: A small buffer in which a core holds writes temporarily. The core can move on without waiting for writes to complete, but other cores see the writes later.

メモリバリア.desc: An instruction guaranteeing that memory operations before it become visible to other cores before those after it, also called a fence, such as RISC-V fence.

アクワイア・リリース.desc: An ordering guarantee: operations after an acquire cannot move before it, and operations before a release cannot move after it. Used for lock acquire and release, it is lighter than a full barrier.

クリティカルセクション.desc: A part of a program that operates on shared data and must be run by only one thread at a time. It is protected by a lock and kept as short as possible.

ロックフリー.desc: A property of an algorithm that some thread can always make progress even if others stall partway. Built with atomic instructions such as CAS.

バリア同期.desc: Synchronization in which threads that arrive first wait until all threads reach the same point, keeping them in step phase by phase. Distinct from a memory barrier.

NUMA.desc: An organization in which each core has near and far memory, and far accesses take longer. Placing data and threads on the same side is faster.

セマフォ.desc: A synchronization mechanism holding a counter of remaining units: decrement before use (waiting at 0) and increment when done. Used to manage resources with a fixed number of units.

条件変数.desc: A synchronization mechanism that puts a thread to sleep until a condition holds and wakes it on a signal from another thread. The condition must be rechecked after waking.

読み書きロック.desc: A lock that admits any number of readers together but only one writer at a time, excluding everyone else while writing.

トランザクショナルメモリ.desc: A mechanism that runs critical sections speculatively, committing them as a whole if there is no conflict and rolling back and retrying if there is.

SerDes.desc: Serializer/deserializer: a circuit that turns parallel on-chip data into a fast serial bit stream for transmission and restores the parallel data at the receiver. It is the heart of high-speed serial physical layers.

差動信号.desc: Signaling that sends opposite signals on two wires and represents 0 and 1 by their voltage difference. Noise picked up equally on both cancels, allowing fast transmission with small swings.

クロック・データ・リカバリ.desc: A receiver circuit that extracts clock timing from transitions in the received data and decides each bit, removing the need for a dedicated clock wire.

8b/10b符号化.desc: Line coding that sends 8 data bits as a 10-bit code with balanced 0s and 1s and short runs. It eases clock recovery but limits efficiency to 80%.

128b/130b符号化.desc: Line coding that sends 128 data bits with a 2-bit header, about 98.5% efficient, relying on scrambling for transitions. Used from PCI Express 3.0 onward.

PCI Express.desc: A high-speed serial expansion interface connecting the CPU with GPUs, SSDs, network cards and more, also written PCIe. Lanes are bundled for bandwidth, and speed roughly doubles each generation.

PAM4.desc: Four-level pulse amplitude modulation, sending 2 bits per symbol. It doubles the bit rate at the same symbol rate but reduces noise margin.

NRZ.desc: Non-return-to-zero: the most basic signaling scheme, sending 1 bit per symbol with two voltage levels.

ルートコンプレックス.desc: The root of the PCI Express tree, connected to the CPU and memory, from which links fan out through switches to devices (endpoints).

MSI(メッセージシグナル割り込み).desc: A scheme in which a device signals an interrupt by writing to a designated address. It needs no dedicated interrupt wire and lets one device have many interrupts.

USB PD.desc: A specification in which source and sink negotiate voltage and current over USB, allowing up to 48 V and 240 W.

アイソクロナス転送.desc: A USB transfer type that reserves bandwidth and sends at fixed intervals without retrying on error. Used for audio and video.

ホットプラグ.desc: Connecting and disconnecting devices with power on while the OS automatically recognizes or detaches them. Used with USB, server SSDs and more.

AXI.desc: An on-chip bus from Arm's AMBA specifications that connects blocks in an SoC, with five independent channels and a VALID/READY handshake. Variants include AXI4-Lite and AXI4-Stream.

ネットワークオンチップ.desc: An on-chip interconnect of routers and links arranged as a network that carries data as packets, moving many transfers between blocks simultaneously.

CXL.desc: A standard on the PCI Express physical layer that enables coherent memory sharing between CPUs and accelerators or memory devices.

about.p: PCI Express (PCIe) moves data efficiently, but it does not keep device memory coherent with CPU caches, so software has to copy buffers and flush or invalidate caches to share data with an accelerator. Compute Express Link (CXL) reuses the PCIe physical layer, connectors and electrical signaling and adds protocols that keep caches coherent and let the CPU access device memory with ordinary loads and stores. CXL 1.x and 2.0 run at the PCIe 5.0 rate of 32 GT/s per lane, and CXL 3.x moves to the PCIe 6.0 rate of 64 GT/s.

CXL.io is essentially PCIe and handles device discovery, configuration, interrupts and DMA. CXL.cache lets a device cache CPU memory in its own cache while hardware keeps it coherent. CXL.mem lets the CPU read and write memory attached to the device as if it were part of system memory. Devices are commonly grouped into three types: Type 1 devices such as smart network cards use CXL.io and CXL.cache; Type 2 accelerators with their own memory use all three; Type 3 memory expanders use CXL.io and CXL.mem.

The DRAM a CPU can attach directly is limited by its number of memory channels and DIMM slots. A CXL memory expander adds capacity, and bandwidth, through PCIe-style links, and with CXL switches a pool of memory can be shared among several servers and assigned where it is needed. Access latency is higher than for directly attached DRAM, often compared with reaching memory on another CPU socket, so operating systems usually present CXL memory as a separate NUMA node and use it as a tier, keeping frequently accessed data in local DRAM.

DRAM and NAND flash differ by about 1000 times in access time, tens of nanoseconds versus tens of microseconds, and storage-class memory was proposed to fill that gap. After Intel announced in 2022 that it would discontinue its phase-change-based Optane products, much of this space has been taken by low-latency SLC NAND on the storage side and CXL-attached DRAM on the memory side. CXL also allows memory controllers on the device to use different memory types than the CPU supports natively.

faq.q: What does CXL stand for?
faq.a: CXL stands for Compute Express Link, an open interconnect standard built on the PCI Express physical layer that adds cache-coherent memory access between CPUs, accelerators and memory devices.

faq.q: What is the difference between CXL and PCIe?
faq.a: They share the same physical layer and slots, but plain PCIe transfers are not cache coherent. CXL adds the CXL.cache and CXL.mem protocols so devices and CPUs can share memory coherently with load/store semantics.

faq.q: What is a CXL Type 3 device?
faq.a: A Type 3 device is a memory expander that uses CXL.io and CXL.mem to give the host additional memory capacity, without caching host memory itself.

イコライザ.desc: A circuit that compensates for a channel attenuating high frequencies more, which smears the signal. Examples include receiver CTLE and DFE and transmitter de-emphasis.

アイパターン.desc: A plot overlaying many bit periods of a waveform. The height of the central eye shows noise margin and its width shows timing margin.

ビット誤り率.desc: The fraction of transmitted bits received incorrectly. High-speed serial links typically require values such as 10^-12 or lower.

特性インピーダンス.desc: The ratio of voltage to current seen by a wave traveling along a transmission line, set by trace width and layer spacing. Changes along the path cause reflections.

リタイマ.desc: A circuit that receives a high-speed serial signal, decides the bits and retransmits a clean signal. Inserted mid-channel to extend reach.

スペクトラム拡散クロック.desc: Slowly varying a clock's frequency slightly to spread electromagnetic emission energy across a wider band and lower its peaks.

クレジット方式のフロー制御.desc: A scheme in which the receiver advertises free buffer space as credits and the sender transmits only within them, so buffers never overflow.

GPIO.desc: General-purpose input/output: microcontroller pins that software can configure as inputs or outputs, used for reading switches, lighting LEDs and so on.

プルアップ抵抗.desc: A resistor connecting a signal line to the supply so it rests at logic 1 when nothing drives it. It keeps input pins from floating and is used on I2C lines and elsewhere.

チャタリング.desc: The rapid on-off flickering of a mechanical switch's contacts when pressed or released, removed by debouncing.

デバウンス.desc: Processing that removes switch bounce, by software that accepts a change only after repeated identical readings or by hardware filtering.

プリスケーラ.desc: A circuit that divides the clock fed to a timer or similar by a fixed ratio, bringing a fast clock into a range the timer can count.

PWM(パルス幅変調).desc: A method that adjusts average voltage or power by varying the high time of an output while keeping the period constant. Used to dim LEDs and control motor speed.

about.p: Pulse-width modulation (PWM) keeps the switching period T fixed and varies the high time t_on. The duty cycle D = t_on/T sets the average output, which is D times the pulse amplitude: a 5 V signal at 40% duty averages 2 V. The information is carried entirely in the timing, so the output stage only ever sits at two levels. A load that responds slowly compared with the period, such as a motor, a heater, the human eye looking at an LED, or an RC or LC filter, sees mainly this average value.

about.h: How a microcontroller timer generates PWM
about.p: A hardware timer counts clock pulses from zero up to a period value and then restarts. The output is set at the start of each period and cleared when the counter matches a compare register. With a period of 1000 counts and a compare value of 250, the output is high 25% of the time. Resolution is set by the number of counts per period, so for a fixed timer clock, higher PWM frequency means coarser duty steps. Once configured, the timer runs without CPU involvement. Analog PWM circuits do the same job by comparing a control voltage with a triangle or sawtooth wave.

The switching transistor is either fully on, with little voltage across it, or fully off, with almost no current, so it dissipates far less power than a transistor held at an intermediate voltage in a linear circuit. Losses come mainly from on-resistance and the brief transitions between states. The frequency is chosen for the load: high enough that LED flicker is not visible and motor current is smoothed by winding inductance, and often above the audible range to avoid motor whine, but not so high that switching losses dominate.

about.h: PWM as a DAC and in power electronics
about.p: Passing PWM through a low-pass filter gives a crude digital-to-analog converter without dedicated DAC hardware; placing the PWM frequency well above the filter cutoff reduces ripple, at the cost of slower response. The same principle runs switch-mode power supplies, where an ideal buck converter outputs D times its input voltage, and inverters, which switch power devices at several kHz to tens of kHz while varying pulse widths to synthesize AC. A three-phase motor inverter uses six switches, two per leg.

faq.q: How do you calculate PWM duty cycle?
faq.a: Divide the high time by the period: duty cycle = t_on / T. For example, 250 counts high out of a 1000-count period is 25%, and the average output is 25% of the pulse amplitude.

faq.q: Does PWM change the frequency or the voltage?
faq.a: Neither, in its basic form: frequency and pulse amplitude stay constant and only the pulse width changes. The average voltage or power delivered to the load changes because the fraction of on time changes.

faq.q: Why is PWM more efficient than a linear regulator for driving a motor?
faq.a: A linear regulator drops the excess voltage across a transistor that carries full current, wasting it as heat. With PWM the transistor is either fully on or fully off, so its voltage-current product, and thus its loss, stays small.

デューティ比.desc: The fraction of each period during which a periodic pulse signal is high. In PWM it sets the average power.

インプットキャプチャ.desc: A timer function in which hardware records the counter value at the instant an input signal changes, allowing precise measurement of pulse width or frequency.

UART.desc: A circuit for asynchronous serial communication without a clock wire, in which both sides agree on a baud rate and characters are framed by start and stop bits.

ボーレート.desc: The number of symbols sent per second in serial communication; for a UART it equals bits per second and must match on both sides.

SPI.desc: Serial Peripheral Interface: synchronous serial communication in which data is exchanged in both directions on a master-driven clock, with devices selected by chip-select lines. Used for fast parts.

I2C.desc: A synchronous serial bus connecting several devices on two wires, clock (SCL) and data (SDA), selecting the partner by address. The lines are open-drain with pull-ups.

ポーリング.desc: A method in which the CPU repeatedly checks a peripheral's status to detect changes. Simple, but it consumes time and power even when nothing happens.

スーパーループ.desc: A firmware structure without an OS in which an infinite loop in main calls each task in turn, with urgent work done in interrupts.

RTOS(リアルタイムOS).desc: An embedded OS that switches tasks by priority so the system responds within set time limits, such as FreeRTOS and Zephyr.

優先度逆転.desc: A situation in which a high-priority task waiting for a resource held by a low-priority task is held up because a medium-priority task preempts the low one.

優先度継承.desc: Temporarily raising a low-priority task holding a resource to the priority of the high-priority task waiting for it, preventing priority inversion.

ハードリアルタイム.desc: A strict timing requirement in which missing a deadline even once is a system failure, as in automotive brake or airbag control. Where occasional lateness is acceptable, it is soft real-time.

ウォッチドッグタイマ.desc: A timer that resets the microcontroller if software does not kick it within a set time, recovering from runaway or hung programs.

ブートローダ.desc: A small program that runs first at power-on, verifying and starting the main firmware or updating it with new firmware.

OTA更新.desc: Updating a device's firmware via wireless communication, often using two flash slots so the device can still boot if an update fails.

スリープモード.desc: A microcontroller state that stops clocks or power to the CPU and peripherals while idle to save power, waking on an interrupt or similar.

ブラウンアウト検出.desc: A function that resets the microcontroller when the supply voltage drops below the operating minimum, preventing unreliable behavior and corrupt flash writes.

JTAG.desc: A standard interface for chip testing and debugging that lets developers halt programs, inspect internal values and program flash. Arm also uses SWD, which needs fewer wires.

読み出し・変更・書き込み.desc: A sequence that reads a value, changes part of it and writes it back. If interrupted midway, other changes can be lost.

GPUカーネル.desc: A function that many threads execute simultaneously on a GPU. It is launched from the CPU-side program, and each thread uses its index to choose its data. Distinct from an OS kernel.

CUDA.desc: NVIDIA's platform for general-purpose computing on its GPUs. Kernels are written in an extended C++, with parallelism expressed as a grid, blocks and threads.

スレッドブロック.desc: A group of GPU threads that runs on a single SM. Threads in a block can share data through shared memory and synchronize.

SIMT.desc: An execution model in which programs are written per thread while hardware bundles threads into warps (32 on NVIDIA) that execute the same instruction in lockstep.

ワープダイバージェンス.desc: The splitting of threads within one warp onto different paths at a conditional branch. The paths execute one after another, lowering efficiency.

メモリコアレッシング.desc: Combining accesses into a few memory transactions when adjacent threads in a warp access adjacent addresses.

シェアードメモリ.desc: Small, fast memory inside each GPU SM that threads of the same block can share. The program decides what is stored there.

バンク競合.desc: In GPU shared memory, multiple threads of a warp accessing different addresses in the same bank at once, which serializes the accesses. Padding can avoid it.

占有率.desc: The ratio of warps actually resident on a GPU SM to the maximum it can hold, determined by register and shared-memory use.

ストリーミングマルチプロセッサ.desc: On NVIDIA GPUs, a unit bundling arithmetic units, registers, shared memory and warp-scheduling circuitry. A GPU is built from many SMs.

レイテンシ隠蔽.desc: Keeping waits, such as for memory, from showing up in performance by doing other work in the meantime. GPUs do it by switching among many warps.

ピン留めメモリ.desc: Memory locked so the OS will not move or evict its physical pages. The GPU can access it directly by DMA, speeding transfers and enabling asynchronous copies.

ユニファイドメモリ.desc: Memory accessible from CPU and GPU through the same pointer, with data migrating automatically on access. It simplifies programs, but migration costs need attention.

テンソルコア.desc: A GPU unit that computes the product and sum of small matrices in one instruction, mainly with low-precision numbers, greatly speeding up AI.

混合精度.desc: Using different numeric precisions for different parts of a computation, such as multiplying in FP16 and accumulating in FP32, to balance speed and accuracy.

並列リダクション.desc: Computing a sum or similar over many values in parallel with a tree that repeatedly combines neighbors, finishing n values in log2 n stages.

プレフィックスサム.desc: Computing the running totals of an array from the start, also called a scan. It can be computed in parallel and is used to find write positions when compacting output.

グリッドストライドループ.desc: Writing a kernel as a loop in which each thread processes elements spaced by the total thread count, decoupling launch size from element count.

定数メモリ.desc: A small GPU region for values that do not change during a kernel. When every thread in a warp reads the same address, one read is broadcast to all, which is fast.

OpenCL.desc: A standard parallel-programming framework for GPUs, CPUs, FPGAs and more from multiple vendors, defined by the Khronos Group industry consortium.

推論.desc: Running only the forward pass with weights fixed by training to produce answers from inputs. It needs less computation and memory than training.

逆伝播.desc: The training computation that propagates the error between output and target backward from output to input to obtain each weight's gradient.

演算強度.desc: Operations performed divided by bytes moved to and from memory. High values tend toward compute-bound, low values toward memory-bound.

Rooflineモデル.desc: A model expressing attainable performance as the smaller of peak compute and memory bandwidth × arithmetic intensity, used to tell compute-bound from memory-bound work.

バッチサイズ.desc: The number of inputs processed together. Larger batches reuse weights for efficiency but increase latency and memory.

KVキャッシュ.desc: Memory in LLM inference holding the attention keys and values of already processed tokens. It avoids recomputation but grows with context length and batch size.

プリフィル.desc: The first stage of LLM inference, processing all input prompt tokens together; it tends to be compute-bound. The following token-by-token generation is called decode.

アテンション.desc: The Transformer mechanism in which each token gathers information by computing its relationship to every other token. Its cost grows with the square of sequence length.

FlashAttention.desc: A fast attention implementation that tiles the computation in on-chip memory and never writes the large intermediate table to HBM. Its results match standard attention.

演算の融合.desc: An optimization that combines several operations into one kernel, avoiding writing intermediate results to memory and reading them back.

計算グラフ.desc: A representation of a model's computation with operations as nodes and tensor flows as edges, underpinning automatic differentiation and AI compiler optimization.

AIコンパイラ.desc: Software that analyzes a model's computational graph, optimizes fusion, data layout and tiling, and generates code for the target hardware, such as XLA and TVM.

ONNX.desc: Open Neural Network Exchange: a common model format for exchanging models between frameworks and inference runtimes.

推論ランタイム.desc: Software that loads a trained model and runs inference quickly through graph optimization, quantization and hardware-specific kernel selection.

学習後量子化.desc: Converting a trained model's weights and activations to lower precision after examining value ranges with representative data.

量子化を考慮した学習.desc: Training that simulates quantization rounding so weights adapt to its error, preserving accuracy even at low bit widths.

プルーニング.desc: Zeroing out low-impact weights in a neural network to reduce computation and memory. Structured pruning, which follows fixed patterns, is easier to accelerate in hardware.

構造化スパース.desc: Sparsity in which zero weights follow a fixed pattern; 2:4 sparsity, with two zeros in every four weights, lets matrix units compute about twice as fast.

知識蒸留.desc: Training a small student model to mimic a large teacher model's outputs so the small model achieves similar performance.

データ並列.desc: Distributed training in which each GPU holds a full model replica, processes its share of the data, and gradients are averaged across GPUs before updating.

テンソル並列.desc: Splitting one layer's weight matrix by rows or columns across GPUs, computing partial products and combining them through communication.

パイプライン並列.desc: Splitting a model's layers across GPUs in sequence, streaming micro-batches to reduce the time GPUs sit idle (the bubble).

オールリデュース.desc: Communication that sums values held by all GPUs element by element and gives the result to every GPU, used to average gradients in data-parallel training.

勾配チェックポイント.desc: Storing only some intermediate forward results and recomputing the rest during backpropagation, trading extra computation for less memory.

TOPS.desc: Trillions of operations per second, a performance figure for AI accelerators, usually a theoretical peak counted at low precision.

MFU.desc: The percentage of hardware peak performance achieved, computed from the operations a model actually requires.

投機的デコーディング.desc: Speeding up inference by having a small model draft several tokens ahead and a large model verify them together, accepting the correct ones at once.

ハードウェア記述言語.desc: A language for describing the structure and behavior of digital circuits, such as Verilog, SystemVerilog and VHDL, converted into circuits by logic synthesis.

Verilog.desc: A hardware description language widely used for digital design and verification, describing circuits as modules with behavior expressed through assign and always.

SystemVerilog.desc: An extension of Verilog adding design features such as the logic type and always_ff/always_comb, and verification features such as classes, constrained random and assertions.

ノンブロッキング代入.desc: Verilog's "<=" assignment, which evaluates every right-hand side at a time step before updating all left-hand sides together. It matches flip-flop behavior and is used for sequential logic.

ブロッキング代入.desc: Verilog's "=" assignment, which updates the left side immediately so the next statement sees the new value. Used in combinational always blocks and testbenches.

センシティビティリスト.desc: The list in @( ) after a Verilog always that names the signals triggering the block. Omissions in combinational logic make simulation and hardware disagree.

意図しないラッチ.desc: A latch created by synthesis when a description intended as combinational logic fails to assign an output under some condition, so the value must be held.

非同期リセット.desc: A reset that initializes flip-flops as soon as the reset signal is asserted, regardless of the clock. Release should be synchronized to the clock.

同期リセット.desc: A reset sampled at clock edges to initialize flip-flops. Timing is easier to analyze, but it does not act while the clock is stopped.

リセット同期化回路.desc: A circuit that applies an asynchronous reset immediately but aligns its release to the clock through two flip-flops before distributing it.

ミーリ型.desc: A state machine whose outputs depend on both the current state and the inputs. Input changes reach outputs within the same cycle, but so can input glitches. A Moore machine's outputs depend only on state.

ワンホット符号化.desc: State encoding that assigns one flip-flop per state with exactly one set at a time. Logic tends to be simple and fast, and it is common on FPGAs.

4値論理.desc: The four values used in HDL simulation: 0, 1, X (unknown) and Z (high impedance). Uninitialized or conflicting signals become X.

X楽観主義.desc: In HDL simulation, the tendency for conditions containing unknown X to resolve to definite values instead of propagating X, hiding bugs.

テストベンチ.desc: Simulation-only code that drives inputs to the design under test and checks its outputs. Since it is never synthesized, delays, display statements and similar can be used freely.

参照モデル.desc: A separate model, often in C, implementing the same function as the circuit. Its results for the same inputs serve as expected values for the design's outputs.

制約付きランダム検証.desc: Verification that generates random input values within constraints allowed by the specification, broadly exercising cases people might not think of.

回帰テスト.desc: Re-running existing tests after each design change to confirm that previously working features still work.

Lint.desc: A tool that checks HDL or other code against rules without simulation, flagging problem-prone constructs such as width mismatches and unintended latches.

ゲートレベルシミュレーション.desc: Simulation of the post-synthesis or post-layout netlist, optionally with delay information, to catch problems invisible at RTL.

generate文.desc: A Verilog construct that expands hardware descriptions by loops or conditions, used for example to instantiate a module repeatedly in a regular pattern.

組み合わせループ.desc: A structure in which combinational output feeds back to its own input without a flip-flop. It can oscillate or fail to settle and defeats timing analysis, so it is avoided.

VCD.desc: A standard file format recording signal value changes during simulation, viewed in waveform tools for debugging.

サイドチャネル攻撃.desc: An attack inferring secrets such as keys from physical information other than the intended output, such as processing time, power consumption or electromagnetic emissions.

タイミング攻撃.desc: A side-channel attack exploiting processing time that varies with secret values, prevented by constant-time implementation.

定数時間実装.desc: A way of writing cryptographic code so that branch directions, loop counts and memory addresses accessed do not depend on secret values.

投機的実行.desc: A CPU technique that executes instructions ahead based on predictions, such as branch outcomes, before they are known. Wrong results are discarded, but traces such as cache state may remain.

Spectre.desc: A class of vulnerabilities, disclosed in 2018, that induces mispredicted speculative execution to read secret data and infers its value from traces left in the cache.

Meltdown.desc: A vulnerability in some CPUs where kernel memory could be read speculatively before the permission exception took effect, with values inferred from cache traces. Mitigated by KPTI and other measures.

KPTI.desc: An OS countermeasure to Meltdown that removes most kernel memory from the page tables while user programs run.

電力解析攻撃.desc: A side-channel attack inferring secrets from a chip's power consumption traces. Differential power analysis (DPA), which processes many traces statistically, is especially powerful.

故障注入攻撃.desc: An attack that deliberately makes a chip malfunction with voltage or clock glitches, lasers and the like to bypass authentication or infer keys.

コールドブート攻撃.desc: An attack reading DRAM contents that persist briefly after power-off to extract keys and other secrets; cooling extends persistence. Prevented by memory encryption.

セキュアブート.desc: A mechanism that verifies the digital signature of the next software at each boot stage and starts only authentic software, forming a chain of trust.

ルートオブトラスト.desc: The component unconditionally trusted as the starting point of security checks, such as immutable ROM boot code and a public key inside the chip.

ロールバック防止.desc: A mechanism recording a minimum version number in unchangeable storage so software cannot be reverted to older vulnerable versions.

TPM.desc: A security chip or function that generates and stores keys, records measurements of booted software and attests to platform state.

測定ブート.desc: A mechanism that cumulatively records hashes of each boot stage's software in a TPM or similar so the boot state can be verified later.

リモートアテステーション.desc: A mechanism in which a device signs the state of its running software with an on-chip key and presents it to a remote server for trust verification.

TEE(信頼できる実行環境).desc: A hardware-protected execution environment isolated even from the normal OS, used for critical work such as key handling and authentication, for example Arm TrustZone.

TrustZone.desc: Arm's processor security architecture, switching between secure and normal worlds and using bus signals to distinguish and restrict access to memory and peripherals.

エンクレーブ.desc: A TEE approach in which part of an application runs in a region whose memory the CPU encrypts and protects, hidden even from the OS and hypervisor.

PUF(物理的複製困難関数).desc: A mechanism using per-chip manufacturing variation to produce values unique to each chip and hard to clone, allowing keys to be regenerated without storing them.

真性乱数生成器.desc: A circuit generating random numbers from unpredictable physical phenomena such as thermal noise or oscillator jitter, serving as the source for cryptographic keys.

ハードウェアトロイ.desc: Malicious circuitry inserted during design or manufacturing to leak information or disable operation. It activates only under rare conditions, making it hard to detect.

偽造チップ.desc: A used, defective or lower-grade chip relabeled and sold as genuine, leading to failures and safety problems.

耐タンパ性.desc: The ability to withstand physical attacks such as opening a chip or probing it, protecting internal secrets, for example by erasing keys on detection.

eFuse.desc: One-time-programmable storage written bit by bit by blowing thin wires with current, used for per-device keys, settings and anti-rollback counters.

動的消費電力.desc: Power consumed in CMOS circuits charging and discharging capacitance when signals switch, expressed as αCV²f with activity factor α, capacitance C, voltage V and frequency f.

活動率.desc: The fraction of a circuit's signals that switch per clock cycle, the α in the dynamic power formula αCV²f. It can be reduced by clock gating and similar.

静的消費電力.desc: Power consumed continuously by leakage currents through off transistors even when signals do not switch, also called leakage power. It rises steeply with temperature.

パワーゲーティング.desc: A low-power technique that switches off the supply to unused blocks, eliminating nearly all their leakage. State saving and wake-up time must be considered.

リテンションレジスタ.desc: A flip-flop that keeps its state in a small always-powered storage element while the block is power-gated, allowing operation to resume where it left off.

アイソレーションセル.desc: A cell placed at a boundary that passes a fixed value to running logic even when the outputs of a powered-off block are undefined.

レベルシフタ.desc: A circuit that converts signal voltages between blocks running at different supply voltages to suit the receiving side.

電源ドメイン.desc: A region of a chip sharing the same supply voltage and power on/off control, allowing voltage and power to be managed per block.

突入電流.desc: The large transient current that flows to charge capacitance the instant power is connected to an unpowered circuit, which can sag the supply voltage.

損益分岐時間.desc: The idle duration needed for the energy saved in a power-saving state to exceed the energy spent entering and leaving it.

C-state.desc: CPU idle states describing sleep depth. C0 is active; higher numbers use less power but take longer to wake.

P-state.desc: Performance levels of a running CPU defined by frequency and voltage combinations, switched by DVFS to match load.

レーストゥアイドル.desc: The strategy of finishing work quickly at high performance and entering deep sleep early, often advantageous when static power or other components' power is large.

ターボ動作.desc: Operation in which a CPU or similar automatically raises frequency above its rated value when power and thermal headroom allow.

サーマルスロットリング.desc: Control that lowers frequency and voltage when a chip gets too hot, reducing heat to protect it.

パワーキャップ.desc: Setting and enforcing an upper limit on server or CPU power, used in data centers to stay within power and cooling limits.

ACPI.desc: Advanced Configuration and Power Interface: the standard mechanism by which an OS manages device power states, power saving and thermals.

適応電圧スケーリング.desc: A technique that measures each chip's speed and temperature on chip and approaches the minimum voltage at which it works, trimming wasted margin.

エネルギー遅延積.desc: A metric multiplying energy per operation by its duration, used to evaluate the balance between energy efficiency and speed.

セルフリフレッシュ.desc: A low-power DRAM state in which the DRAM refreshes itself to retain contents without commands from the memory controller, used during system sleep.

PMIC.desc: An IC that generates multiple voltages from a battery or similar and manages power-up sequencing and voltage changes.

パワーシーケンス.desc: The specified order for applying and removing multiple supply voltages to a chip; violating it can cause malfunction or latch-up.

ニアスレッショルド動作.desc: Operating with supply voltage near the transistor threshold, greatly cutting energy per operation at the cost of speed and greater sensitivity to variation.

PUE.desc: Total data center power divided by IT equipment power; values closer to 1 indicate higher efficiency.

ティックレスカーネル.desc: An OS kernel that stops the periodic timer tick on idle CPUs so they can sleep until the next work.

CPI.desc: The average number of clock cycles per instruction, one factor in execution time = instruction count × CPI × cycle time, and the reciprocal of IPC.

速度向上率.desc: Execution time before an improvement divided by the time after; a value of 2 means twice as fast.

グスタフソンの法則.desc: The observation that when processors are added and the problem is enlarged, the parallel fraction grows, giving gains nearly proportional to processor count.

強いスケーリング.desc: Parallel performance evaluation that fixes problem size and measures how much time drops as processors are added.

弱いスケーリング.desc: Parallel performance evaluation that fixes problem size per processor while growing the total and checks whether time stays constant.

ベンチマーク.desc: A representative program run under fixed conditions to compare computer or program performance. Choosing ones close to actual use is important.

SPEC CPU.desc: A standard CPU benchmark suite of many programs based on real applications, reporting ratios against a reference machine combined by geometric mean.

幾何平均.desc: The nth root of the product of n values, used to average performance ratios because the comparison does not depend on the reference chosen.

調和平均.desc: The reciprocal of the mean of reciprocals, used to average rates over equal amounts of work.

マイクロベンチマーク.desc: A benchmark timing a tiny isolated operation; beware pitfalls such as the compiler optimizing the computation away.

壁時計時間.desc: The actual elapsed time from start to finish, including I/O waits and time when other programs ran.

CPU時間.desc: The total time the CPU spent executing a program's instructions, excluding waits; with parallel execution it can exceed wall-clock time.

スループット.desc: The amount of work, requests or data processed per unit time, a different metric from latency, which describes how fast one task completes.

about.p: Throughput counts how much work finishes per unit time; latency measures how long one piece of work takes from start to finish. The two often trade against each other. A five-stage CPU pipeline ideally completes one instruction per clock, raising throughput about fivefold, even though each instruction's latency grows slightly. Batching requests in a server or AI inference engine raises throughput but makes each request wait. CPUs spend circuitry on making one thread fast, while GPUs run thousands of simpler threads to maximize total throughput.

Peak memory throughput is transfer rate times bus width. DDR memory transfers on both clock edges, so DDR4-3200 runs a 1600 MHz clock at 3200 MT/s, and a 64-bit channel peaks at 25.6 GB/s. Multiple DRAM banks overlap activate and precharge operations to keep data flowing. Link encoding also matters: PCI Express 3.0 moved from 8b/10b (80% efficient) to 128b/130b (about 98.5%), nearly doubling effective throughput while the signaling rate rose only from 5 to 8 GT/s.

The roofline model shows which kind of throughput limits a program. Plotting performance against arithmetic intensity, in operations per byte moved from memory, gives a slanted ceiling set by memory bandwidth and a flat ceiling set by peak compute. With 1 TB/s of bandwidth and 100 TFLOPS of compute, any kernel below 100 FLOP per byte is memory-bound, so improving data reuse helps more than adding arithmetic units.

Manufacturing uses the same idea. Tool throughput is quoted in wafers per hour, and choices often trade it against other goals: batch cleaning of about 50 wafers per bath is fast but risks cross-contamination, higher EUV dose reduces stochastic defects but lowers scanner throughput, and thermocompression bonding is slower than mass reflow. At factory level, Little's law states WIP = throughput × cycle time, so a fab shipping 50,000 wafers a month with a three-month cycle time holds about 150,000 wafers in process.

faq.q: What is the difference between throughput and latency?
faq.a: Throughput is the amount of work completed per unit time, such as requests per second or GB/s. Latency is the time a single request takes to complete; a system can have high throughput and still high latency, for example when it batches work.

faq.q: How do you calculate memory bandwidth?
faq.a: Multiply the transfer rate by the bus width in bytes. For example, DDR4-3200 on a 64-bit (8-byte) channel gives 3200 MT/s × 8 B = 25.6 GB/s peak; sustained throughput is lower because of refresh, bank conflicts and turnarounds.

faq.q: What is Little's law?
faq.a: Little's law says average work in progress equals throughput multiplied by average time in the system. It applies to fabs, queues and processors alike, so cutting cycle time at constant throughput requires less WIP.

テールレイテンシ.desc: The slow end of the response-time distribution, such as the 99th percentile, which governs overall latency when a task waits on many components.

リトルの法則.desc: The relationship that the average number in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends there: L = λW.

プロファイラ.desc: A tool that measures which functions or parts of a program consume execution time, using sampling or instrumentation.

フレームグラフ.desc: A profiling visualization stacking call chains vertically, with each function's width showing its share of time.

性能カウンタ.desc: A hardware counter in the CPU that tallies events such as instructions executed, cache misses and branch mispredictions.

トップダウン分析.desc: A method using performance counters to divide CPU issue slots into frontend bound, backend bound, bad speculation and retiring, narrowing down bottlenecks.

STREAMベンチマーク.desc: A benchmark that copies and adds large arrays to measure the memory bandwidth actually achievable.

並列効率.desc: Parallel speedup divided by the number of processors, indicating how effectively the cores are used.

プローブ効果.desc: The phenomenon in which adding a measurement mechanism changes the behavior of the program being measured.
